# Spectral Micro

> Documentation for the Spectral Micro BLDC motor controller by Source Robotics.

Every page of this site is also available as Markdown at its address followed by `index.md`, with its links absolute; `llms-full.txt` holds every page in one file. The version box on the landing page names the release the pages describe.

Full text of every page, in the order of the site's navigation. Source: https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/

[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/) [About this manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/about/)

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document for the Spectral Micro BLDC driver. It is revised as the product and
its firmware change; the document number, firmware version, revision and date above identify the version you are
reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. Take care that the firmware version named
under *Applies to* matches what `#Info` reports on your driver: the version selector in the header switches
between firmware releases. The text and the images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

# Quick start

From the box to a calibrated motor that follows commands, in four parts. The quickest way through is
[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) in the browser; every step also shows the terminal commands.

!!! danger "Read first"
    Reversed supply polarity, a daisy-chain cable the wrong way round, or 5 V on the UART port destroys the driver.
    The motor turns during calibration. The [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/02-safety/) chapter is two minutes long.

## Before you start

You start from the box: a driver, a motor and the parts below. The wiring needs a multimeter and a soldering iron.

Nothing else is assumed: no experience with motor drivers, a terminal or a program.

## The four parts

| Part | What you do | What you end with |
|---|---|---|
| [1. Fit the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/1-motor/) | Fit the magnet, mount the board behind the motor, solder the three phases | A driver on its motor, wired |
| [2. Connect](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/2-connect/) | Connect the supply and the PC, open Motor GUI or a terminal | A driver that talks to your PC |
| [3. Calibrate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/3-calibrate/) | Restore the defaults, calibrate, set the current limit, save | A calibrated driver that keeps its settings |
| [4. First moves](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/4-first-moves/) | Turn the motor at a speed, move it to a position, stop it | A motor that follows commands |

Each step links the page that explains it. Follow the link when a step is not clear or something fails.

## What you need

| | Where to get it |
|---|---|
| **Spectral Micro driver** | [single driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-bldc-controller) or the [starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-bldc-starter-kit), which has everything below except the motor, the bracket and the supply |
| **A brushless motor** with a phase resistance of 2 to 24 Ω and 2.8 A or less: a gimbal motor, from the 2804 class to the 8108 class | the [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/tested-motors/) are safe choices |
| **The encoder magnet**, diametrically magnetised; the stock one is 6 × 2.5 mm, another thickness is fine if it gives the 1 mm gap | [magnet](https://source-robotics.com/products/6x2-5mm-diametrical-neodymium-magnet) |
| **A bracket** that holds the board behind the motor, and M3 screws | the [example bracket](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files) to adapt and print; a NEMA 17-format motor needs only a spacer |
| **USB-to-serial adapter**, 3.3 V, and its cable | [serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter), [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable) |
| **Power cable** | [power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable) |
| **A 12 to 29 V supply**, 24 V recommended | a bench supply with a current limit is the safest start |
| For CAN later: **CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter** and a **CAN cable** | [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter), [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable) |
| Optional: **100 kΩ NTC thermistor** for motor temperature protection | [thermistor](https://source-robotics.com/products/100k-ntc-thermistor) |
| **Software**: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, or a serial terminal | [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/); PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino serial monitor |

More: [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/01-overview/what-you-need/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/1-motor/ -->

# 1. Fit the motor

The driver goes behind the motor, over a magnet on the end of the motor shaft.

## 1. Fit the magnet

1. Press the magnet onto the end of the motor shaft, centred.
2. Glue it, so that it cannot turn on the shaft.

The magnet must end up about **1 mm** above the encoder chip in the middle of the board.

![About 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip in the middle of the board.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/mag_dist.webp){ width="560" }

A magnet that slips is the usual cause of a calibration that "succeeds" and a motor that then runs badly.

!!! success "Check"
    The magnet sits centred on the shaft, and once the glue has set it does not move when you push it with a
    finger. If it does: [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/).

More: [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/).

## 2. Mount the board

1. Bolt the bracket to the bottom of the motor.

    ![The example bracket. The motor bolts to one side, the board to the other; the hole in the middle is for the shaft and the magnet.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/brack.webp){ width="500" }

2. Bolt the board to the bracket, with the encoder chip (the bottom of the board) towards the magnet.
3. Check the gap between the magnet and the encoder chip: 1 mm, not touching.

A NEMA 17-format motor takes the board on a spacer with its own rear screws.

!!! success "Check"
    The board sits parallel to the motor, with about 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip, and the rotor
    turns by hand without the magnet touching the chip. If not: [Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/).

More: [Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/).

## 3. Wire the motor

Solder the motor's three wires to **U, V and W**. The order does not matter: calibration detects it.

![The connectors. The motor phases go to U, V, W; the supply to DC+ and DC−.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/con2.webp){ width="700" }

!!! success "Check"
    With the driver unpowered, a multimeter shows about the same resistance between U and V, V and W, and W
    and U, and no strand bridges two groups. If not: [Wiring the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/wiring/).

More: [Wiring the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/wiring/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/2-connect/ -->

# 2. Connect

The supply powers the motor, the serial adapter connects the PC.

## 1. Connect power and the PC

1. Connect the supply to a power connector: **DC+ to positive, DC− to negative**. Check twice.
2. Connect the serial adapter to the UART connector with the UART cable: TX to RX, RX to TX. 3.3 V only.

    ![The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/UART_connection.webp){ width="700" }
    ![The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/UART_connection_dark.webp){ width="700" }

3. Power on.

The LED blinks for about two seconds while the bootloader waits for a host. Then the firmware starts, and the LED
stays on steadily: the driver is not calibrated yet, which it reports as an error state.

![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" }

??? info "The serial adapter alone"
    The serial adapter alone powers the driver's logic: it answers over UART without the supply, but reports a
    Vbus error and will not calibrate or move.

More: [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/) ·
[Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/connectors/).

## 2. Open Motor GUI or a terminal

=== "Motor GUI"

    1. Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/) in Chrome or Edge.
    2. Choose the serial connection.
    3. Press **Connect**, and choose the adapter's port.

    ![Motor GUI connection bar with UART transport, baud rate and Connect](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/motor-gui/connection.jpg){ width="800" }

    The driver's identity and state appear: hardware and firmware version, serial number, *Not calibrated*, *No
    errors*.

    If nothing connects: the port, the cable's TX/RX, the browser (Web Serial needs a Chromium browser).

    More: [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/).

=== "Terminal"

    1. Open a terminal on the adapter's port: 256000 baud, line ending CR+LF.
    2. Type `#Info`.

    The driver prints its hardware and firmware version, its CAN ID, whether it is calibrated, and the motor's
    parameters.

    More: [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/terminal/).

!!! success "Check"
    The driver's identity and live state appear before you change settings. A missing connection is covered in
    [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/#opening-the-port) or [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/3-calibrate/ -->

# 3. Calibrate

The driver learns your motor. There is nothing to enter: calibration measures the motor's resistance and
inductance and finds its pole pairs and phase order by itself.

## 1. Restore the defaults

First the factory defaults, so that calibration does not start from another motor's values or from junk in the
EEPROM.

=== "Motor GUI"

    Press *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"

    ```
    #Default
    ```

??? info "What else #Default resets"
    It also sets the hardware version and batch date to factory values; from firmware 109 it keeps the CAN node ID.

## 2. Calibrate

!!! tip "We recommend a Motor GUI preset"
    In Motor GUI's **Presets** tab, apply *Generic motor*, *BLDC motor on Spectral Micro (soft)* before you
    calibrate. It writes a low current limit and soft loops and leaves the resistance, the inductance and the pole
    pairs to the calibration, which measures them, so the motor calibrates safely. Raise the limits and the gains
    from there ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/)). More: [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/).

1. Fix the motor to the bench, with nothing on the shaft.
2. Set the supply to 24 V.
3. Start the calibration:

    === "Motor GUI"

        Start the calibration. The GUI switches to *Calibration mode* and shows the driver's log step by step.

    === "Terminal"

        ```
        #Cal
        ```

4. Keep the shaft free until the end, about a minute more after the log below.

The LED flashes, the motor clicks, then turns in both directions, and the driver reports each step: the magnet,
the supply, the resistance and inductance, the pole pairs, the phase order, the motor constants, and finally

```
Calibration success!
Next, by itself: the encoder table, then anti-cogging (about a minute; keep the shaft free). Everything is saved when they finish (#Encal state, #Cogcal state)
Going to idle!
```

The driver then goes on to measure the encoder table and the anti-cogging, and saves everything when they succeed.

A failed step names itself:

- `Magnet test: Failed` is the magnet;
- `Resistance test: Failed` means a phase is not connected or the motor is outside the 2 to 24 Ω range;
- `Open loop: Failed` means the rotor did not follow the field: check the three wires and that the shaft is free;
- `Commutation/alignment check failed!` means the motor did not respond: check the three wires, the supply, and
  that the magnet does not slip.

!!! success "Check"
    The calibration log ends with `Calibration success!`. If it does not, use the failed step in
    [Calibration troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/#troubleshooting); do not treat a stopped motor as
    success.

More: [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/), with the whole log and every message.

## 3. Set the current limit and save

The current limit is the current the motor may draw, in mA; it is also the grip of the motor against a load.

From firmware 109 calibration puts back the limit that was in force (107 and older left 1600 mA), so check it now,
before you save. 1000 mA suits the gimbal motors in the tested list; a small 2804 is better at 500 mA, a motor
rated for more can go up to 2800 mA.

=== "Motor GUI"

    Set the current limit in the limits, then **Save** (the GUI warns about unsaved changes until you do).

=== "Terminal"

    ```
    #Ilim 1000
    #Save
    ```

Without saving, the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The LED now shows three short flashes and a
pause: normal operation.

![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" }

!!! success "Check"
    After **Save**, Motor GUI no longer marks unsaved changes, and after a power cycle `#Info` prints
    `Calibrated`. [Saving](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/) explains which settings are kept.

More: [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/) · [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/4-first-moves/ -->

# 4. First moves

The motor is calibrated and saved. Now it moves on command.

## 1. Move it

=== "Motor GUI"

    Use the jog controls:

    - *Jog velocity* turns the motor at a speed;
    - *Jog position* moves it to a position;
    - *Jog current* applies a torque;
    - *Send setpoint* sends a value in the current control mode.

    The plots show position, speed and current while it moves.

    ![Motor GUI simulated motor: device state, controls and live telemetry](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/motor-gui/motor-demo.jpg){ width="800" }

=== "Terminal"

    ```
    #V 16384        one revolution per second
    #V 0
    #P 0            back to where it started
    #P 16384        one revolution forward
    #Idle
    ```

Position is in encoder ticks, 16384 per revolution; speed in ticks per second; current in mA. If the motor hums
or whines, lower the current limit or tune the loops.

!!! success "Check"
    The position and speed feedback follow the request, and **Idle** stops driving the motor. A motor that
    does not follow needs [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/) before a load is attached.

More: [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/) · [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/).

## 2. Where to go next

| You want to | Read |
|---|---|
| get to know Motor GUI: the screen, the plots, recordings, several motors | [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/), [Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/motor-gui/) |
| control the driver from a program over CAN | [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/can/), then [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/python/) |
| put several drivers on one bus | give each a node ID and terminate the ends: [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/) |
| protect the motor from overheating | [Thermistor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/thermistor/) |
| update the firmware | [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/) |
| look up a message or a command | [API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/) |
| build something: a wheeled robot, a leg, a compliant arm | [Guides](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/) |
| understand why it does not work | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/), [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/) |

# About this manual

## Scope and audience

The Spectral Micro Manual covers the Spectral Micro BLDC driver from unpacking to a tuned motor on a CAN bus: what
the driver is, how to mount it on a motor and wire it, the first setup with Motor GUI or the serial terminal,
calibration and tuning, how the driver is controlled over UART and CAN or from Python, and how its firmware is
updated. The API reference lists every CAN message and UART command of the firmware release named on the landing
page. The Guides are worked examples.

It is written for someone who builds a robot or a machine with the Spectral Micro: a maker, a student or an
engineer who can solder three motor wires and open a serial terminal. It does not assume any knowledge of
field-oriented control; the Theory corner in the appendix explains the concepts the control modes rely on.

Read the Safety chapter before you power anything. The [Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/) is the whole first setup,
in four short parts; the chapters are in the order you need them and go deeper.

## Finding your way

The header has four tabs. **Spectral Micro Manual** is the document you read from the start: the quick start, then
safety, technical data, mounting, the first setup, operation and firmware updates, in numbered chapters. Motor
GUI, the tool in the browser, is the usual way to do what the chapters describe; each procedure shows it first
and the terminal command beside it. **API reference** lists every CAN message, every UART command and the Python
library's calls for the firmware release this site describes, with the defaults and the error flags, and is where
you look things up. **Guides** are worked examples with code. **Support** says where to get help and how to report
a problem.

The whole site describes one firmware release. The dropdown next to the site name switches between releases, and a
page from an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the
firmware repository; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.
## Warnings and notes

Three kinds of highlighted text appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the
step it belongs to.

!!! note "Note"
    Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

!!! warning "Notice"
    The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

!!! danger "Danger"
    Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.
## Related documents

| Document | Number | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| Spectral Micro Manual | SR-5002 | the Spectral Micro BLDC driver: quick start, safety, technical data, mounting, setup with Motor GUI or a terminal, operation, firmware; the API reference; guides |

A document marked with a firmware version describes that firmware release, here 110; the version selector in the header switches between releases. The compatibility table says which firmware, Python library and hardware revisions work together.

The STEPFOC stepper driver has similar hardware and firmware and is run the same way; its documentation is at
[docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/). The SSG-48 gripper, which
is driven by a Spectral Micro, is documented at
[docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/).

## Document history

The Spectral Micro Manual describes one firmware release; one revision is kept per release, and the version
selector in the header switches between them. The earlier version of this site, for firmware 101, is kept as
version `101`.

The text and the images of this documentation are licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), the code examples under the [MIT licence](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-docs/blob/main/LICENSE-CODE). The Source Robotics name, the product names and the logos are not covered by either.

| Revision | Date | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.C | 2026-11-13 | Firmware 110: the gripper (each end read under a light push, 0 and 255 clear of the stops, the soft start, a clean arrival and hold, an object after 50 ms, its own current limit), `#Estop` over UART, `#Close` during a calibration, brake or coast kept by Save, the watchdog while idle, parameters 90 to 93; the upgrade from 109 |
| 2026.B | 2026-11-10 | Firmware 109: the parameters and buffers (CAN 36 to 43), the identity and telemetry frames, the watchdog actions, the encoder table and the anti-cogging, the current loop from R, L and a bandwidth, the speed estimate, the commutation delay compensation, the EEPROM blocks, status and diagnostics, sound through the motor (CAN 44 and 45, `#Tone`), upgrading from older firmware; new pages Encoder table and anti-cogging, The watchdog, Status and diagnostics, Sound, Upgrading from older firmware, Parameters and buffers, Sound (CAN) |
| 2026.A | 2026-11-03 | First version in this form: the manual chapters, the generated CAN and UART reference, firmware 107 |

# Overview

What the Spectral Micro is and what it is made of, how it relates to the STEPFOC stepper driver that is built on
it, and what you need around it to get a motor turning.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The introduction video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/FRhTW86H9zU/hqdefault.jpg){ width="480" }
  <figcaption><a href="https://youtu.be/FRhTW86H9zU">The introduction video</a>: the driver, the motors it runs and what it does with them.</figcaption>
</figure>

## In this chapter

- [The driver at a glance](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/01-overview/driver-at-a-glance/)
- [Spectral Micro and STEPFOC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/01-overview/spectral-and-stepfoc/)

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/01-overview/driver-at-a-glance/ -->

# The driver at a glance

The Spectral Micro is a field-oriented controller for small three-phase brushless motors: gimbal motors and other
low-current motors with a phase resistance of a few ohms. It mounts behind the motor, reads the rotor position
from a magnet on the motor shaft, and drives the three phases with sinusoidal currents placed from that position,
the way a servo drive does.

The motor can be commanded in position, speed, current (torque) or impedance, holds a position at standstill, reports
where it is, and runs quietly and efficiently. It is made for robot joints, legs, arms and grippers.

![The Spectral Micro driver, 39 × 39 mm, with the encoder chip in the middle of the board.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/spectral-Photoroom.webp){ width="520" }

## What is on the board

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| STM32F103CB microcontroller | runs the control loops at 5 kHz and the CAN and UART interfaces |
| 14-bit magnetic encoder (MT6816) | reads the position of the magnet on the motor shaft: 16384 ticks per revolution |
| Three-phase driver stage with inline current sensing | drives the phases with up to 2.8 A and measures the phase currents |
| 16 Kbit EEPROM | keeps the configuration and the calibration over a power cycle |
| Two CAN connectors and two power connectors | daisy-chain several drivers on one bus and one supply |
| CAN termination switch | the 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node need |
| UART connector (3.3 V) | the serial terminal: every setting, calibration, tuning |
| Thermistor pads | an NTC in the motor windings for temperature protection |
| PIN header | a spare pin for your own use: an analog input or a digital input/output |
| HALL header | pads for hall sensors; not implemented in the firmware |
| JTAG pads (1.27 mm) | the programming adapter, for installing the bootloader or for development |
| Status LED | normal operation, calibration or error, see below |

The connectors and their pinout are in [Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/connectors/).

## What the firmware does

The firmware closes three nested loops on the motor: a current (torque) loop, a velocity loop around it and a
position loop around that, plus an impedance (PD) loop that makes the motor behave like a spring and damper.

A command picks the loop: a current setpoint, a speed, a position or a PD setpoint. An open-loop mode and a
voltage-torque mode exist beside them; [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/) describes each.

Calibration measures the motor: its phase resistance and inductance, its pole pairs and the order of its phases,
the angle between the encoder and the rotor field, and its torque and velocity constants. Nothing about the motor
has to be typed in; see [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/).

The driver protects itself and the motor: it stops on a supply voltage outside the limits, on an encoder fault, on
an over-speed, on a motor over-temperature (with the thermistor), on a hardware fault of the driver stage, on an
E-stop command and on a watchdog that runs out. The status LED and `#Error` tell which; see
[Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/).

## How it is controlled

- **UART**, a 3.3 V serial port at 256000 baud: human-readable commands such as `#P 16384`, and the only way to
  run the calibration. See [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/uart/).
- **CAN**, 1 Mbit/s, up to 14 drivers on one bus: compact frames for real-time control from a PC with the CANvas
  adapter, a microcontroller or a robot control box. See [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/can/).
- **Python**, the `Spectral-BLDC` library on top of CAN. See [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/python/).
- **Motor GUI**, in the browser, over serial or CAN: the usual tool for setup, testing and tuning. See [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/).

## The status LED

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| three short flashes and a pause | normal operation: no error, calibrated |
| fast flashing, about 10 times a second | the calibration routine is running |
| on, not flashing | error mode: at least one error is active, or the motor is not calibrated |

The LED can be turned off with `#LED 0`.

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Fast flashing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/01-overview/spectral-and-stepfoc/ -->

# Spectral Micro and STEPFOC

The Spectral Micro and the [STEPFOC stepper driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/) are sister
drivers: similar hardware and similar firmware, each made for its kind of motor. The Spectral Micro drives
three-phase brushless motors; STEPFOC drives two-phase stepper motors.

They are not the same board and do not run the same firmware, but they are controlled and run practically the same
way: the same CAN and UART commands, the same Python library, Motor GUI and bootloader.

What this means in practice:

- **The commands are practically the same.** The CAN messages and UART commands of the API reference exist on both drivers,
  with the same IDs, names and layouts; STEPFOC adds a few that only make sense on a stepper (homing against a
  sensor, open-loop stepping). A program written for one runs on the other. The idle behaviour is the exception
  over UART: the Spectral Micro sets it with `#Brake 0` or `#Brake 1` and coasts by default, STEPFOC has the
  actions `#Brake` and `#Coast`. Send_Settings over CAN is the same on both.
- **The firmware releases go in step, and from 109 share their numbers.** From release 109 the two drivers are
  released together under the same version number; the Spectral Micro went from 107 straight to 109, so there is
  no Spectral Micro 108. Before, the numbers did not always match (Spectral Micro 107 went with STEPFOC 108); the
  [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/compatibility/) lists the pairs. Some defaults differ, each measured on its
  own driver: the direct PLL speed estimate at 100 Hz and 234 µs delay compensation here, 60 Hz and 166 µs on
  STEPFOC.
- **Calibration differs.** The Spectral Micro measures the motor's resistance and inductance and finds its pole
  pairs; STEPFOC cannot, so there the three values are entered from the motor's datasheet first. See
  [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/).
- **The motor terminals differ.** U, V and W for the three phases, instead of A+, A−, B+, B− for the two coils of
  a stepper.
- **The grippers differ.** The [SSG-48 gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/) is driven by
  a Spectral Micro, the [MSG gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/) by STEPFOC; both use the
  driver's [gripper mode](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/).

The guides under the Guides tab were written with the Spectral Micro; the code in them runs unchanged on STEPFOC.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/01-overview/what-you-need/ -->

# What you need

This page lists what a Spectral Micro setup is made of, what comes with the driver, and what you buy or make
yourself.

## The driver

The Spectral Micro is sold as a single driver or as a starter kit in the Source Robotics shop:

- [Spectral Micro BLDC controller](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-bldc-controller)
- [Spectral Micro starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-bldc-starter-kit), which adds
  the adapters, the magnet, the cables and a thermistor listed below

Every driver is end-of-line tested and ships with the current firmware release and the bootloader already
installed, so a driver works out of the box with a serial terminal, the Python library or Motor GUI. The firmware
can be updated later without a programming adapter; see [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/).

## A brushless motor

The Spectral Micro drives three-phase brushless motors with a phase resistance of about 2 to 24 Ω and a current
of 2.8 A or less: gimbal motors from the small 2804 class up to the 8108 class, and other brushless motors of
similar resistance, such as the NEMA 17-format 42BLS40. The [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/tested-motors/)
are known to work. The motor needs a place for the encoder magnet on the axis of its shaft, on the side where the
board is mounted.

!!! danger "Low-resistance motors"
    The calibration routine's default voltages are made for motors of 2 Ω and more. A motor with a much lower
    resistance, such as a drone motor, draws a destructive current at those voltages. Do not calibrate one without
    lowering the calibration voltages (`#Resv`, `#Openv`, `#Vp`) first. The current limit does not protect it:
    calibration sets its own, up to 1600 mA.

## The encoder magnet

A diametrically magnetised 6 × 2.5 mm neodymium magnet on the end of the motor shaft, about 1 mm above the
encoder chip in the middle of the board: [6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet](https://source-robotics.com/products/6x2-5mm-diametrical-neodymium-magnet).
An axially magnetised magnet, or one that wobbles, makes calibration fail or report bad positions. The 6 × 2.5 mm
size is the stock one, not a requirement: another thickness is a way to set the 1 mm gap when a shaft or a bracket
leaves the wrong distance. [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/) says how to fit it.

## A mounting bracket

The board does not bolt to a gimbal motor directly: a bracket holds it behind the motor, with the encoder chip on
the shaft's axis and 1 mm from the magnet. The firmware repository has an
[example bracket](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files) to
adapt to your motor; see [Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/). A motor with the NEMA 17 hole
pattern, such as the 42BLS40, takes the board on a spacer with its own screws.

## Adapters and cables

| Part | Needed for | Shop |
|---|---|---|
| USB-to-serial adapter (3.3 V) | the serial terminal: calibration, tuning, any `#` command | [Serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) |
| CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter | CAN control from a PC, the Python library, Motor GUI over CAN | [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) |
| CAN cable and power cable | daisy-chaining several drivers | [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable) |
| 100 kΩ NTC thermistor | motor temperature protection (optional but recommended) | [Thermistor](https://source-robotics.com/products/100k-ntc-thermistor) |
| JTAG programming adapter | only for installing the bootloader on an older board, or for firmware development | [Programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch) |

!!! danger "Cable orientation"
    The daisy-chain cables for CAN and power are keyed by their orientation, not by their connector. A cable
    plugged in the wrong way round destroys the driver. Use the cables from the shop or follow
    [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/) exactly when you make your own.

## A power supply

12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended; see [Ratings and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/ratings/). Calibrate at 24 V:
the resistance, inductance and motor constants come out wrong at a lower voltage. A bench supply with a current
limit is the safest way to start.

## Software

- [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), in the browser, over the serial adapter or the CAN adapter: the usual tool
  for setup, calibration, tuning, plots and firmware updates; see [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/).
- Or a serial terminal: PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor in VS Code, or the Arduino serial monitor; see
  [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/terminal/).
- The Python library `Spectral-BLDC` for CAN control from your own programs; see [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/python/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/02-safety/ -->

# Safety

The Spectral Micro is a bare circuit board that drives a motor from a supply of up to 29 V. Read this chapter before you
connect anything; the few rules here are the ones that destroy a driver, a motor or a finger when they are ignored.

## Electrical

!!! danger "Supply polarity"
    Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the driver at once. Check the polarity of every power cable
    before you plug it in, every time.

!!! danger "Cable orientation on the daisy chain"
    The CAN and power cables that link one driver to the next are keyed by their orientation, not by their
    connector: a cable plugged in the wrong way round puts the supply on the wrong pins and destroys the driver.
    Use the cables from the Source Robotics shop, or make yours exactly as shown in
    [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/).

!!! danger "UART is 3.3 V"
    The UART port runs at 3.3 V. A 5 V serial adapter destroys the board. Use a 3.3 V adapter, such as the one
    from the shop.

!!! warning "Supply voltage"
    12 to 29 V DC. The driver raises a Vbus error below 9 V and above `#Vmax`, 29 V after `#Default`. 29 V is
    also the hardware limit: do not connect a supply that can rise above it, and allow for the voltage a
    decelerating motor pushes back into the supply. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to
    start.

!!! warning "Do not disconnect a running motor"
    Never unplug a motor, or a power cable in the daisy chain, while the driver is powered. The inductive kick of
    the windings and the arcing at the connector damage the driver stage.

!!! warning "Static electricity"
    Static electricity damages the microcontroller, the encoder chip and the driver stage. Unplug the supply and
    touch earthed metal before you handle the board, and hold it by its edges, away from the chips and the pads.

## Mechanical

!!! danger "Moving parts"
    A calibrating or running motor turns without warning, in both directions, and a motor in position mode
    pushes back hard against a hand. Keep fingers, hair and cables away from the shaft and whatever is mounted on
    it, fix the motor to the bench before the first test, and test without a load on the shaft.

!!! danger "A powered motor can move with nobody at it"
    The driver moves its motor whenever a command arrives, over UART or from any host on the CAN bus, and keeps
    following the last one. A speed command goes on turning the motor after the program that sent it has crashed
    or its cable has come out, unless the watchdog is set ([Stopping the motor](#stopping-the-motor)). Before you
    reach for the motor or the mechanism it drives, put the driver in idle (`#Idle`, Send_Idle) or switch the
    supply off.

!!! warning "The encoder magnet"
    The magnet sits about 1 mm above the encoder chip. A magnet that touches the chip, or sits far too close, can
    damage the microcontroller; a magnet too far away gives a wrong position. Mount it as described in
    [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/).

!!! warning "Hot motor and driver"
    A motor running at its rated current gets hot enough to burn, and so do the driver's chips and the board
    around them. Switch off and let both cool for a few minutes before you touch them. Set the current limit for
    your motor ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/)), use the thermistor, and give the driver
    airflow when it runs near 2.8 A. `#Ilim` is clamped to 2800 mA, and from firmware 109 so are the current limit of
    Send_Limits over CAN and the current of a gripper move. The motor's rating is usually lower: a host must keep
    them within it.

## Stopping the motor

- `Send_ESTOP` over CAN, or `#Idle` over UART, stops the motor at once; the E-stop error stays until it is cleared.
- Cutting the supply stops the motor as well; the motor then holds nothing, so a vertical axis drops.
- The watchdog ([Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/)) stops the motor by itself when the host stops talking.
  From firmware 109 its action can instead hold the position or let a joint down at a limited speed, for a set
  time at most, then brake or coast ([The watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/watchdog/)): while that runs the motor is still
  driven.

Nothing on the driver is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop
that cuts the motor supply, independent of the driver.

## Firmware updates and programming

When you connect a programming adapter to the JTAG connector, disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter
first. Updating over the bootloader needs no adapter; see [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/).

## Liability

The Spectral Micro is sold as a component for people who build their own machines. Its hardware designs, firmware and this
documentation are under development and may contain errors.
Whoever builds a machine with it is responsible for its safe design, assembly and operation.

# Ratings and limits

## Electrical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Supply voltage | 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V typical; 10 V absolute minimum |
| Vbus error limits (firmware) | below 9 V or above `#Vmax`, 29 V after `#Default` |
| Phase current, continuous | 1.5 A typical |
| Phase current, maximum | 2.8 A (`#Ilim` and, from firmware 109, Send_Limits over CAN are clamped to 2800 mA); needs good cooling and short bursts |
| Power, maximum | 80 W |
| Power, idle | 0.3 W |
| PWM frequency | 25 kHz |
| Control loop frequency | 5 kHz |
| Electrical frequency, maximum | 500 Hz |
| Current sensing | inline, on two phases |
| Encoder | 14-bit magnetic, 16384 ticks per revolution, diametrical magnet 1 mm above the chip |
| UART | 3.3 V, 256000 baud by default (1 000 000 tested) |
| CAN | CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers, node IDs 0 to 13 (14 and 15 are reserved by the bootloader), 120 Ω termination by switch |
| Thermistor input | 100 kΩ NTC, 54.9 kΩ pull-down |
| PIN | analog input or general-purpose input/output, 3.3 V |
| Driver stage protection | hardware overcurrent (trips at 3 to 5 A), undervoltage lockout (6.3 to 8 V) and thermal shutdown (150 to 180 °C); shown as a driver error |

!!! warning "Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the board."

## Thermal and environmental

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Operating temperature of the board | −20 to 130 °C |
| Motor temperature limit (firmware, with the thermistor) | 75 °C by default (`#Tlim`), −20 °C minimum |

## Mechanical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 39 × 39 mm |
| Mass | 8 g |
| Mounting | four holes on the NEMA 17 pattern, 31 mm apart; the encoder chip in the middle of the board |

## Firmware limits

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Position | signed 24-bit over CAN (±8.4 million ticks, ±512 revolutions), 32-bit internally |
| Speed | signed 24-bit over CAN, encoder ticks per second |
| Current setpoint | signed 16-bit over CAN, mA |
| Motors the calibration defaults are made for | a phase resistance of 2 to 24 Ω |
| Configuration | kept in the EEPROM with `#Save` / `Send_Save_config` |

The defaults of every setting are listed in the [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/defaults/) reference.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/connectors/ -->

# Connectors and pinout

![The connectors. The motor phases go to U, V, W; the supply to DC+ and DC−.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/con2.webp){ width="900" }

| Connector | Pins | Type | Cable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Motor | U, V, W | solder pads, three per phase | the motor's own leads, see [Wiring the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/wiring/) |
| Power, two of them | DC+, DC− | JST XH, 2 pins | [Power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable); the second connector feeds the next driver |
| CAN, two of them | CANL, CANH | JST ZH, 2 pins | [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable); the second connector feeds the next driver |
| UART | 3V3, GND, TX, RX | JST SH, 4 pins | [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable) |
| Thermistor | TERM, 3V3 | solder pads | the 100 kΩ NTC from the shop or any 100 kΩ NTC, see [Thermistor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/thermistor/) |
| JTAG | 3V3, GND, SWCLK, SWDIO | 1.27 mm pads | [Programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch), pressed onto the pads |
| PIN | GND, PIN, 3V3 | solder pads | your own signal: an analog input or a digital input/output, 3.3 V |
| HALL | 5V, GND, HALL1, HALL2, HALL3 | solder pads | hall sensors: not implemented in the firmware, see the note below |

![The pinout. Left the top of the board with the CAN connectors, the motor pads and the termination switch; right the bottom with the UART connector, the power connectors, the thermistor pads and the encoder chip.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/PINOUT1.webp){ width="900" }

!!! note "Hall sensors are not implemented"
    The HALL header and the twelve resistor pads above it are on the board for hall-sensor commutation, but the
    Spectral firmware does not implement it: the magnetic encoder is the only position source. Leave the header
    unpopulated.

!!! danger "Polarity and orientation"
    DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative; a cable the wrong way round destroys the driver. The daisy-chain
    cables have an orientation too: see [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/).

!!! note
    - UART is TX to RX and RX to TX between the driver and the adapter.
    - The UART port and the PIN header are 3.3 V. 5 V on either destroys the board.
    - The thermistor pin has a 54.9 kΩ pull-down; the firmware's temperature table is for a 100 kΩ NTC.
    - The CAN termination switch is next to the CAN connectors; **ON** connects the 120 Ω resistor.
    - The encoder chip sits on the bottom of the board, in the middle: that side faces the magnet.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/dimensions/ -->

# Dimensions and CAD

The board is 39 × 39 mm with four mounting holes on the NEMA 17 pattern (31 mm apart). The encoder chip is
exactly in the middle of the board, so a bracket that centres the board on the motor shaft puts the chip on the
shaft's axis.

<div class="gripper-viewer" data-base="../../assets/models/spectral/" markdown="0">
  <canvas class="gripper-viewer__canvas" aria-label="The Spectral Micro driver in 3D: drag to turn, scroll to zoom"></canvas>
  <div class="gripper-viewer__controls">
    <button type="button" name="reset" class="md-button">Reset view</button>
  </div>
  <p class="gripper-viewer__hint">Drag to turn the board, scroll to zoom. The model is the board's STEP file from the <a href="https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files">repository</a>, the PCB and everything mounted on it.</p>
</div>

![Board dimensions and hole pattern.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/micro_dimensions_dark.webp){ width="600" }

![The board's model, from its STEP file: the PCB and everything mounted on it.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/renders/spectral_board_studio.webp){ width="520" }
![The board's model, from its STEP file: the PCB and everything mounted on it.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/renders/spectral_board_studio_dark.webp){ width="520" }

The STEP files of the board and of an example mounting bracket are in the firmware repository, in
[STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files):
`Spectral_micro_STEP.STEP` is the board, `Spectral_micro_bracket.STEP` the bracket to adapt to your motor
([Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/)).

[Downloads and files](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/cad-files/) lists everything that can be downloaded.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/tested-motors/ -->

# Tested motors

The Spectral Micro drives three-phase brushless motors with a phase resistance of about 2 to 24 Ω: the
calibration routine's default voltages are made for that range. The motors below have been run on it. Calibration
measures each motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs, so nothing has to be looked up before the first run.

| | Motor | Kind | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| ![BGM8108](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/BGM8108.webp){ width="90" } | BGM8108 | gimbal motor, 8108 class | [AliExpress](https://es.aliexpress.com/item/2008157492.html) |
| ![GM8112](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GM8112.webp){ width="90" } | GM8112 | gimbal motor, 8112 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_Dc6I1bx) |
| ![GM7008H](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GM7008H.webp){ width="90" } | GM7008H | gimbal motor, 7008 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DBY6U9T) |
| ![GM6008H](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GM6008H.webp){ width="90" } | GM6008H | gimbal motor, 6008 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DDPsXZn) |
| ![GBM5208](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GBM5208.webp){ width="90" } | GBM5208 | gimbal motor, 5208 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_okWNA7Z) |
| ![GM5208](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GM5208.webp){ width="90" } | GM5208 | gimbal motor, 5208 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_Dd82dTF) |
| ![GBM5010](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GBM5010.webp){ width="90" } | GBM5010 | gimbal motor, 5010 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DlJ8vJb) |
| ![GB4114](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/GB4114.webp){ width="90" } | GB4114 | gimbal motor, 4114 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DDVlOFR) |
| ![2804](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/2804_motor.webp){ width="90" } | 2804 | gimbal motor, 2804 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DlEUo81) |
| ![2804 (RCTimer)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/RCTIMER.webp){ width="90" } | 2804 (RCTimer) | gimbal motor, 2804 class | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DlQJp3T) |
| ![2804 100KV](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/2804_100kv.webp){ width="90" } | 2804 100KV | gimbal motor, 2804 class, 100 KV | [AliExpress](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DdeNXK1) |
| ![42BLS40-24-01](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/NEMA17%20format%20BLDC.webp){ width="90" } | 42BLS40-24-01 | NEMA 17-format brushless motor, 24 V, 26 W, 1.8 A, 219 g | [Stepperonline](https://www.omc-stepperonline.com/24v-4000rpm-0-0625nm-26w-1-8a-42x42x40mm-brushless-dc-motor-42bls40-24-01) |

Before the first test, set the current limit for the motor with `#Ilim` (firmware 107 and older leave 1600 mA
after a calibration; from 109 calibration puts your limit back). The
factory default of 1000 mA suits the gimbal motors above; a motor rated for more can go up to the driver's
2800 mA. See [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/).

!!! tip "Choosing a motor"
    A lower phase resistance and inductance give a higher speed at a given supply voltage; the velocity constant
    `KV` that calibration finds tells how fast the motor can turn: roughly 0.8 × Vbus × KV revolutions per minute.
    A high pole-pair count (the large gimbal motors have 11 to 14) gives smooth torque at low speed and limits the
    top speed through the driver's maximum electrical frequency. Motors with visibly uneven windings, a resistance
    that differs between the phases or an uneven back-EMF calibrate badly and run rough.

!!! danger "Drone motors"
    Motors with a phase resistance well under 1 Ω draw a destructive current at the calibration routine's default
    voltages. The Spectral Micro is not made for them.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/ -->

# Mounting and wiring

How the driver goes onto the motor and what gets connected to it: the encoder magnet on the shaft, the board on a
bracket behind the motor, the three phases to the motor terminals, the supply and the CAN bus, and the thermistor.
Do the pages in order; the magnet first, because it is the one thing you cannot check from the outside later.

## In this chapter

- [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/)
- [Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/)
- [Wiring the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/wiring/)
- [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/)
- [Thermistor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/thermistor/)

When all of it is done, continue with [First setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/ -->

# The encoder magnet

The encoder reads a diametrically magnetised magnet on the end of the motor shaft. The magnet must sit centred on
the shaft's axis, parallel to the board, about **1 mm** above the encoder chip, and it must not move. Every
calibration problem that is not a wiring problem comes from this magnet.

![About 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip in the middle of the board.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/mag_dist.webp){ width="700" }

## The magnet

A neodymium disc, **diametrically** magnetised (north and south across the diameter, not through the thickness).
The shop's [6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet](https://source-robotics.com/products/6x2-5mm-diametrical-neodymium-magnet)
is the stock size. An axially magnetised magnet looks the same and does not work: the magnet test may even pass,
and the position is wrong.

!!! note "The size is not fixed"
    6 × 2.5 mm is the stock size, not a requirement. Any diametrically magnetised disc of about 6 mm diameter
    works, and the thickness is a way to set the gap: a thicker magnet brings its face closer to the encoder, a
    thinner one farther, so with a shaft or a bracket that leaves the wrong distance you can pick the thickness
    that gives 1 mm instead of changing the bracket. What matters is the 1 mm from the magnet's face to the chip,
    the magnet centred on the shaft, and the diametrical magnetisation.

## Fitting it

1. The magnet goes on the end of the shaft that faces the board. On most gimbal motors the shaft ends at the
   bottom of the motor, flush with the housing or a little proud of it, and the board is mounted on that side
   ([Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/)). On a motor whose shaft ends inside the housing, a short holder pressed
   into the shaft's end carries the magnet out to where the board can see it.
2. Press the magnet on, centred on the shaft's axis. A magnet that sits off-centre wobbles its field as the shaft
   turns and gives a position error that repeats every revolution.
3. Fix it with a drop of glue. A magnet that can turn on the shaft is the classic cause of a calibration that
   reports success and a motor that then runs badly: the magnet slipped between calibration and use.
4. Check the height after the board is mounted: 1 mm, the magnet not touching the chip. A magnet that touches
   the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet 2 mm away or more gives a weak signal.

!!! success "Check"
    The magnet sits centred on the shaft, and once the glue has set it does not move when you push it with a
    finger.

## Checking it

With the driver powered and the serial terminal open, `#Magnet` answers `Magnet Good` when the chip sees enough
field, `Magnet Bad` when it does not. The calibration routine runs the same test first. 

!!! warning "What the magnet test checks"
    Only that a magnet is close enough to the encoder. It passes with a magnet that is not glued, sits off-centre or
    can slip on the shaft, and fails only when there is no magnet or it is too far away. The 1 mm gap, the centring
    and the glue are yours to check.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/mounting/ -->

# Mounting on the motor

The board sits behind the motor, with the encoder chip, in the middle of the board, on the axis of the shaft and
1 mm from the magnet. The board's four holes are on the NEMA 17 pattern, 31 mm apart.

## Gimbal motors

A gimbal motor has no standard mounting for a board; a bracket holds the board at the right distance. The
firmware repository has an example to adapt to your motor, `Spectral_micro_bracket.STEP` in
[STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files): change
its hole pattern to the motor's bottom holes and its height so that the magnet ends up 1 mm from the chip.

![The example bracket. The motor bolts to one side, the board to the other; the hole in the middle is for the shaft and the magnet.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/brack.webp){ width="500" }

1. Bolt the bracket to the bottom of the motor. The magnet on the shaft's end sits in the bracket's centre hole.
2. Bolt the board to the bracket with M3 screws, with the encoder chip (the bottom of the board, see
   [Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/connectors/)) towards the magnet. Tighten the screws evenly; the
   board must be parallel to the magnet's face.
3. Check the gap between the magnet and the encoder chip: about 1 mm, the magnet not touching it. If it is wrong,
   change the bracket's height or the magnet's thickness ([The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/)).

!!! success "Check"
    The board sits parallel to the motor, with about 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip, and the rotor
    turns by hand without the magnet touching the chip. If the gap is wrong: [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/).

## Motors with the NEMA 17 pattern

A brushless motor in the NEMA 17 format, such as the 42BLS40 in the [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/tested-motors/),
takes the board directly, with the motor's own rear screws: remove the four screws, put on a spacer that sets the
magnet height, the board on the spacer with the chip towards the magnet, and longer M3 screws in. Check the gap.

!!! warning "The board is bare"
    Nothing on the board may touch the motor's housing or a metal bracket. Keep the bracket clear of the
    components on both sides of the board (the connectors on the bottom need room), and keep metal swarf and
    screws away from the board while you work. Touch earthed metal before you pick the
    board up and hold it by its edges: static electricity damages its chips.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/wiring/ -->

# Wiring the motor

A three-phase brushless motor has three wires. They go to the terminals **U, V and W** on the board (see
[Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/connectors/)), in any order: calibration finds the order of the
phases. Firmware 105 and newer compensates it in software; firmware 101 asks you to swap two wires when it is
reversed.

## Soldering

1. Cut the leads to a comfortable length: long enough to reach the pads with the board mounted, short enough not
   to get into the rotor. With firmware older than 105, leave them long enough to swap two of them later.
2. Tin the leads and solder each to one group of pads, U, V or W. The three pads of a group are one terminal.
3. Make sure no strand bridges two groups and that nothing touches the rotor or the housing.

A motor that comes with a connector keeps it: solder a short lead with the mating connector to each pad group.

!!! success "Check"
    With the driver unpowered, a multimeter shows about the same resistance between U and V, V and W, and W
    and U, and no strand bridges two groups.

!!! warning
    Never connect or disconnect the motor while the driver is powered.

## Phase order and direction

Calibration spins the motor in open loop and watches the encoder, then checks that a current command moves the
rotor the expected way.

With firmware 105 and newer, the order of the phases is detected and compensated, so the motor calibrates identically
with any wiring, and positive commands turn the motor the same way whatever the wiring: counter-clockwise seen from
the encoder side of the board, see [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/). To turn the other way, use negative
setpoints.

Firmware older than 105 does not compensate the order: calibration stops with
`Phase order is wrong! Switch motor phases and try again!`. Swap any two of U, V and W and calibrate again.

If the motor does not respond to the commutation check, calibration says so (`Commutation/alignment check
failed!`). That means a phase is not connected, `#Iqoffset` is set too low or the magnet slipped, not that the
wires are in the wrong order; see [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/power-and-can/ -->

# Power and the CAN daisy chain

Each driver has two power connectors (JST XH) and two CAN connectors (JST ZH). The second connector of each pair
feeds the next driver, so a chain of drivers hangs on one supply cable and one CAN cable.

![Power and CAN pass from driver to driver. The first and the last node on the bus have their termination switch on.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Daisy_chain-Photoroom.webp){ width="700" }

## Power

- 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended. **DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative**; reversed polarity destroys
  the driver.
- The power connectors are rated for 4 A. A chain of drivers shares that: with motors at 1.5 A each, plan for at most two or three drivers per chain that draw their full current at the
  same time (three or four with 10 Ω gimbal motors), and feed a longer chain from
  both ends or from several supplies.
- A motor that decelerates pushes energy back into the supply. A lab supply or a battery absorbs it; a supply that
  cannot (some switch-mode supplies) sees its voltage rise, and the driver raises a Vbus error above `#Vmax`
  (29 V after `#Default`).

## The cable orientation

!!! danger
    The daisy-chain cables are keyed by their orientation, not by the connector: the same 2-pin cable fits both
    ways, and the wrong way puts DC+ on DC−. Every cable must run as in the picture below, the same way at both
    ends. A wrong cable destroys the driver at the moment it is powered.

![The orientation of the daisy-chain cables, the same for the 2-pin power and CAN cables.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/daisy-chain-cable.svg){ width="600" }
![The orientation of the daisy-chain cables, the same for the 2-pin power and CAN cables.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/daisy-chain-cable_dark.svg){ width="600" }

The cables from the shop are made this way: [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable),
[power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable), and all of them under
[connectors and cables](https://source-robotics.com/pages/connectors-and-cables).

## CAN

- CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. Up to 14 drivers on one bus, each with its own node ID, 0 to 13 (0 by default;
  set it with `#CANID` or Send_CAN_ID and save). The firmware accepts 14 and 15 too, but the
  [bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/the-bootloader/) reserves them: a driver on one of those IDs cannot be updated
  over CAN.
- Twisted-pair wire; keep the bus short at 1 Mbit/s (a few metres at most).
- **Termination:** the first and the last node on the bus need a 120 Ω resistor between CAN H and CAN L. The
  switch next to the CAN connectors turns the driver's resistor on (**ON**). Drivers in the middle stay off. A bus
  with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered.
- A PC joins the bus with the [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter),
  which has its own termination.

![The termination switch, ON for the first and the last node.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/TERM.webp){ width="520" }
![The termination switch, ON for the first and the last node.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/TERM_dark.webp){ width="520" }


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/thermistor/ -->

# Thermistor

A 100 kΩ NTC thermistor in the motor lets the driver stop before the motor overheats. It is optional, and off by
default; use it on any motor that runs near its current limit for long, and on a motor that holds a load at
standstill, which heats one winding without any movement to show it.

!!! warning "Without it, nothing protects the motor from overheating"
    The driver limits the current, not the temperature. A motor that runs continuously, holds a load for long, or
    is set up badly (a current limit above its rating, loops that oscillate, a wrong resistance or inductance) can
    overheat and burn its windings without any warning. With the thermistor fitted and enabled, the driver stops
    first. The starter kit includes one.

![The thermistor on the TERM and 3V3 pads.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/TERM1-Photoroom.webp){ width="520" }

## Fitting it

Solder the thermistor's leads to the two thermistor pads, TERM and 3V3 ([Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/connectors/)).
Put its bead inside the motor's windings, where the heat is: on a gimbal motor the windings are open at the
bottom and can be reached through one of the mounting holes or past the edge of the stator.

Thermal cement holds the bead in place and conducts the heat; keep the leads clear of the rotor.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Thermal cement](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Thermal_cement.webp){ width="220" }
  ![Thermal cement](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Thermal_cement_dark.webp){ width="220" }
  <figcaption>Thermal cement: it sets hard and conducts heat. Thermal paste stays soft and lets the bead move, ordinary glue insulates it. <a href="https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_c3dBOwTD" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Where to buy it</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

![The thermistor placed in the windings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/TERM2-Photoroom.webp){ width="520" }

## Enabling it

```
#Term 1
#Tlim 75
#Save
```

`#Temp` then prints the temperature; with the thermistor disabled it prints `Temp Off`. Above the limit the driver
raises a temperature error and stops; it clears with `#Clear` once the motor has cooled.

Below −20 °C it raises the same error, so `#Term 1` without a thermistor, or with a broken lead, stops the driver too.
75 °C is the default limit and a safe one for the enamel of most small motors; do not go higher unless the motor is
rated for it.

Over CAN, Send_Respond_Temperature returns the temperature, and the temperature error is one of the bits of
Send_Respond_State_of_Errors.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/ -->

# First setup

From a mounted and wired driver to a calibrated, tuned motor. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual tool for it;
every step also gives the terminal command, for a terminal or for the console in Motor GUI.

1. [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/): the browser, the serial adapter, opening the port, what is on the screen.
2. [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/terminal/): the alternative — PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino monitor,
   and the `#` commands.
3. [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/): the factory defaults, then the run that measures the motor and finds its pole
   pairs, phase order and constants.
4. [Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/): two corrections the driver can measure on itself after a
   calibration, how to run them and how to check them.
5. [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/): the current limit for the motor, the loop gains if the defaults do
   not suit it, the speed estimate and the delay compensation.
6. [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/): nothing survives a power cycle until it is saved; where it is kept.

A driver that has been through these pages is ready for [Operation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/). The
[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/quick-start/) is the same path in four short parts.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/ -->

# Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) is the usual way to set up, test and tune a driver: a tool in the browser that
connects to one driver over the serial adapter or to a bus of drivers over the CANvas adapter, shows the state,
moves the motor, runs the calibration, tunes the loops with live plots, records telemetry and updates the
firmware. Nothing is installed. Everything it does, the driver also does from a terminal or from Python — the
GUI reads and writes the same settings — so every procedure in this manual shows the GUI first and the terminal
command beside it.

## The browser

Motor GUI reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access (Web Serial), which Chromium-based
browsers have: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera. Firefox and Safari cannot open serial ports.

## Two ways to connect

| | Adapter | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **One driver over serial** | the 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter on the driver's UART connector, 256000 baud | the first setup and calibration (calibration runs over UART only), tuning on the bench |
| **A bus over CAN** | the CANvas adapter; it appears as a serial port and speaks slcan | every driver on the bus by its node ID: testing a machine, updating firmware on all joints |

## Opening the port

1. Plug in the adapter and the motor supply. The adapter alone powers the driver's logic, enough to open the
   port and read the settings, but the driver reports a Vbus error and will not calibrate or move until the
   supply is on.
2. Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/), choose the connection kind, and **Connect**. The browser asks
   which port; pick the adapter's.
3. The driver's identity appears: hardware version, firmware version, serial number, batch date, whether it is
   calibrated and activated, and the active errors. In a terminal, `#Info`, `#SERNUM` and `#Error` print the same.

If the port is not offered, the browser is not Chromium-based, or another program holds the port (a terminal left
open, PlatformIO's monitor), or the operating system does not give the browser the port:

=== "Windows"
    The adapter is `COM` and a number. Device Manager lists it under **Ports (COM & LPT)**: the entry that
    disappears when you unplug the adapter is yours. An adapter that shows a warning sign there instead needs the
    driver of its USB chip (on most 3.3 V adapters a CP210x or a CH340) from the chip maker.

=== "Linux"
    The serial adapter is `/dev/ttyUSB0` on most adapters, the CANvas adapter `/dev/ttyACM0`;
    `ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM*` lists them. To open them without root, join the `dialout` group once, then
    log out and in again:

    ```
    sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
    ```

=== "macOS"
    The serial adapter is `/dev/cu.usbserial-` and a few characters on most adapters, the CANvas adapter
    `/dev/cu.usbmodem` and a number; `ls /dev/cu.*` lists them. Use the `cu.` name, not the `tty.` one, in a
    terminal or a script.

The browser's port picker lists the same adapters. If the port opens and nothing appears: the driver is
unpowered, or TX and RX are crossed on an adapter that is not the Source Robotics one.

## What is on the screen

- **State**: the identity above, the control mode the driver is in, the errors, and **Clear errors**.
- **Jog**: *Jog position*, *Jog velocity* and *Jog current* move the motor in the matching control mode; *Send
  setpoint* sends a value in the current mode. *Live stream while dragging* follows a slider as you move it.
- **Plots** of position, speed and current, panning and zooming, with the value under the pointer.
- **Settings**: the motor parameters (pole pairs, resistance, inductance), the limits (current, velocity,
  voltage), the loop gains with *Apply gains* and *Apply preset*, the CAN node ID, the watchdog, the thermistor.
  The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you **Save** to the driver's EEPROM; *Default* restores the factory values.
- **Calibration**: starts `#Cal` and shows the driver's log step by step; afterwards the resistance, inductance and pole pairs it measured, the phase order and direction, Kt, KV
  and the flux linkage.
- **Telemetry**: the stream from the driver, and recordings of it for a test or a bug report.
- **Firmware update**: the releases from GitHub, flashed through the bootloader; *Scan bootloaders* on a bus.
- **Gripper**: the gripper controls, for a driver in gripper mode.
- **Console**: type any `#` command by hand; the answer appears below it.
- **Wiring diagrams** and **Keyboard shortcuts** under help.

## Screen guide

!!! success "Check"
    After connecting real hardware, the state and identity belong to your driver. If they do not appear, check
    the transport, the selected port, the supply and the TX/RX wiring before trying to move.

## Try it without hardware

Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)**, and press **Connect**. The motor and gripper panels run in the browser without a port picker. Motor calibration (`#Cal`) still requires a real UART connection; the CAN demo does not perform it.

## What next

[Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/) is the first thing to do with a connected driver;
[Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/motor-gui/) covers everyday use: moving the motor, the plots, recordings,
several motors on a bus.
