<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/terminal/ -->

# The serial terminal

Motor GUI is the usual way to work with the driver; a plain serial terminal is the alternative, and it is what
the console inside Motor GUI is.

Everything in this manual that is done in the GUI is also one `#` command, and the terminal shows the driver's answers
exactly as it prints them, which is useful when something does not work.

The driver talks on its UART connector at 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V. Any terminal that sends a line ending in
CR+LF works.

![The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/UART_connection.webp){ width="700" }
![The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/UART_connection_dark.webp){ width="700" }

## Connecting

1. Plug the [USB-to-serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) into the UART
   connector with the [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable). With another adapter: 3.3 V
   only, and cross TX and RX: the driver's TX to the adapter's RX, the driver's RX to the adapter's TX.
2. Connect the motor supply. The adapter's 3.3 V powers the driver's logic, so the driver answers over UART with
   only the adapter plugged in, but it reports a Vbus error and refuses calibration and every motion command
   until the 12 to 29 V supply is on.
3. Find the adapter's port:

=== "Windows"
    The adapter is `COM` and a number. Device Manager lists it under **Ports (COM & LPT)**: the entry that
    disappears when you unplug the adapter is yours. An adapter that shows a warning sign there instead needs the
    driver of its USB chip (on most 3.3 V adapters a CP210x or a CH340) from the chip maker.

=== "Linux"
    The serial adapter is `/dev/ttyUSB0` on most adapters, the CANvas adapter `/dev/ttyACM0`;
    `ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM*` lists them. To open them without root, join the `dialout` group once, then
    log out and in again:

    ```
    sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
    ```

=== "macOS"
    The serial adapter is `/dev/cu.usbserial-` and a few characters on most adapters, the CANvas adapter
    `/dev/cu.usbmodem` and a number; `ls /dev/cu.*` lists them. Use the `cu.` name, not the `tty.` one, in a
    terminal or a script.

!!! danger
    5 V on the UART pins destroys the board.

## A terminal

=== "PuTTY"
    PuTTY needs to send CR+LF when you press Enter, which the stock build cannot. Use the
    [modified PuTTY](https://www.grzegorz.net/pliki/putty-crlf.zip): under *Terminal → Keyboard* select the CR LF
    option, then open the serial port at 256000.

    | Keyboard setting | Session |
    |---|---|
    | ![PuTTY keyboard tab](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/PUTTY2.PNG){ width="420" } | ![PuTTY session](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/PUTTY1.PNG){ width="420" } |

=== "VS Code (PlatformIO)"
    With the [firmware project](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/Bootloader_main/Spectral%20BLDC%20Firmware)
    open in VS Code with the PlatformIO extension, the serial monitor (the plug icon in the status bar) uses the
    speed and the `send_on_enter` filter from `platformio.ini`, so a line goes out with CR+LF when you press
    Enter.

    | platformio.ini | The monitor |
    |---|---|
    | ![platformio.ini](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/vscode1.PNG){ width="420" } | ![The serial monitor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/vscode2.PNG){ width="420" } |

=== "Arduino IDE"
    Select the adapter's port under *Tools*, any board (the monitor does not care), open the serial monitor, set
    256000 baud and *Both NL & CR* as the line ending.

    ![The Arduino serial monitor at 256000 baud, with Both NL & CR as the line ending](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Arduino3.PNG){ width="420" }

## The first commands

```
#Info
```

prints the driver's identity: the hardware and firmware version, the CAN ID, the calibration state and the motor
parameters. `#Help` (firmware 106 and newer) prints a short command reference, `#Error` the active errors,
`#SERNUM` the serial number and `#Param` the gains.

!!! success "Check"
    `#Info` answers with the driver's identity, the hardware and firmware version first. If nothing comes back:
    the baud rate, the CR+LF line ending, TX and RX, see
    [The driver does not answer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/#the-driver-does-not-answer).

Every command starts with `#`, and a Set/Get command takes one number after a space: `#P 16384` moves to position
16384; `#P` alone prints the position. Names are case-sensitive. The whole set is in the
[UART commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/) reference, and [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/uart/) explains the
protocol.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/ -->

# Calibration

Calibration teaches the driver its motor. It checks the magnet and the supply, then measures the motor's phase
resistance and inductance and computes the current loop gains from them.

It spins the motor in open loop to find the pole pairs and the direction, checks the order of the phases and
aligns the encoder to the rotor field, and measures the motor constants Kt, KV and the flux linkage. Nothing about
the motor has to be entered first.

It runs once per motor; the result is kept by saving. From firmware 109 every `#Cal` goes on by itself to two more
runs, the [encoder table and the anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/), and saves. `#Calonly` is the calibration alone.

!!! danger "The motor turns"
    Calibration spins the motor in both directions, fast at times. Fix the motor to the bench and take everything
    off the shaft.

!!! tip "Supply voltage"
    Calibrate at 24 V. At a lower voltage the resistance, the inductance, KV and Kt come out wrong.

## The settings

The routine uses six settings, which it prints when it starts. The defaults suit motors with a phase resistance
of 2 to 24 Ω; change them only for a motor outside that range.

| Setting | Default | Command | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current loop bandwidth | 160 Hz | `#Cbw` | the bandwidth the current loop gains are computed for (Kpiq ≈ ω·L, Kiiq = ω·R·T, with ω = 2π × the bandwidth and T the 200 µs control period); too high makes the motor vibrate and whine. 500 Hz up to firmware 107 |
| Resistance voltage | 1000 mV | `#Resv` | the voltage the resistance measurement starts at; it rises until the power reaches the limit below |
| Max power dissipation | 12 W | `#Calpwr` | the power the resistance and inductance measurements may put into the motor |
| Open loop voltage | 5000 mV | `#Openv` | the voltage of the open-loop spin that finds the pole pairs |
| Open loop speed | 20 rad/s | `#Opens` | the electrical speed of that spin |
| Phase search voltage | 5000 mV | `#Vp` | the voltage of the spin that checks the phase order |

A seventh setting is not printed: `#Iqoffset`, 300 mA by default, the current of the angle-offset search and of
the commutation check. None of the seven is saved; after a power cycle they are back at these defaults. The
current gains the bandwidth gives are saved with the calibration.

!!! danger "Low-resistance motors"
    These voltages are made for motors of 2 Ω and more. On a motor with a much lower resistance, such as a drone
    motor, they drive a destructive current. The Spectral Micro is not made for such motors; if you must try one,
    lower the three voltages first. Lowering the current limit does not help: calibration sets its own.

!!! warning "Calibration sets its own current limit"
    The routine does not use the current limit you set. It raises the limit to 1600 mA, and drives the motor with
    up to 1250 mA while it measures Kt and KV and with `#Iqoffset` while it aligns the encoder. From firmware 109 it
    puts the limit that was in force back when it ends; firmware 107 and older left 1600 mA in force (known issue
    KI-2).

## 1. Restore the defaults

The EEPROM of a new driver, or of one that ran another motor, can hold values that do not fit: another motor's
parameters, or junk that shows as `-1` in `#Info`. Calibration starts from what is there, so start from the factory
values.

=== "Motor GUI"
    *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Default
    ```

This also sets the hardware version and batch date to factory values, and clears an encoder table and an
anti-cogging set from another motor; note what `#Info` printed if you need them. From firmware 109 the CAN node
ID is kept. [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/) says what else it does.

## 2. Run it

!!! tip "We recommend a Motor GUI preset"
    In Motor GUI's **Presets** tab, apply *Generic motor*, *BLDC motor on Spectral Micro (soft)* before you
    calibrate. It writes a low current limit and soft loops and leaves the resistance, the inductance and the pole
    pairs to the calibration, which measures them, so the motor calibrates safely. Raise the limits and the gains
    from there ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/)). More: [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/).

=== "Motor GUI"
    Start the calibration. The driver enters *Calibration mode* and the GUI shows its log step by step; when it
    finishes, the resistance, inductance and pole pairs it measured, the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the
    flux linkage appear in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Cal
    ```

The LED flashes fast, about 10 times a second, while the routine runs, and the driver prints each step as it
goes. The numbers below are those of one tested motor; yours will differ:

```
----------------
Calibration mode
-----Settings-----
Current loop bandwidth: 160.00Hz
Resistance voltage: 1000mV
Max Power dissipation: 12.00W
Open loop voltage: 5000mV
Open loop Speed: 20.00Rad/s
Phase search voltage: 5000mV
----------------
Magnet test: Passed
Vbus test: Passed
Resistance = 7.026575Ohm
Inductance = 0.001492H
Kp_iq = ...
Ki_iq = ...
Pole pair = 11
Dir = 1
Calibrating angle offset... stage 1/13, sweep point 0
Calibrating angle offset... stage 2/13, sweep point 0
...
Phase order = 2
Phase order is good!
KV is: ...
Kt is: ...
KV runs: ... ... ... ... (same direction within ... %)
Flux linkage is: ...
----------------
Calibration success!
Next, by itself: the encoder table, then anti-cogging (about a minute; keep the shaft free). Everything is saved when they finish (#Encal state, #Cogcal state)
Going to idle!
----------------
```

The `Calibrating angle offset...` lines come every half second while the encoder is aligned, which can take
about 40 seconds; the routine has not stopped.

`#Calonly` runs the same calibration and nothing after it; it ends with `Save config with #Save` instead.

From firmware 110 `#Estop` or `#Close` stops a running calibration; `#Idle` does not. It ends as a failed
calibration (`Calibration failed!`): the motor is released, and the driver is not calibrated until it calibrates
again. After `#Estop`, send `#Clear` first.

On firmware 109 a reset (`#Reset`) was the only clean way over UART: `#Close` switched the mode under the running
calibration and left it half done.

What the steps are:

| Step | What happens | Fails with |
|---|---|---|
| Magnet test | the encoder sees enough field: a magnet is there and close enough. The test says nothing about centring, the gap or the glue | `Magnet test: Failed`: magnet missing, too far, or axially magnetised |
| Vbus test | the supply is within limits | `Vbus test: Failed` |
| Resistance | a rising voltage is put on the windings and the current measured; the motor clicks. The resistance follows from the two | `Resistance test: Failed`: no current flows, a phase is not connected, or the motor is far outside the 2 to 24 Ω range |
| Inductance | a voltage step and the rate at which the current rises give the inductance. Kp_iq and Ki_iq are computed from R, L and the bandwidth | `Inductance test: Failed` |
| Open loop | the stator field is turned at the open-loop speed and the encoder watched: the pole pairs are the ratio of electrical to mechanical turns, and 1 to 49 are accepted. The direction the rotor turned is remembered as the commutation direction (`Commutation dir` in `#Info`); `Dir` is always 1 after a calibration | `Open loop: Failed`, then `The rotor did not follow the open-loop field (pole pairs must come out as 1 to 49).` and `Check the motor's three wires and that the shaft is free.` |
| Phase order | a current command must move the rotor the expected way, and the encoder's zero is aligned to the rotor field (the angle offset, `#Offset`). A motor that does not respond gets a second try at another angle | `Commutation/alignment check failed!`, `Motor did not respond as expected to a current command...` and a line `Spin-confirm delta: … ticks (need > 8192), Vbus: … mV` that says how far the motor turned (half a revolution is needed) and at what voltage |
| Kt, KV, flux linkage | four spins from standstill, about a second each and alternately forward and back; KV is the mean speed per volt available, and the constants follow from it. `KV runs:` in the log shows all four and how far they agree | nothing. `KV runs disagree` is a warning, not a failure: two runs in the same direction differ by more than 5 %. The shaft was not free, or something held it; calibrate again |

!!! note "The measured values are estimates"
    The resistance, the inductance and the motor constants differ a little from one run to the next, and KV, and
    with it Kt and the flux linkage, can be off by a factor of two or three on cheap motors with uneven windings.
    For the loops this does not matter; for a torque estimate in newton-metres, measure Kt yourself.

## What follows the calibration

Half a second after `Calibration success!` of a `#Cal` the driver starts two runs on its own: the encoder table,
then the anti-cogging identification. Keep the shaft free for about a minute more.

When they succeed, everything is saved. A command from a host (a motion command, `#Idle`) stops them; then nothing is
saved, and the calibration is kept only if you `#Save` it.

A host that takes the drive before they start has 3 s: after that the runs are dropped and do not start later. `#Cal`
always runs them; `#Calonly` never does. [Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/) explains both.

!!! warning "Set the current limit before you calibrate"
    The encoder table turns the field with a current of 80 % of the current limit, for about 20 s. Calibration uses
    its own 1600 mA for its steps and puts the limit that was in force back before the encoder table runs. So set
    `#Ilim` for the motor before `#Cal` (known issue KI-19).

## 3. Set the current limit and save

Calibration puts back the current limit that was in force when it started (firmware 107 and older left
1600 mA). If that is not your motor's yet, set it now ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/)), then save. After
`#Cal` the driver saves by itself when the runs succeed; save anyway once they are done, or after `#Calonly`.

=== "Motor GUI"
    Set the current limit in the limits, then **Save**. The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you do.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Ilim 1000
    #Save
    ```

Without it the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. After `#Calonly` the driver is idle. After `#Cal` it
ends the two runs holding the position the shaft reached: `#Idle` releases it. The LED shows normal
operation; `#Info` shows *Calibrated*, the pole pairs, the resistance and inductance, Kt and KV, the phase order
and the commutation direction.

!!! success "Check"
    After a power cycle `#Info` still prints `Calibrated`, and Motor GUI shows *Calibrated*. `Not calibrated`
    means the save did not happen: calibrate and save again.

## When to calibrate again

- After changing the motor, the magnet or the wiring.
- After restoring the defaults.
- After an update from firmware 107 or older to 109, where the motor can turn freely: the older calibration stored
  the resistance and the inductance too low. An assembled SSG-48 keeps its calibration and gets its preset
  ([Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/)).
- After a firmware update that clears the calibration (a release note says so when it does).

A calibration that reports success but a motor that runs badly afterwards usually means the magnet moved on the
shaft between calibration and use: fix the magnet and calibrate again.

## Troubleshooting

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Magnet test: Failed` | no magnet, magnet too far (more than about 1.5 mm), or an axially magnetised magnet |
| `Vbus test: Failed` | supply off, too low, or the cable the wrong way round (if the driver survived it) |
| `Resistance test: Failed`, `Inductance test: Failed` | a phase not connected or shorted; a motor far outside the 2 to 24 Ω range |
| the motor wobbles left and right and the routine fails | one phase is not connected |
| `Open loop: Failed` | the rotor did not follow the field, or the pole pairs came out outside 1 to 49: a phase open, the shaft not free, the open-loop voltage (`#Openv`) too low for a high-resistance motor, the supply's current limit set too low |
| `Commutation/alignment check failed!` | the motor did not respond to the current command: a phase open, `#Iqoffset` set too low, a magnet that slips. Run `#Cal` again. Firmware 101 printed `Phase order is wrong! Switch motor phases and try again!` here; since 105 the wiring is compensated and swapping wires does not help |
| `Cal: not started, the E-stop is latched (#Clear first)`, or `Stopped by an E-stop: #Clear, then calibrate again.` after `Calibration failed!` | an E-stop is latched or ended the calibration: `#Clear`, then `#Cal`; the alignment starts again from its first stage |
| the routine stops in a step and prints nothing more | stop it with `#Close` (firmware 110) or reset the driver (`#Reset`), and try again |
| success, but the LED stays on and no error is reported | `#Info` shows `-1` somewhere: the EEPROM holds a value from an older release ([The check at power-up](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/#the-check-at-power-up)); restore the defaults and calibrate again |
| the resistance, KV or Kt look wrong | the supply was not 24 V, or the motor is one of the uneven ones; see the note above |

Calibration runs over the serial connection only: a terminal, or Motor GUI over the serial adapter, not over CAN.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/ -->

# Encoder table and anti-cogging

Firmware 109 measures two corrections on the drive itself, with nothing but the motor on the bench. The
**encoder table** corrects the small error of the encoder's angle reading. The **anti-cogging** is a current that
cancels the motor's own torque ripple. The same routines run on the sister driver STEPFOC.

After `Calibration success!` of a `#Cal` both run by themselves, and everything is saved when they succeed
([What follows the calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/#what-follows-the-calibration)). `#Calonly` is the calibration
alone. This page explains what they are, how to run them again, and how to check them.

On the Spectral Micro bench (gimbal motor, 2026-11-10) a full `#Cal` measured the encoder table and identified the
anti-cogging, and saved both. Check the result ([Checking them](#checking-them)) before you keep it.

!!! danger "The motor turns"
    Each run turns the motor one revolution forward and one back, slowly. Keep the shaft free: nothing on it and
    nothing it could drive. A mechanism that cannot turn a whole revolution, a gripper's jaws for example, has to
    come off first.

## The encoder table

The magnetic encoder reads the shaft angle with a small error that changes slowly around the turn. The magnet is
never exactly on the axis, and the chip itself is not perfectly linear. On the bench gimbal motor it was 0.50° peak
to peak.

The STEPFOC bench stepper read 0.61 to 0.65° from run to run. Two of its tables agreed within 0.021°.

The commutation multiplies it by the pole pairs. On an 11-pole-pair motor 0.50° spans about 5.5 electrical
degrees. The electrical offset sits near the middle of that span, so the field is a few electrical degrees off at
places. That costs torque and makes the current uneven around the turn.

To measure it, the driver turns the field open loop, one shaft revolution forward and one back at 2048 ticks/s
(about 20 s). A current of 80 % of the current limit holds the rotor to the field.

At each 1/128 of a turn it records how far the encoder's angle is from the field's. Forward and backward are
averaged, so friction, which pulls the rotor behind the field in each direction, cancels. The motor's own pull at
higher orders is left out by keeping only the harmonics 1 to 16 per turn.

![Illustration, not a measurement: friction pulls the forward and the backward pass to either side of the encoder's error, and the motor's own pull adds a fast ripple; their average, kept to the harmonics 1 to 16 per turn, is the table.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/encoder_measurement.svg){ width="800" }
![Illustration, not a measurement: friction pulls the forward and the backward pass to either side of the encoder's error, and the motor's own pull adds a fast ripple; their average, kept to the harmonics 1 to 16 per turn, is the table.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/encoder_measurement_dark.svg){ width="800" }

The result is a table of 128 corrections. From then on the encoder reading is corrected with it. The electrical
offset is moved by the table's mean error, so the commutation stays right.

The plot shows a measured table from the sister driver STEPFOC, which runs the same routine, on its bench
NEMA 17. Its right-hand scale multiplies by the stepper's 50 pole pairs. On an 11-pole-pair motor the same error
is about 4.5 times smaller in electrical degrees.

![Measured with the STEPFOC on its bench NEMA 17: the encoder's error at each 1/128 of a turn, 0.61° peak to peak, about 31° electrical on the right-hand scale for 50 pole pairs (about 7° on an 11-pole-pair motor); the dashed line is its once-per-turn part.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/encoder_table.svg){ width="800" }
![Measured with the STEPFOC on its bench NEMA 17: the encoder's error at each 1/128 of a turn, 0.61° peak to peak, about 31° electrical on the right-hand scale for 50 pole pairs (about 7° on an 11-pole-pair motor); the dashed line is its once-per-turn part.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/encoder_table_dark.svg){ width="800" }

A check of the routine on a simulated 11-pole-pair motor at the Spectral Micro's loop rate took the commutation
error from 30 to 0.4 electrical degrees.

A table over 4° peak to peak, or one that would move the offset by more than 60 electrical degrees, is rejected
as implausible: the magnet is loose or far off its place.

## Anti-cogging

A motor's magnets pull towards the stator's teeth. Errors in the current measurement add a ripple once and twice
per electrical turn.

At low speed both show as a ripple in the speed and the position. Anti-cogging adds a current to the current
setpoint that cancels it: a function of the electrical angle, added in velocity and position modes.

To find it, the driver runs in velocity mode at 1500 ticks/s (parameter 44), one motor revolution forward and one
back. It records the current the velocity loop asks for in 256 bins over the electrical angle. Then it averages
the two directions, each without its mean, so friction drops out.

From that it keeps two forms of the same correction:

- **harmonics** (parameter 37 = 1): the 8 largest of the harmonics 1 to 32 of the electrical angle, each
  a·cos(h·θ) + b·sin(h·θ) in mA;
- **table** (parameter 37 = 2): 256 values in mA over one electrical turn, interpolated between them.

The plot shows both forms on the STEPFOC's bench NEMA 17. Its cogging current was about the size of the Spectral
Micro's bench gimbal motor's (7.1 and 6.8 mA rms); the shape over the turn depends on the motor.

![Measured with the STEPFOC on its bench NEMA 17: the anti-cogging over one electrical turn, identified at 1500 ticks/s before that drive had the encoder table and the zero trim: above, its two forms; below, the current the velocity loop asks for with it off and on.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/anticogging.svg){ width="800" }
![Measured with the STEPFOC on its bench NEMA 17: the anti-cogging over one electrical turn, identified at 1500 ticks/s before that drive had the encoder table and the zero trim: above, its two forms; below, the current the velocity loop asks for with it off and on.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/anticogging_dark.svg){ width="800" }

The identification switches the harmonics on. On the bench gimbal motor it found 6.8 mA rms. Parameter 38 scales
the correction from 0 to 200 % for experiments; 100 % is as identified.

The angle here comes from the encoder alone, without the calibration's offset. The part of the correction that
comes from the current measurement is tied to the motor's electrical angle, though, which the offset defines.
That is one reason `#Cal` identifies the anti-cogging again.

The identification records the current the loops ask for, so it depends a little on the gains. After a large
change of the current or velocity gains, identify it again.

### The current-sense zero trim

The STEPFOC firmware can also correct the current-sense zeros from the anti-cogging's once-per-turn part (the
**zero trim**, 43 = 4 or 5). The Spectral Micro firmware 109 skips that step until the map of its current channels
is measured.

So here `#Cogcal trim` (43 = 4) and 43 = 5 identify like 1 and 2. The state reads 3, never 11 (done without the
trim). The combined runs and the runs after a `#Cal` ask for the trim too, with the same result.

Parameters 62 and 63 hold the 1st harmonic before and after a trim, in 0.1 mA. After a run that asked for the
trim, both read the 1st harmonic of the set found.

The trims (parameters 59 and 60, up to ±60 counts) change only when written. They are saved with the encoder
table and added to the zero the driver measures at every start-up.

Parameter 56 has no effect on the Spectral Micro. It keeps its number so that the two drivers' parameters match.
`#Cal` always runs both corrections, `#Calonly` neither.

## Running them

The driver must be calibrated and without an error. Each run has a UART command and a CAN parameter:

| What | UART | CAN: Send_Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| the encoder table, used at once | `#Encal` | 52 = 1 |
| the encoder table, used and saved | `#Encal save` | 52 = 2 |
| the encoder table, then the anti-cogging, then save all | `#Encal all` | 52 = 3, or 43 = 3 |
| the anti-cogging, switched on | `#Cogcal` | 43 = 1 |
| the anti-cogging, switched on and saved | `#Cogcal save` | 43 = 2 |
| stop a run | `#Encal stop`, `#Cogcal stop` | 52 = 0, 43 = 0 |

`#Encal stop` does not stop the anti-cogging part of a combined run (`#Encal all`). `#Cogcal stop` stops a run
in either part, and so do 52 = 0 and 43 = 0 over CAN.

1. Make sure the shaft is free: nothing on it and nothing it could drive.
2. Send the run's command from the table, on the UART or over CAN.
3. Send nothing else while the motor turns, one revolution forward and one back for each run.
4. Read the result with `#Encal state` or `#Cogcal state`, or parameter 52 or 43 over CAN.

!!! success "Check"
    The state reads 3, done. The motor holds the position the shaft reached. Any other state is in the table
    "When a run fails" under [Checking them](#checking-them).

Both runs keep the CAN watchdog fed while they go, and end by holding the position the shaft reached. They stop at
once when a host sends a command (a motion command, Idle) or an error comes up. Nothing is saved then.

While a run turns the motor a capture is not armed. During the anti-cogging run parameters 34 and 35 refuse a
write: the runs use the capture's memory and the histogram.

A save from a run is the whole configuration, as `#Save` writes it. After a change of the motor, the magnet or
its position, run the encoder table and the anti-cogging again, in that order, or calibrate again.

Two guards keep a correction from running on the wrong data:

- parameter 37 refuses 1 or 2 while no set is stored for that form;
- an encoder table measured on its own (52 = 1 or 2) switches an anti-cogging set from before off, because that
  set was found on the uncorrected encoder. The anti-cogging state then reads 10 until it is identified again.

## Checking them

`#Info` ends with what is in force:

```
In force:
  encoder table: on, error 0.61 deg p-p
  anti-cogging: on (harmonics), saved
  current-sense zero trim: 0 / 0 counts
  delay compensation: 234 us
  speed estimate: direct PLL, 100 Hz
  input filter: off; integral deadband: off
```

The example shows the defaults, with an example encoder error. While a run goes, a line
`running: encoder table` or `running: anti-cogging identification` follows.

`#Encal state` and `#Cogcal state` print one run's state without starting it. After a finished identification
(state 3) it also lists the harmonics. Parameter 43 gives the same state over CAN.

Over CAN the same is in the parameters (the [parameter table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#every-parameter)):

| Parameter | What it tells | On the bench gimbal motor |
|---|---|---|
| 52 | the encoder table's state: 3 done, 4 aborted, 5 error or not calibrated, 6 the rotor did not follow, 7 rejected | 3 |
| 54 | the table's error peak to peak, 0.01° of the shaft | 50 (0.50°) |
| 55 | the amplitude of its once-per-turn part, 0.01° of the shaft | |
| 57 | how far the last table moved the electrical offset, 0.1° electrical | |
| 43 | the anti-cogging state: 3 done, 6 the shaft did not turn | 3 |
| 45 | the cogging current found, 0.1 mA rms | 68 (6.8 mA) |
| 79 | the bits of what is in force, see [What is in force](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#what-is-in-force-parameter-79) | |

Send_Buffer_Read reads the corrections themselves: kind 4 the encoder table (128 values in 1/16 count), kind 2
the harmonics, kind 3 the anti-cogging table ([Respond_Buffer_Data](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#respond_buffer_data)).

A capture of the speed while the motor turns slowly, with the anti-cogging off and on
([Status and diagnostics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/diagnostics/#a-capture)), shows whether it helps on your motor.

On the STEPFOC's bench NEMA 17 the speed ripple that repeats with the angle was 1.2 to 2 times smaller with the
anti-cogging on, at 1500 to 6000 ticks/s. The Spectral Micro has not been measured this way yet.

![Measured with the STEPFOC: the speed of its bench NEMA 17 turning at 6000 ticks/s, minus its mean, before that drive had the encoder table and the zero trim: with the anti-cogging on, the part that repeats with the angle is about half as large.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/anticogging_speed.svg){ width="800" }
![Measured with the STEPFOC: the speed of its bench NEMA 17 turning at 6000 ticks/s, minus its mean, before that drive had the encoder table and the zero trim: with the anti-cogging on, the part that repeats with the angle is about half as large.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/anti-cogging/anticogging_speed_dark.svg){ width="800" }

When a run fails:

| State | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 52 = 6, 43 = 6 | the rotor did not follow: the shaft is blocked, or the current is too low to turn it | free the shaft; for the encoder table raise the current limit (it uses 80 % of it) |
| 52 = 5, 43 = 5 | the driver was in error or is not calibrated | `#Error`, clear it, calibrate |
| 52 = 4, 43 = 4 | a command came first | run it again and send nothing meanwhile |
| 52 = 7 | the table is implausible | check the magnet: glued, centred, at the right distance ([The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/)), then calibrate |
| 43 = 8 | the encoder table of a combined run failed | parameter 52 says why |

When a run fails after a `#Cal`, the calibration itself is still good: save it with `#Save`.

## Switching them off

| | UART | CAN: Send_Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| the encoder table off / on | `#Encal off`, `#Encal on` | 53 = 0, 53 = 1 |
| the anti-cogging off, harmonics, table | `#Par 37,0`, `#Par 37,1`, `#Par 37,2` | 37 = 0, 1, 2 |
| how much of the anti-cogging | `#Par 38,` and the percentage | 38 = 0 to 200 (%) |

`#Save` keeps the switches with the corrections. `#Default` clears both corrections and the trims.

!!! note "STEPFOC"
    The STEPFOC firmware 109 has the same encoder table and anti-cogging, and the current-sense zero trim as
    well. Its [manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/) says more.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/ -->

# Current limit and loop tuning

Calibration leaves the driver with current loop gains computed for your motor and with conservative velocity and
position gains. Two things remain: the current limit, which you must set for your motor, and the loop gains, which
you tune if the defaults do not suit it.

Motor GUI shows the motor's response on its plots while you change a gain, which is what makes tuning quick.

## The current limit

Set the current limit to the rated phase current of your motor in mA. Calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its
steps and, from firmware 109, puts your limit back when it ends (107 and older left 1600 mA: set it again after
calibrating there).

The factory default (`#Default`) of 1000 mA suits the gimbal motors in
[Tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/tested-motors/); a motor rated for more can go up to the driver's 2800 mA.

`#Ilim` clamps the limit to 2800 mA; from firmware 109 Send_Limits over CAN does too. The firmware does not trip on
phase current by itself; the MOSFET driver's hardware protection only catches a hard fault. A limit above the motor's
rating overheats the motor.

=== "Motor GUI"
    In the limits set the current limit, then **Save**.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Ilim 1500
    #Save
    ```

Crunching and whining sounds at speed usually mean the current limit, or the current loop gains, are too high.

## The loops

![The position loop commands the velocity loop, which commands the current loop.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/cascadeloop.webp){ width="800" }

Tune from the inside out: the current loop first, then velocity, then position. Before you start:

- The motor must be calibrated and without active errors; the driver refuses the control modes otherwise.
- Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft. A loop that oscillates can shake a loose motor off the table.
- If the defaults oscillate, lower all gains until the motor is quiet, then raise them one at a time in small steps.

=== "Motor GUI"
    The gains are in the settings: change one, *Apply gains*, command a move with the jog controls and read the
    response on the plots. *Apply preset* loads a starting set for a kind of motor: a product preset writes its
    own current and velocity gains; the *Generic motor* presets set soft limits and velocity gains and leave the
    current gains to `#Cbw` and the calibration. Apply a preset before you calibrate, so that the calibration
    computes the current gains.
    **Save** when you are done.

=== "Terminal"
    Each gain is a command: `#Kpiq 0.5`, `#Kpv 0.02`, …, then `#Save`. Command a move with `#Iq`, `#V` or `#P`
    and judge the response by ear and by `#Cyc 20`, which streams position, speed and current.

### The current loop

The current loop is a PI controller that turns a current request into a voltage.

Its gains `Kpiq` and `Kiiq` follow from the motor's resistance R, its inductance L (both measured by calibration) and
one number, the bandwidth: Kpiq ≈ ω·L and Kiiq = ω·R·T, with ω = 2π × the bandwidth and T the 200 µs control period
(Kiiq is applied once per control loop).

The PI then cancels the coil's own lag, and the current follows a request like a first-order filter at that bandwidth.
Calibration computes them this way at 160 Hz, the default from firmware 109; so does setting the bandwidth:

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Cbw 200          new gains at once from R and L; it prints them
    #Save             keeps the gains (the bandwidth itself is 160 again after a power cycle)
    ```

=== "CAN"
    Send_Parameter(49, 200), then Send_Save_config. Reading parameter 49 gives the bandwidth the gains in force
    amount to with the R and L in force.

The bandwidth can be 10 to 500 Hz (a tenth of the 5000 Hz control loop). A higher one follows a request and
rejects a disturbance faster, and is louder. Gains set by hand with `#Kpiq` and `#Kiiq` work too; parameter 49
then tells which bandwidth they amount to.

!!! note "Drives calibrated with older firmware"
    Firmware 107 and older computed the gains for 500 Hz on the 5000 Hz loop, which is fast for that loop rate.
    Their saved gains stay as they are after an update to 109: parameter 49 reads about 500 Hz until the drive is
    calibrated again. Calibrate again after the update where the motor can turn freely. A calibration made with
    107 or older stored the resistance about 10 % and the inductance about 45 % too low, so `#Cbw` on the old
    values gives gains for a lower bandwidth than it names (on an SSG-48 apply its preset instead, which writes
    the gains). 160 Hz is the default; on the gimbal-motor bench 300 Hz settled a speed step 3.6 times faster at the
    same holding noise, and 500 Hz added half again the current noise. The SSG-48 preset sets 300 Hz. See
    [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/).

Test with a current setpoint of a few hundred mA (*Jog current*, or `#Iq 300`): the motor should push with a
steady, quiet torque. Keep the current well under the limit.

### The velocity loop

1. Raise `Kpv` until the motor oscillates at a steady speed command, then back off 20 %.
2. Raise `Kiv` slowly until it oscillates, then back off a little. `Kiv` is an integrator: too much makes the
   motor unstable, none leaves a steady-state error.
3. Test with a speed setpoint (*Jog velocity*, or `#V 20000`; 16384 ticks per second is one revolution per
   second) and with different speeds.

### The position loop

1. Raise `Kpp` until the motor overshoots or oscillates when it reaches a target, then back off.
2. Test with a position step (*Jog position*, or `#P 16384` and `#P 0`): one revolution and back. The response
   should be quick, without overshoot; the plot shows both.

### Testing

Run the motor over the whole range of speeds and loads it will see, with a load if you can, and adjust. Then save.

## The speed estimate

The velocity loop needs the speed, which the driver estimates from the encoder count. From firmware 109 parameter
50 picks how:

| Parameter 50 | Estimate | How it behaves |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | moving average of the last 20 count differences | about 2 ms late, in steps of 250 ticks/s: the estimate of every release before |
| 1 | PLL, the speed is its integrator | smooth, a little late |
| 2 (default) | direct PLL, integrator plus the proportional term | almost no lag, a little more noise |

Both PLLs are critically damped at the natural frequency of parameter 51, 100 Hz by default (10 to 250 Hz). The
lag of the moving average is what limits the velocity gain.

On the gimbal-motor bench the direct PLL at 100 Hz allowed twice the `Kpv` of the moving average before the motor
vibrated (0.11 against 0.056), lowered the speed ripple 1.3 to 3.4 times between 1500 and 48000 ticks/s, and cut the
overshoot of a speed step from about 67 % to 12 % at the same gains.

At 60 Hz it overshot more, at 200 Hz it held with more current noise. Calibration and the gripper's stop detection
always use the moving average. Neither parameter is kept by Save. The speed in Respond_data_pack_1 and
Send_Respond_Encoder_data, the watchdog descend and the capture is the picked estimate.

## Commutation delay compensation

The voltage a control loop sets reaches the motor later than the angle it was computed from was read: the rest of
the loop, the wait for the PWM update and half a control period.

By then the rotor has turned on, and the voltage lands a little behind the angle it was meant for. Parameter 64 turns
the output voltage forward by the angle the rotor covers in that delay, in the closed-loop modes above 100 ticks/s; 1
to 500 µs are accepted.

The default is 234 µs, the Spectral Micro's own delay measured on the bench: 20 points between 24000 and 120000
ticks/s gave one delay within 2 to 4 % of theory at every speed.

Without it the field lags about 6° electrical at 120000 ticks/s. The delay belongs to the driver's timing, not to the
motor, so it suits any motor; 0 switches it off. It is not kept by Save.

## The finer points of the velocity loop

Two settings for special cases, both off by default and not kept by Save; both were tested on the STEPFOC bench:

- **Position input filter**, parameter 74 (Hz, 0 to 200). A host that sends positions at a fixed rate sends a
  staircase; without the speed the steps are all the loops see. The filter turns the staircase into a smooth path
  and makes its own speed from it, in position and PD modes. Use it only for a host that sends positions
  **without** the speed feedforward, at about the host's rate ÷ 12 (8 Hz for 100 Hz); with a host that sends the
  speed it makes the tracking worse.
- **Velocity-integral deadband**, parameter 75 (ticks, 0 to 2000). In position mode the velocity integral sees the
  position error less this band, so a holding motor stops pushing against a small error it cannot correct. It
  trades accuracy for holding current.

## Impedance (PD) mode

![The impedance loop: a spring (KP) and a damper (KD) around the position setpoint, plus a current feedforward.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/PDloop.webp){ width="800" }

In PD mode the motor behaves like a spring and a damper: the torque is `KP × (setpoint − position) + KD × (speed
setpoint − speed) + feedforward current`.

Set `KP` and `KD` (the gains, or `#KP`, `#KD`, or Send_PD_Gains), then command with `#PD`, `#PDV` and `#PDI` or
Send_data_pack_PD. Start with a small `KP` and `KD` of 0, raise `KP` until the motor holds position firmly, then add
`KD` until it stops ringing. The [theory corner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/theory/) explains the loop.

## Limits

- The velocity limit (`#Vlimit`) clamps the speed the loops may command, in encoder ticks per second. A rough
  maximum for your motor is 0.8 × Vbus × KV × 16384 / 60 ticks per second, with KV from calibration.
- The voltage limit (`#Vlim`) clamps the voltage of the current loops in mV; 0 uses the supply voltage.
- `#Rstint 1` resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which avoids windup when a program sends one setpoint
  after another with large steps.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/ -->

# Saving the configuration

Nothing you set survives a power cycle until you save it.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Save**. The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you do.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Save
    ```

Saving writes the configuration to the EEPROM: the motor parameters and the calibration, every gain and limit,
the CAN node ID, the heartbeat and watchdog settings, the thermistor and LED settings, the temperature and voltage
limits and the gripper flag.

From firmware 109 also the tool id and the watchdog fallback, the anti-cogging set with its mode and scale, and the
encoder table with its on/off switch, parameter 56 and the current-sense zero trims. From firmware 110 also the idle
behaviour (`#Brake`, Send_Settings or parameter 18).

Over CAN, Send_Save_config does the same. Saving also copies the node ID into the bootloader's board ID
([The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/the-bootloader/#the-board-id)). Save after calibration, after tuning, and after
changing the node ID.

!!! warning "Set the current limit before you save a calibration"
    Firmware 107 and older left the current limit at 1600 mA after a calibration, and a save stored it. From
    firmware 109 calibration puts the limit that was in force back; check that it suits your motor (`#Ilim`)
    before you save.

## What is not saved

These settings are lost at a power cycle, whatever you save. The driver starts with the values in the
[Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/defaults/) reference:

- the calibration settings `#Cbw` (160 Hz; the gains it computed are kept), `#Resv`, `#Calpwr`, `#Openv`,
  `#Opens`, `#Vp` and `#Iqoffset`: set them again before each calibration that needs other values;
- the parameters of firmware 109 that tune the loops: the speed estimate (the direct PLL at 100 Hz), the
  commutation delay compensation (234 µs), the sin/cos table (off), the position input filter and the velocity-integral deadband
  (off), the anti-cogging identification speed, the d-axis current, and the capture and histogram settings. The
  [parameter table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#every-parameter) says for every parameter whether it is kept;
- the cyclic output (`#Cyc`, `#Cyca`);
- the serial number. Saving writes it, but the firmware does not read it back at power-up: after a power cycle
  the driver reports 1, and the next save writes that 1 over the stored number.

## The defaults

=== "Motor GUI"
    *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Default
    ```

Restoring the defaults writes the factory values to the EEPROM and loads them. It erases the calibration (the
driver reports *Not calibrated*), clears the gripper flag, the heartbeat rate and the watchdog, sets the hardware
version to 1 and the batch date to 24092024, and stores 1111 as the serial number.

From firmware 109 it also clears the tool id, the watchdog fallback, the anti-cogging set, the encoder table and its
zero trims, and sets parameter 56 back to 0. From firmware 110 it also sets the idle behaviour back to coasting.

The CAN node ID is kept from firmware 109 (it is 0 only when no valid ID is stored); firmware 107 and older set it
to 0.

Note what the driver reports before you use it. The values are listed in the [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/defaults/)
reference.

Use it before the first calibration of a motor, after a firmware update when the driver behaves oddly, and when
the state shows nonsense values (a `-1` where a number should be).

## The check at power-up

The configuration lives in an EEPROM chip on the board (a 24C16, 2 KB), apart from the firmware: flashing a new
firmware never touches it, and only the firmware's check at power-up decides to reset a part of it. Since
firmware 106 the saved configuration is in blocks, each with its own checksum; firmware 109 adds three:

| Block | Bytes | Checksum at | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| calibration | 60-188, reserved 204-228 | 200 | the motor's resistance, inductance, pole pairs, phase order, direction, angle offset, Kt, KV and the current loop gains |
| settings 1 | 44-180 | 196 | the other gains, the limits, the node ID, the watchdog, the heartbeat and the flags |
| settings 2 (109) | 260-312 | 256 | tool id, watchdog fallback, the product stamp, the calibration ID, from 110 the idle behaviour; reserved slots |
| anti-cogging (109) | 324-879 | 320 | the harmonics, the table, mode and scale |
| encoder table (109) | 884-1147 | 880 | the table, its on/off switch, parameter 56, the current-sense zero trims |

At power-up the driver checks each. A block that fails, after a power loss during a save for instance, is replaced
by its factory values without a message, and the others are kept.

A failed settings block gives the default gains and limits (from firmware 109 the node ID stays, if it was valid);
a failed calibration block leaves the driver *Not calibrated*.

The new blocks need the chip's upper banks; on a smaller chip they keep their defaults in RAM and are not saved, which
`#Info` says (`Settings block 2: not available`, `block 3 not available`).

Going back to an older firmware is safe: the first two blocks are unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything
from byte 256 on. [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/) says what changes when you update.

A board that comes from a release before 106 has no checksums yet: the driver keeps its values once and seals
them; from firmware 109 every board that was ever saved is trusted this way.

A value that was already wrong (a `-1` in `#Info`, for instance) then stays, and `#Default` with a new calibration is
the fix. A blank EEPROM gets the defaults.

## What the driver reports

- `#Info` prints the identity and the motor: hardware version, batch date, firmware version, CAN ID, whether the
  motor is calibrated, temperature, supply voltage, the phase order and direction, the pole pairs, resistance,
  inductance, Kt and KV, and from firmware 109 the build, the board ID and the calibration ID, the tool id, the
  watchdog, the EEPROM blocks and, at its end, what is in force;
- `#SERNUM` prints the serial number;
- `#Param` the gains and limits;
- `#Error` the active errors.

They are the first thing to look at when something is off, and the thing to copy into a bug report.
[Status and diagnostics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/diagnostics/) explains the new lines.


---

# Operation

How a calibrated driver is used: the control modes and what each one does, the two ways to talk to the driver and
the two tools on top of them, what happens when something goes wrong, and gripper mode.

## In this chapter

- [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/)
- [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/uart/)
- [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/can/)
- [The watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/watchdog/): what the driver does when the host stops talking
- [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/python/)
- [Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/motor-gui/)
- [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/)
- [Sound](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/sound/): tones, tunes and recorded sound through the motor
- [Status and diagnostics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/diagnostics/): what is in force, the identity, telemetry, captures
- [Gripper mode](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/)

The exact layout of every message and command is in the [API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/).
