<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/ -->

# Errors and recovery

When the driver detects a fault it disables the motor, goes to idle, turns the status LED on steadily and sets
the error bit in every CAN frame it sends. A disabled motor coasts, also when `#Brake 1` is set. The driver stays
there until the error is cleared.

## Seeing the error

- **The LED**: on and not flashing means error mode (or not calibrated). Three short flashes and a pause is
  normal operation; fast flashing, about 10 times a second, is calibration.
- **`#Error`** prints `In error state!` or `No errors!`, followed by one line per active error.
- **Send_Respond_State_of_Errors** returns every flag as a bit; **the error bit** of any frame says whether there
  is one.

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Fast flashing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |

In error mode the LED does not flash: it stays on, as in the photo on the right.

## The errors

| Error | `#Error` line | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vbus | `Vbus error` | the supply voltage is below 9 V or above `#Vmax` (29 V after `#Default`). From firmware 109 a low voltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, while the supply ramps up | check the supply and the cable; a decelerating motor can push the voltage up |
| Encoder | `Encoder error` | the magnet is not detected or the reading is invalid | magnet distance and type, see [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/) |
| Driver | `Drv error`, and `FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault` while the fault lasts (firmware 107 and older printed `FAULT pin is HIGH`) | the MOSFET driver's own protection tripped: undervoltage, thermal shutdown or overcurrent | lower the current limit, cool the driver, check for a short between the motor leads |
| Velocity | `Velocity error` | the measured speed exceeded 20,000,000 ticks/s (about 1220 revolutions per second), a fixed limit that `#Vlimit` does not change | a runaway or an encoder fault: check the magnet and the encoder, see [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/04-mounting/magnet/) |
| Temperature | `Temp error` | the thermistor reads more than `#Tlim` (75 °C by default) or less than −20 °C, with `#Term 1` | let the motor cool; lower the current limit |
| E-stop | `Received ESTOP command` | Send_ESTOP was received, or from firmware 110 `#Estop` over UART | clear it when it is safe |
| Watchdog | `Watchdog error` | no motion command or answered request over CAN within the watchdog time (Send_Watchdog); what the motor does then is the watchdog's action, see [The watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/watchdog/) | the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear. See [The watchdog](#the-watchdog) |
| Wrong product | `Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)` | from firmware 109: this board was calibrated by the other product (a STEPFOC firmware on a Spectral Micro, or the other way round), so the firmware drives nothing ([The product lock](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/diagnostics/#the-product-lock)) | flash the right firmware; it does not clear otherwise |
| Not calibrated | `Not calibrated` | the motor has not been calibrated since `#Default`, or the EEPROM is invalid | run `#Cal` and `#Save` |
| Current | `Current error` | reserved; this firmware never raises it | — |

## Clearing

`#Clear` or Send_Clear_Error clears the flags and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes
straight back: a Vbus error at 2 V stays until the supply is right; once the supply is 24 V, one `#Clear` returns
the driver to normal operation.

The calibration error clears only by calibrating (or, for a motor you know is calibrated, `#Calibrated 1`).

## The watchdog

The watchdog is set with Send_Watchdog over CAN, or with parameters 6 (time) and 7 (action): over UART,
`#Par 6,<ms>` and `#Par 7,<action>`. It counts the motion commands (Send_data_pack_1, Send_data_pack_PD, Send_gripper_data_pack) and the requests
the driver answers (the Send_Respond_ remote frames, Send_Get_Parameter, Send_Buffer_Read).

Other CAN frames and UART commands do not reset it. Send_Save_config keeps it over a power cycle, like the heartbeat
interval. What the driver does when it runs out is the watchdog's action ([The watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/watchdog/)).

A driver with a saved watchdog that is used over UART only, or by a host that sends no motion command, raises a
watchdog error each time the watchdog time runs out, also right after `#Clear`.

To turn it off, send Send_Watchdog with 0 and then Send_Save_config over CAN. Over UART, `#Par 6,0` and then `#Save`
do the same; nothing else is changed.

## When the driver does not answer

- No LED at all: no power. Check DC+ and DC− and the cable orientation.
- LED on, no answer on UART: the baud rate (256000), TX and RX crossed, the adapter's port.
- No answer on CAN: the node ID, the termination (about 60 Ω across the bus, unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter.
- `#Info` shows `-1` or nonsense: the EEPROM holds values the firmware does not expect, usually from an older
  release (see [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/#the-check-at-power-up)); `#Default`, then
  calibrate again.

[Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/) goes through the symptoms one by one.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/diagnostics/ -->

# Status and diagnostics

What the driver tells about itself, from firmware 109: what is in force, who it is, its state in one frame, how
long its control loop takes, and recordings of its own signals made inside the control loop. The error flags and
what to do about each are on [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/).

## What is in force

`#Info` ends with the section `In force:`, and parameter 79 holds the same as bits
([What is in force: parameter 79](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#what-is-in-force-parameter-79)):

| Line | Says |
|---|---|
| `encoder table:` | `on, error … deg p-p`, `measured, off` or `not measured` ([Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/)) |
| `anti-cogging:` | `on (harmonics)`, `on (table)`, `identified, off` or `not identified`, and `, saved` when it is the saved set |
| `current-sense zero trim:` | the two trims in counts, and whether the zero measured with the bridge switching is in use |
| `delay compensation:` | the commutation delay in µs, or `off` ([Commutation delay compensation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/#commutation-delay-compensation)) |
| `speed estimate:` | `moving average`, `PLL, … Hz` or `direct PLL, … Hz` ([The speed estimate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/#the-speed-estimate)) |
| `input filter:`, `integral deadband:` | parameters 74 and 75, or `off` |
| `running:` | only while one runs: `calibration`, `encoder table`, `anti-cogging identification`, or `the runs after the calibration` |

Before that section `#Info` prints, beside what it printed before:

- `Build:` the git commit the firmware was built from, 7 hex digits, with a `+` when it was built with
  uncommitted changes. `Board ID:` this board, 8 hex digits made from the chip's unique number; it never changes,
  and it is not the bootloader's board ID (0 to 13). `Calibration ID:` a new number at every successful
  calibration, kept by Save; `00000000` before the first. Over CAN they are parameters 84, 86 and 87; parameter
  85 is the build time in Unix seconds.
- `CAN RX overruns` and `CAN TX dropped`: frames the driver lost because its receive buffer was full, and answers
  it gave up after waiting 1 ms for a free transmit mailbox. Both should stay 0; they count from power-up. From
  firmware 109 the CAN controller passes only the frames addressed to the driver's own node ID, and the driver
  sends from all three transmit mailboxes, so a busy bus costs it less.
- `Product:` this firmware, Spectral Micro.
- `Current sense zero:` the zeros in use, in ADC counts from 2048, measured at start-up with the bridge off (one
  count is about 1.6 mA), and what the second measurement with the bridge switching found. On the bench the zeros
  were −8 and −7 counts, and the current read 3.9 mA with nothing flowing, where it read −20 to +19 mA before. A zero more than 200
  counts from 2048 is not trusted: the driver then uses 2048 and says `not measured or out of range`.
  The current sensors need the motor supply. If the driver starts without it (USB plugged in before the supply),
  it waits up to half a second for the supply, then uses 2048 and says
  `no motor supply at start-up: 2048 used; measured once the supply is there`. When the supply comes, the driver
  measures the zero by itself at rest, coasting for about 100 ms even if it is set to brake, and the line shows the
  new zeros. The Vbus error the late supply latched stays until `#Clear`.
- `Tool ID`, `Watchdog: … ms, action …, fallback …`, `Settings block 2: ok` and `Anti-cogging: …, scale … %` with
  whether it is saved.

## Who the drive is: the identity frame

Send_Respond_Identity (ID 39, a remote frame) answers with the product (1 STEPFOC, 2 Spectral Micro), the tool id,
the firmware release, the hardware version, the pole pairs, whether it is calibrated, and eight flags: set up as
a gripper, brakes in idle, coils reversed, settings block 2 available, wrong product, current-sense zero measured,
anti-cogging saved, switching zero in use ([Send_Respond_Identity](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/status/#send_respond_identity)).

A host can read it before it commands or flashes a drive, to know it talks to the drive it expects.

The **tool id** says what the drive is built into:

- 0: none (a joint or a bare driver);
- 1: an SSG-48;
- 11 to 33: an MSG (the tens digit the rail, 1 = 100, 2 = 150, 3 = 200 mm; the units digit the stepper, 1 = 21.5,
  2 = 40, 3 = 60 mm);
- 200 to 254: your own tools.

Set it with `#Tool` or parameter 1 and save.

## Everything at once: telemetry

Send_Respond_Telemetry (ID 40, a remote frame) answers with the temperature, the supply voltage, both error bytes
and the current, all from the same moment: one request instead of four, for a host that watches many drives
([Send_Respond_Telemetry](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/status/#send_respond_telemetry)).

## The product lock

STEPFOC and the Spectral Micro use the same bootloader and the same file name for their firmware, and each
firmware drives the other board wrongly: the Spectral Micro firmware on a STEPFOC drove a coil at about 1.7 A in
every mode on the bench.

From firmware 109 a board remembers which product calibrated it, a stamp in the EEPROM written at the first start-up
of a calibrated board and at every save.

A firmware that finds the other product's stamp, or no stamp but a calibration its own product cannot make (the
Spectral Micro firmware treats 50 pole pairs or more as a STEPFOC calibration), reads and writes nothing more, drives
no pin (its gate driver is enabled only after the check) and starts no control loop.

It stays reachable: it reports an error, `Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)` in `#Error`, the
`wrong_product` bit in the error state and the identity, and a warning in `#Info`. Flash the right firmware and the
board runs as before; nothing was written.

`#Product` shows the stamp. On a board the rule misjudges, `#Product claim` stamps it as this product and
`#Product clear` removes the stamp; power-cycle after either. Both are UART commands only.

## How long the control loop takes

The control loop runs every 200 µs (5000 Hz) and has to finish inside that. `#Info` prints the last loop's time.
On the bench an early build of firmware 109 took about 80 µs of the 200; anti-cogging and the commutation delay
compensation each add some 10 µs (measured on STEPFOC).

The section timing and the register fast paths of the STEPFOC firmware (its parameters 66 to 72) are not in the
Spectral Micro firmware.

## A capture

The capture records three signals inside the control loop, sample by sample, 1024 samples per channel: what the
loop saw and did, which a host polling over the bus cannot see. Parameters 24 to 33 set it up and report on it,
Send_Buffer_Read with kind 0 reads it ([Reading the capture](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#reading-the-capture);
the signals are listed under [Capture and histogram](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#capture-and-histogram)).

A step response, 1024 samples of speed, current and position error, one every 2 loops (0.41 s):

```python
import time
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral

comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

def read_all(seconds):
    end = time.time() + seconds
    while time.time() < end:
        message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.01)
        if message is not None:
            motor.UnpackData(message, ids)

for number, value in ((24, 4), (25, 1), (26, 7), (27, 2), (28, 1)):
    motor.Send_Parameter(number, value)     # A speed, B Iq, C position error; every 2nd loop; start now
motor.Send_data_pack_1(1000, 0, 0)          # the step: to position 1000
read_all(0.5)
motor.Send_Get_Parameter(32)                # how many samples
read_all(0.1)
count = motor.parameters.get(32, 0)
motor.Send_Buffer_Read(0, 0, count)         # kind 0, from sample 0
read_all(3.0)
for i in sorted(motor.capture):
    speed, iq, position_error = motor.capture[i]
    print(i, speed, iq, position_error)
```

Trigger 2 records up to an error instead: armed with a pre-trigger, it keeps the moments before a trip, the
watchdog's included, and the time after it. The capture calls (`Send_Parameter`, `Send_Get_Parameter`,
`Send_Buffer_Read`) need the Spectral-BLDC library 1.21 or newer.

## Memory

The drive's microcontroller has 128 KB of flash, of which the bootloader takes 12 KB, and 20 KB of RAM. Firmware
109 uses about 91.5 % of the 116 KB application flash and 65 % of the RAM for fixed data, which leaves about
7 KB for the stack and the heap.

Parameter 83 (`#Par 83`, or Send_Get_Parameter(83)) is the margin check: the bytes of that RAM the stack has never
reached since start-up. The stack needs about 1.5 to 2 KB; read parameter 83 after the drive has run its hardest work
(a calibration, the encoder table, the anti-cogging, sound) and see that plenty is left.

## A histogram

The histogram adds one signal into 256 bins over the electrical angle or over one motor turn, every control loop,
until it is stopped or a bin holds 65535 samples (about an hour): the mean per bin shows what repeats with the
angle, such as the cogging current at a steady speed.

Parameter 35 picks the signal, 34 starts it (1 electrical angle, 2 motor turn) and stops it (0), 36 counts the
samples, and Send_Buffer_Read with kind 1 reads the count and the sum of each bin. The anti-cogging identification
uses it the same way.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/sound/ -->

# Sound

From firmware 109 the driver plays sound through its motor: tones, chords, tunes from a queue it plays by itself,
and recorded sound such as speech. A current at an audio frequency in the windings makes a small force at that
frequency, and the motor, and above all whatever it is fixed to, radiate it as sound.

## How it works

- **Where:** the driver adds the sound to its output voltage, after the current loop. By default it goes on the q
  axis (parameter 82 = 1), where it makes torque: the rotor rocks at the tone's pitch. On the bench that was much
  louder than the d axis (82 = 0), which makes no torque at all.
- **When:** only while the driver holds or moves: position, velocity, current or PD mode. Idle, or any error,
  stops all sound. A joint keeps holding its pose while it plays.
- **Tones:** up to 4 at once (channels 0 to 3), a chord on one motor, each with its own pitch, loudness and length.
- **Loudness** is given as a current, in mA. The coil's impedance rises with the pitch (√(R² + (2πfL)²), from the
  motor's R and L), so the same voltage would sound much quieter high than low; the driver turns the current into
  the voltage that pitch needs, and a note is as loud low as high.
- **Pitch:** 20 Hz up to just below 2500 Hz, half the 5000 Hz control loop. Tones are clean up to about a third of
  the loop rate; melodies sit well between C4 and C6 (262 to 1047 Hz).
- **The queue:** 31 events, each setting one channel's pitch and loudness and then waiting. The control loop plays
  them with loop-exact timing, so the host's own timing never reaches the music: it loads the queue and starts it.
- **Samples:** recorded sound, 8 bits, played from a 1024-place buffer at a rate the host sets, up to the loop
  rate. Speech comes through recognisable but muffled: the telephone band reaches 3400 Hz, the motor 2.5 kHz.
- **The cap:** all sound together is limited to the voltage of parameter 81, 2000 mV by default; 0 refuses sound.
  On a gimbal motor's high resistance the cap comes early: 250 mA in a 7 Ω coil already takes 1.75 V. None of the
  sound settings is saved.

## A tone over UART

```
#Tone 440,250,1000      440 Hz, 250 mA, 1000 ms
#Tone 880,200,0         until stopped
#Tone off               stops all sound
```

From idle, a calibrated driver first holds the position it is at and says so (`Holding the position while it
plays (#Idle releases it)`); `#Idle` releases it afterwards. Left out, the loudness is 200 mA and the length
500 ms.

`Tone: not played` means the driver is not calibrated or in an error, the pitch is outside 20 Hz to half the loop
rate, or parameter 81 is 0.

## Over CAN and from Python

Send_Sound (ID 44) carries every operation: a tone now, an event for the queue, play the queue, play the samples,
stop. Send_Sound_Samples (ID 45) fills the sample buffer ([Sound](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/sound/) in the CAN
reference). The Python calls below need the Spectral-BLDC library 1.21 or newer, as does its `music` module (note
names, ringtone melodies, MIDI files, WAV files).

Over CAN the host makes the driver hold first, for example with a position frame to where the motor is:

```python
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
from Spectral_BLDC import music

comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

def read_answers(seconds=0.1):
    message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=seconds)
    while message is not None:
        motor.UnpackData(message, ids)
        message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.005)

motor.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()                # where the motor is
read_answers()
motor.Send_data_pack_1(motor.position, 0, 0)     # hold it there
read_answers()

motor.Send_Tone(440, current_mA=250, duration_ms=1000)        # one tone
for channel, note in enumerate(('C4', 'E4', 'G4')):            # a chord: three channels at once
    motor.Send_Tone(music.note_hz(note), current_mA=200, duration_ms=1500, channel=channel)
```

A tune goes into the queue and plays by itself. A melody becomes two events per note (the note, then a short
silence, so repeated notes are heard as two), so up to 15 notes fit at once:

```python
name, melody = music.parse_rtttl('scale:d=8,o=5,b=120:c,d,e,f,g,a,b,c6')
for channel, freq, current, wait in music.melody_events(melody, current_mA=250):
    motor.Send_Sound_Event(freq, current, wait, channel=channel)
motor.Send_Sound_Play()
```

For a longer tune, keep loading events while it plays: bits 0 to 7 of parameter 80 say how many are still
queued. `music.read_midi` reads a MIDI file, `music.split_voices` splits it into lines for the four channels, and
`music.lines_events` makes the queue's events from them.

Recorded sound: convert a WAV file to samples at the rate the motor plays, fill the buffer, start it, and keep it
filled:

```python
rate = 2500
samples = music.wav_samples('hello.wav', rate, coil_tau_s=0.00149 / 7.0, clip_percentile=0.95)
motor.Send_Samples(samples[:1000])               # fill the buffer first
motor.Send_Samples_Play(rate, full_scale_mV=2000)
sent = 1000
while sent < len(samples):
    motor.Send_Get_Parameter(80)
    read_answers(0.02)
    buffered = (motor.parameters.get(80, 0) >> 8) & 0x7FF
    room = 1000 - buffered
    if room > 0:
        motor.Send_Samples(samples[sent:sent + room])
        sent += room
```

`coil_tau_s` is the coil's L ÷ R (here 1.49 mH and 7.0 Ω, the motor of the calibration example): the function
raises the high frequencies the coil would otherwise swallow, and `clip_percentile` levels speech so that it plays
about four times louder.

At 2500 samples a second a driver takes about 313 frames a second, some 4 % of the bus. When the buffer runs dry the
playing stops and bit 27 of parameter 80 says so.

Send_Sound and Send_Sound_Samples do not reset the watchdog: with a watchdog set, keep sending a status request
while the sound plays.

## Limits and care

- **Fix the motor to something that rings.** A box or a table is far louder than a motor in free air, and a loose
  motor jumps and distorts the sound. On the STEPFOC bench the motor was taped down.
- **Keep tones short and moderate.** `#Tone` and Send_Tone default to 200 mA; the bench played notes at 250 mA.
  The sound current comes on top of the holding current and heats the motor like any other current; a motor is
  made to turn, and long loud tones are hard on it.
- **On the q axis a tone is a small torque ripple:** a held joint vibrates slightly at the tone's pitch. Choose the
  d axis (parameter 82 = 0) when that matters; it is quieter.
- **The cap**, parameter 81, limits all sound together; the output also clamps at the supply voltage.

Sound has not been tested on a Spectral Micro yet; the code is the same as STEPFOC's. On the STEPFOC bench
(2026-11-08, a bare NEMA 17 taped down), tones, scales, a tune from the queue, four-note chords and streamed speech
all played.

The q axis was much louder than the d axis, speech was audible but muffled, and there were no errors, no warming and
only small vibrations.

## The arm as an instrument

Every joint of a robot can play its own line, and because the sound rides on top of the control, the arm keeps
holding its pose while it plays.

Load each driver's queue first, then start them one after another: the starts are meant to fall within about a
millisecond of each other, and from then on each driver keeps its own time (whether they stay together over a whole
song is still to be measured).

Split a MIDI file into as many lines as there are channels, four per driver, and give each driver its four. Through a
gearbox the sound changes with the joint; try each joint's range. Playing on an assembled arm has not been tested yet.

## Checking what plays

| Parameter | Says |
|---|---|
| 79, bit 24 | sound is playing |
| 80 | bits 0-7 events queued, 8-18 samples buffered, 24 a tone sounds, 25 the queue plays, 26 samples play, 27 the samples ran dry |
| 81 | the sound's voltage cap, mV |
| 82 | the axis: 1 q, 0 d |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/ -->

# Gripper mode

A driver can run a gripper instead of a joint: the same board, with a state machine that moves a jaw to a
position between open and closed, at a speed, with a current limit that becomes the grip force, and that reports
when it holds something. The [SSG-48 gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/) is built on the Spectral Micro this way.

## Turning it on

```
#Gripper 1
#Save
```

`#Default` clears the flag again. Over CAN the flag is parameter 92 from firmware 110: write 1 while the driver is
idle (in any other mode the write is refused), then Send_Save_config.

A driver in gripper mode still answers every other command; the gripper commands only work with the flag set,
except the gripper calibration, which runs with or without it.

## Calibrating the gripper

After every power-up the gripper has to find its end stops: `#Gripcal` or Send_gripper_calibrate. The jaws open
slowly at 500 mA until they stop. Then the push eases to 100 mA for a quarter of a second, and the driver reads the
open end where the jaws rest against the stop. The closed end is found the same way.

Position 0 (open) lies 32 ticks inside the open end, and 255 (closed) 16 ticks inside the closed end. So a move to 0
or 255 ends in free travel: it does not press on the stop and reports no object.

Firmware 109 read the ends during the 500 mA push, so 0 and 255 lay inside the stops, and a full open or close kept
pressing on them.

If it has not found both ends within about 30 s it gives up, and the gripper stays uncalibrated. From firmware 110
it also stays uncalibrated when the two ends lie less than 1000 ticks apart: the jaws did not travel.

Check the result with `#Gripinfo` or the `gripper_calibrated` bit of Respond_Gripper_data_pack. From firmware 110
parameter 93 gives the stroke between 0 and 255 in ticks, and 0 while the gripper is not calibrated. The motor
itself must be calibrated (`#Cal`) and saved before that, once.

While the gripper calibrates, send only empty status polls. A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error
or `#Clear` stops the calibration without a message. From firmware 110 the next calibration starts from its first
step, and `#Gripcal` or Send_gripper_calibrate during a calibration starts it again. Firmware 109 went on where
the stopped one left off ([known issue KI-7](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/)).

## Moving

Over UART:

```
#Gripvel 100       speed, 0 to 255
#Gripcur 400       current limit of the move in mA, the grip force
#Grippos 200       go to position 200 (0 open, 255 closed); also activates the gripper
```

Over CAN, Send_gripper_data_pack carries position, speed and current in one frame with the activate and action
bits; the driver answers with Respond_Gripper_data_pack: the position, the measured current, whether it is moving,
and the object detection:

| Object detection | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | moving |
| 1 | an object was detected while closing: the jaws stopped on it and hold it with the current limit |
| 2 | an object was detected while opening |
| 3 | the position was reached |

From firmware 110 an object (1 or 2) is reported once the jaws have stood still at nearly the move's current for
50 ms. Firmware 109 reported it at the first slow control cycle, also at the start of a move.

From firmware 110 a move starts at the slowest speed and picks up to its own speed within 0.1 s. It slows down over
the last stretch, so it arrives slowly. A new command in the same direction keeps the speed the jaws have, so a host
that streams positions is not slowed.

At the position the driver holds with a small dead zone, a quarter of a position count and at most 16 ticks, and
friction keeps the jaws there: a few mA are left after a move.

On firmware 109 the current took a second or more to settle after every move. From firmware 110 the position the
driver reports is also rounded to the nearest count; 109 cut it off.

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack (0 bytes) only asks for the state. The answer to a 5-byte command goes out
before the driver acts on it, so its object detection and error bits are still those of the moment before
(KI-6); the answers to the next frames show the new move.

The action bit in the answer is a copy of the last command's action bit and stays 1 after the move ends (KI-8): the
object detection tells when it has ended.

Send_gripper_data_pack's E-stop bit raises the gripper E-stop error; `#Gripstop 1` does the same over UART. The
error stays: while the E-stop bit is 1 the driver raises it again on every control cycle (KI-5). To recover,
clear the bit (`#Gripstop 0`, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit 0), then `#Clear` or Send_Clear_Error.

!!! warning "Current"
    From firmware 109 the current you give a gripper move stops at the board's 2800 mA; firmware 107 and older
    did not limit it. The safe range depends on the gripper's mechanics and motor and is lower; the
    [SSG-48 manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/) gives it for that gripper.

From firmware 110 the move's current is the gripper's own limit. The driver's current limit (`#Ilim`, parameter 16)
stays as you set it, and a `#Save` stores that. Firmware 109 wrote the current of each move into the driver's limit,
and a `#Save` then stored the gripper's current.

## Where the details are

The bytes of the two gripper frames are in the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gripper/), the UART commands in
the [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/gripper/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/ -->

# Firmware

The driver's firmware is open source and released as numbered builds. Release 104 is the first release built
for the bootloader: a driver that runs 104 or newer carries a bootloader and updates itself over UART or CAN. A
driver that runs 101 or older needs the bootloader installed once with a programming adapter. A driver that
reports 101 can be either ([Drivers that report 101](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/releases/#drivers-that-report-101) says how to tell).

## In this chapter

- [Releases and versions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/releases/): how releases are numbered, how to see which one a driver runs, what the
  release notes contain
- [The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/the-bootloader/): what it is, how the driver boots, how it is entered, its protocol and tools
- [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/): the normal update, with Motor GUI, the bootloader's command-line
  tool, or a PAR6 control box
- [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/): what a driver keeps when it is updated to this release, what works
  at once and what has to be run
- [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/): for a driver that runs firmware 101 or older
- [Building from source](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/building/): PlatformIO, the memory layout, uploading with a programming adapter

The release notes of every release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix,
[Firmware release notes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/firmware-release-notes/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/releases/ -->

# Releases and versions

A firmware release is a number: 101, 104, 105, … Every release is a tag `V<number>` in the
[firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller) and a GitHub release that
carries the image `spectral-bldc-firmware-V<number>.bin`, a manifest `firmware.json` with the image's size, SHA-256 and
the commit it was built from, and the release notes. The notes are the firmware's changelog; the
[appendix](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/firmware-release-notes/) collects them.

## Which release does my driver run?

```
#Info
```

prints `Software version: <number>` among the rest; Motor GUI shows the same number in the driver's identity, and
over CAN Send_Respond_Device_Info returns it as the third byte. From firmware 105 the number is the build's own
version.

Before that it was read from the EEPROM, where the last `#Default` wrote it, so it names the firmware that last
restored the defaults, not necessarily the one running: 101 and 104 both write 101.

### Drivers that report 101

A driver that reports 101 runs either release 101 from the `main` branch, without a bootloader, or release 104
(or an earlier build of `Bootloader_main`), which also writes 101 and runs above the bootloader. Drivers sold before
release 105 shipped with firmware 101 or 103.

To tell whether yours has the bootloader:

- Watch the LED as you switch the driver on: with the bootloader it blinks for about two seconds before the
  firmware starts.
- Or power it up while `bl_flash.py list` or Motor GUI's *Scan bootloaders* is polling: a driver with the
  bootloader answers in its first two seconds.

With the bootloader, update it to the current release as in [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/); the release
it ran before does not matter then. Without one, install it first:
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/).

## Which release does this site describe?

The one in the version box on the [landing page](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/) and in the version selector in the header. When a
newer release changes what a page says, a new version of the site is published and the previous one stays
reachable from the selector. The [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/compatibility/) says which releases go with
which bootloader, Python library and PAR6 runtime.

## The STEPFOC counterpart

Most Spectral Micro releases have a [STEPFOC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/) release with the
same changes. From release 109 the two drivers share their version numbers and are released together: the
Spectral Micro went from 107 straight to 109, so there is no Spectral Micro 108.

Before that the numbers did not always match (Spectral Micro 107 went with STEPFOC 108); the
[compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/compatibility/) lists the pairs.

## The two branches

Releases from 104 on are built from the `Bootloader_main` branch of the repository, whose firmware is linked to
run above the bootloader; 104 is the first of them.

The `main` branch holds the firmware linked to run without a bootloader: release 101 and earlier, and a few later
changes that were never tagged as a release (among them the Kt request and the voltage limit message). It is not
updated.

Version `101` of this site documents a board running 101. It also fits 104, which adds the Send_Respond_Kt
request, Send_Voltage_Limit (in the release image) and the bootloader.

The 104 release image was built from commit `20765c9` on `Bootloader_main`, not from the source at the tag `V104`,
which does not have Send_Voltage_Limit yet. To move a board without a bootloader to a current release, see
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/the-bootloader/ -->

# The bootloader

Every driver that runs firmware 104 or newer (104 is the first release built for the bootloader) carries a small
bootloader in the first 12 KB of its flash.

It starts the firmware on a normal boot, and it loads a new firmware over UART or CAN when a host asks, so a driver is
updated without a programming adapter and without opening anything. The bootloader is open source:
[stm32f103c-bootloader](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader), shared with STEPFOC.

## Memory layout

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| `0x08000000` – `0x080022FF` | the bootloader (about 9 KB) |
| `0x08002C00` – `0x08002FFF` | the bootloader's configuration page: the board ID, the firmware's page count and CRC, the bootloader's build version |
| `0x08003000` – `0x0801FFFF` | the firmware (up to 116 KB) |
| RAM `0x20001000` | a magic word the bootloader sets to hand over to the firmware |

The firmware is linked to start at `0x08003000` and sets its vector table there (`VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000`); the
first `0x3000` bytes belong to the bootloader and the firmware never touches them.

## What happens at boot

1. On a reset, the bootloader runs first. If the magic word is in RAM and the reset was a software reset, it
   checks the firmware's stack pointer and reset vector and jumps straight into the firmware: about 10 ms, the
   normal boot.
2. Otherwise it initialises the clocks, CAN, UART and its watchdog, and **listens for a host for 2 s**.
3. With no host, and a firmware whose stored CRC is valid, it sets the magic word and resets; the next boot takes
   the fast path.
4. With a host talking, it stays as long as the host keeps talking: 3 s after the last command, 60 s once a flash
   is in progress. Any `PING` resets the timer.
5. With no valid firmware (never flashed, or a flash that was interrupted), it stays in bootloader mode and waits.
   The LED is off; the driver answers nothing on `#Info`.

## Entering the bootloader

- **From the firmware**: `#Reset` over UART or Send_Reset (command 14) over CAN. Since firmware 104 both reset
  the driver into the bootloader's 2 s window; the host tools send them for you.
- **At power-on**: the 2 s window after every power-up, if the host is already polling.
- **Always**, when there is no valid firmware.

## The board ID

The bootloader has a board ID of its own, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. 14 and 15 do not exist
for it: its command frame, identifier `0x700`, decodes as node 14 in the firmware's identifier scheme, so those
two node IDs are reserved.

**Give drivers node IDs 0 to 13.** The firmware accepts `#CANID 14` and `15`, but the bootloader then keeps its old
board ID and a firmware update over CAN cannot reach the driver.

The firmware keeps the board ID in step with its CAN node ID when the configuration is saved: `#Save` or
Send_Save_config writes the node ID into the bootloader's board ID, so a saved driver answers the host tools under its
node ID. Setting the node ID alone (`#CANID`, Send_CAN_ID) does not: until you save, the bootloader keeps the old ID.

A replacement board ships as ID 0; two boards with the same ID on one bus corrupt each other's flash stream, so give
the new board its ID alone on the bus first (`set-id` in the host tool).

## Transports and protocol

Over **CAN** (1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers) the host commands on identifier `0x700` with 8 data bytes
(`board_id`, `cmd`, two parameters). The board replies on `0x701 + board_id` with 5 bytes (`board_id`, `cmd`,
error code, a 16-bit parameter).

The firmware image streams in bulk frames on `(board_id << 7) | sequence`, 16 frames of 8 bytes per chunk, with no
reply per frame.

Over **UART** (256000 baud) the same commands travel in framed packets `[0xBB][CMD][LEN][BOARD_ID][DATA…][CRC16]`
with the same 5-byte reply.

Commands: `WBUF` (1), `WPAGE` (2), `WCRC` (3), `PING` (4), `SET_ID` (5), `ERASE_APP` (6), `STREAM_BEGIN` (7),
`STREAM_STATUS` (8). Error codes: `0` OK, `1` invalid offset, `2` invalid CRC, `3` flash write failed, `4` invalid
page number.

A flash is: ping, reset the firmware if it answers, ping until the bootloader answers, `ERASE_APP` (about 3.5 s), then
for each 1 KB page `STREAM_BEGIN`, 8 chunks of 16 frames, `STREAM_STATUS`, `WPAGE` with the page's CRC32; finally
`WCRC` with the page count and the image's CRC32.

The bootloader stores the CRC and reboots into the new firmware. The full wire protocol is in the bootloader
repository's `docs/PROTOCOL.md`.

## The host side

| Tool | Transport | Use |
|---|---|---|
| [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/) | serial adapter (Web Serial) or CANvas | one driver on the bench, releases fetched from GitHub |
| `host_tools/bl_flash.py` in the bootloader repository | slcan or gs_usb CAN adapters, or UART | scripts, several boards, `list`, `set-id`, `flash --erase-first` |
| the PAR6 control box's `flash_motor_firmware.py` and the dashboard's Firmware tab | the robot's own CAN bus | every joint of a robot, from the box |

[Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/) has the commands.

## Recovery

An interrupted flash leaves an invalid CRC; the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits, so the board is
not lost: flash again. A board that answers nothing at all: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch
the 2 s window.

The one thing the tools refuse, and that would need a programming adapter to undo, is flashing an image linked for
`0x08000000` (a firmware from the `main` branch) over the firmware region.

## Installing it

Boards that run firmware 101 or older have no bootloader. [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/)
puts it there once, with a programming adapter at `0x08000000`; from then on the board updates like any other.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/ -->

# Updating through the bootloader

A driver with the bootloader (firmware 104 or newer) is updated over the UART connector or the CAN bus: the host
tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it.
No programming adapter, and nothing to open.

!!! warning "Before you update"
    - Park the mechanism: the motor loses torque during the update and until the new firmware is calibrated and
      commanded.
    - An update may clear the calibration (the release notes say so when it does); plan to calibrate and `#Save`
      afterwards, and note the gains `#Info` prints. An update to 109 keeps it, and the driver runs on it; calibrate
      again where the motor can turn freely, or apply the SSG-48 preset on an assembled gripper (over UART, with
      *Gripper CAN ID* set to the gripper's node):
      [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/) says why, what changes and what to run.
    - On a bus with several drivers, update each node; a bus with mixed releases behaves unpredictably.

## With Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) in Chrome or Edge, connected over the serial adapter or the CANvas adapter:
choose the release, and the GUI fetches the image and its manifest from the GitHub release, verifies the size and
the SHA-256, resets the driver into its bootloader and flashes it. This is the way for one driver on the bench.

## With the bootloader's command-line tool

The [bootloader repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader) has `host_tools/bl_flash.py`,
which flashes an image over CAN (slcan or candleLight/gs_usb adapters) or over UART:

=== "Windows"
    ```
    cd host_tools
    pip install -r requirements.txt

    # over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter on COM6, driver with board ID 0
    python bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel COM6 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

    # over UART on COM7
    python bl_flash.py --transport uart --port COM7 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
    ```

=== "Linux"
    ```
    cd host_tools
    pip install -r requirements.txt

    # over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/ttyACM0 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

    # over UART with the serial adapter
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
    ```
    Your user needs the `dialout` group for both ports ([Motor GUI: the port](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/motor-gui/#opening-the-port)).

=== "macOS"
    ```
    cd host_tools
    pip install -r requirements.txt

    # over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0; ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* gives the name
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

    # over UART with the serial adapter; ls /dev/cu.usbserial* gives the name
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/cu.usbserial-0001 --baudrate 256000 flash spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
    ```

The tool sends the reset command to the running firmware (`#Reset` over UART, Send_Reset over CAN), catches the
bootloader's two-second window, erases the application pages and streams the image page by page, each page
verified by a CRC; `list` shows the boards in bootloader mode, `set-id` changes a board's bootloader ID. The image
is the `spectral-bldc-firmware-V<number>.bin` from the GitHub release.

!!! note "Board ID and node ID"
    The bootloader has its own board ID (0 to 13), kept in its configuration page, separate from the firmware's
    CAN node ID. The firmware copies the node ID into the board ID when the configuration is saved (`#Save`,
    Send_Save_config), so a saved driver's bootloader ID is its node ID. After `#CANID` or Send_CAN_ID without a
    save, `--board` still needs the old ID.

!!! success "Check"
    After the flash, from Motor GUI or the tool, the driver starts the new firmware: `#Info` prints the release
    you flashed as `Software version`, and Motor GUI shows it in the driver's identity. If the driver does not
    answer, see [When it fails](#when-it-fails).

## From a PAR6 control box

A robot built on the Robot Control Box updates every joint from the box itself, over its own CAN bus, from the
dashboard's Firmware tab or with `tools/flash_motor_firmware.py`; the
[PAR6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/) describes it.

## What happens in the driver

1. The host sends the reset; the firmware reboots into the bootloader.
2. The bootloader listens for two seconds. With no host it starts the firmware; with a host it stays as long as
   the host keeps talking (60 s during a flash).
3. The application pages are erased, then written page by page; each page is checked by a CRC.
4. The bootloader checks the whole image's CRC, records it, and starts the new firmware.

## When it fails

A flash that fails or is cancelled part way is not a brick: the stored CRC is invalid, so the bootloader refuses to
start the firmware and waits for a host.

Run the flash again; `bl_flash.py list` (or a passive scan from the control box) finds the board. A board that answers
nothing: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch the two-second window.

An image linked for `0x08000000` (a firmware from the `main` branch, release 101 and earlier) must never be
flashed through the bootloader: it would overwrite the bootloader's own region if the tool did not refuse it.
The tools validate the image first.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/ -->

# Upgrading from older firmware

Firmware 109 adds more to the Spectral Micro than any release before it: parameters, the watchdog actions, the
identity and telemetry frames, captures, the current loop from one bandwidth, a choice of speed estimates, and the
encoder table and anti-cogging.

This page says what a driver keeps when it is updated to 109, what works at once, what can be run, and how to go back.
[Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/) is how to flash it.

There is no firmware 108 for the Spectral Micro: from 109 the Spectral Micro and STEPFOC share their version
numbers, so a Spectral Micro goes from 107 straight to 109. The step from 109 to 110 is smaller:
[From 109 to 110](#from-109-to-110).

## From 109 to 110

Firmware 110 changes the gripper, adds `#Estop` and parameters 90 to 93, and saves brake or coast; nothing has to
be measured again. A driver updated from 109 keeps everything it saved: the settings, the motor calibration, the
encoder table and the anti-cogging. 110 keeps the idle behaviour in a slot of settings block 2 that was reserved.

- **Brake or coast** (parameter 18) is saved from 110 on. A driver that has not saved it yet coasts in idle, as on
  109; send `#Brake 1` and `#Save` once if it should brake.
- **The gripper calibration** is kept in RAM, as it always was: calibrate the gripper after the update, as after
  every power-up. Positions 0 and 255 then lie a little inside the two ends
  ([Gripper mode](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/#calibrating-the-gripper)).
- **Motor GUI 0.7.0** is the version made for 110: its STOP sends `#Estop` over UART, and its presets write
  parameters 90 to 92 over CAN.

Going back to 109 is safe: 109 ignores the saved idle behaviour and coasts at every power-up again.

## What is kept

Flashing never touches the EEPROM, where the configuration lives
([The check at power-up](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/#the-check-at-power-up)). A driver updated from 106 or 107 starts
with everything it had:

- the calibration: pole pairs, R, L, the angle offset, Kt, KV, the phase order and direction, the current gains;
- the CAN ID, the gains, the limits, the watchdog, the heartbeat, the thermistor and the gripper settings.

!!! warning "Calibrate again after the update, where the motor can turn freely"
    In every firmware before 109 the enable input of phase B was fed by a clock signal instead of a steady level,
    so phase B could drop out, also while the calibration measured the motor. A calibration made with 107 or older
    stored the resistance about 10 % and the inductance about 45 % too low (reference gimbal motor: about 6.4 Ω and
    1.25 mH, where 109 measures about 7.0 to 7.2 Ω and 1.75 to 1.9 mH).

    The driver keeps running on such a calibration: on the bench an SSG-48 updated to 109 without a new
    calibration reached every target and gripped as before. Only the current gains are computed from the low
    values. So:

    - **A motor that can turn freely:** run `#Cal` once after the update. The current gains then follow the true
      values, and the encoder table and the anti-cogging are measured too.
    - **An assembled SSG-48 gripper,** whose motor moves the jaws: do not run `#Cal`. Apply Motor GUI's SSG-48
      preset over UART instead: it writes 300 Hz current gains for the gripper's motor and saves. Set *Gripper CAN
      ID* to the gripper's node first: it starts at 6, the PAR6 gripper's; a PAROL6 gripper is node 0. A motor
      calibration needs the body opened and the linear guide with the jaws off; then use `#Calonly`, because
      `#Cal` also runs the encoder table and the anti-cogging.

A driver from 101 to 105, saved before the configuration had checksums, is trusted and sealed at its first start
of 109 when it was ever saved; a blank EEPROM gets the defaults. Release 101 and older from the `main` branch have
no bootloader: such a board needs the programming adapter once
([Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/)).

The new settings start from their defaults: tool id 0, the watchdog fallback 2000 ms / 0 mA / 1000 ticks/s /
legacy, parameter 56 = 0.

## What works at once

These need no measurement and are on from the first start of 109:

- the **current-sense zero**, measured at every start-up with the driver asleep: on the bench the current read
  3.9 mA with nothing flowing, where it read −20 to +19 mA before, depending on the rotor's position;
- undervoltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, so a supply that ramps up slowly no longer
  leaves a Vbus error behind (overvoltage always is);
- the **watchdog actions**: the action byte the host already sends is acted on. Byte 0, what the Python library and
  the PAR6 runtime send, gives the legacy response, so an unchanged host sees no difference;
- phase B's enable pin is driven properly, and the control loop keeps the gate driver awake in every driving
  mode: either could leave a motor that took a command and did not move, or that pushed unevenly;
- the limits refuse a negative value, and Send_Limits and the gripper's current stop at 2800 mA;
- setting the watchdog time starts a fresh window, so switching it on again no longer trips it at once;
- `#Default` and a settings reset **keep the CAN ID**;
- the first motion frame after Idle is followed (the driver's wake-up now comes with it), and a position or speed
  frame after another mode no longer kicks with a stale velocity integral;
- the product lock, the new CAN commands and parameters, the identity frame, telemetry, the capture, `#Info`'s
  `In force:`, and [sound through the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/sound/) (not yet tested on a Spectral Micro).

## What can be run or switched on

The encoder table and the anti-cogging are off after the update until they are measured (`#Cal` measures both);
the speed estimate and the delay compensation are new defaults, on from the first start:

- the **encoder table** and the **anti-cogging** ([Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/));
  they cannot be switched on before they are measured;
- the **direct PLL speed estimate** at 100 Hz (parameters 50 and 51) and the **commutation delay compensation** of
  234 µs (parameter 64), both on by default from 109
  ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/#the-speed-estimate)). They change how the velocity loop
  behaves with the gains you had: a speed step overshoots less. Check your velocity gains after the update.

## What does not change by itself

- **The current gains.** The saved Kpiq and Kiiq stay as they are: on a driver calibrated before 109 they were
  computed for 500 Hz (parameter 49 reads about 500), from a resistance and an inductance that were too low. A
  calibration with 109 measures both again and computes the gains at 160 Hz. `#Cbw 160` on the old calibration
  does not replace it: it uses the old values and gives gains for a lower bandwidth than it names. 160 Hz is the
  new default; it was chosen on the STEPFOC bench.
- **The velocity gains** stay as they are; their defaults, Kpv 0.03 and Kiv 0.0003, did not change.

## The whole upgrade

1. Flash 109 ([Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/)). `#Info` prints the new firmware version and ends with
   `In force:`.
2. Check that the current limit suits your motor (`#Ilim`): calibration puts back the limit that was in force, and
   the encoder table in the next step runs at 80 % of it.
3. Calibrate, with the shaft free: `#Cal`, so that the resistance, the inductance and the current gains are
   measured again. It goes on to the encoder table and the anti-cogging, and saves everything. `#Calonly` is the
   calibration alone.
4. After `#Calonly`: `#Save`; and if you want them, run the encoder table and the anti-cogging with the shaft free
   (`#Encal all`) and check them.

With Motor GUI's presets: apply the preset first, then calibrate. A product preset writes its own current and
velocity gains, so one applied after the calibration puts its current gains back. The *Generic motor* presets set
soft limits and velocity gains and leave the current gains to `#Cbw` and the calibration.

## Going back

Flashing 107 or older over 109 is safe for the configuration: the calibration and the first settings block are
unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything 109 saved from byte 256 on (tool id, fallback, anti-cogging,
encoder table). Flash 109 again and they are all still there.

!!! note "Not yet tested on the bench"
    A downgrade and the sound on a Spectral Micro had not been tested on the bench when this page was written;
    the rest of this page was.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/ -->

# Installing the bootloader on an older board

A driver running firmware 101 or older has no bootloader: its firmware starts at the beginning of the flash. A
driver that reports 101 may run 104 and have the bootloader all the same; check first, as in
[Drivers that report 101](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/releases/#drivers-that-report-101).

To run any release from 104 on (104 is the first release built for the bootloader), which is linked to start above the
bootloader, the bootloader must be installed once, with a programming adapter on the JTAG connector. After that, every
update goes over UART or CAN.

!!! warning
    Disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter before connecting the programming adapter. The adapter
    powers the board at 3.3 V.

## What you need

- The [programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch) (an ST-LINK
  with the 1.27 mm pogo-pin adapter for the JTAG pads), or any ST-LINK, J-Link or OpenOCD-compatible probe wired
  to 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO and SWCLK.
- [STM32CubeProgrammer](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html) or the older
  [STM32 ST-LINK Utility](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link004.html) on the PC, with the
  [ST-LINK drivers](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link009.html).
- The bootloader binary from the [bootloader repository's `bin/` folder](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader/tree/main/bin);
  its `README.md` names the current file.

=== "Windows"
    STM32CubeProgrammer or the ST-LINK Utility, and the ST-LINK USB driver (STSW-LINK009) for the adapter.

=== "Linux"
    STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver, but your user
    needs access to its USB device: install the udev rules that come with STM32CubeProgrammer, or run it with
    `sudo`.

=== "macOS"
    STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver.

![The JTAG pads. The adapter is pressed onto them; a little pressure makes the contact.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/FLASHING2.webp){ width="520" }
![The JTAG pads. The adapter is pressed onto them; a little pressure makes the contact.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/FLASHING2_dark.webp){ width="520" }

## Steps

1. Connect the adapter to the JTAG pads and the PC.
2. In the programmer, connect to the target (SWD). The STM32F103CB shows up with 128 KB of flash.
3. Erase the chip, or at least the application region: the old firmware and the bootloader must not overlap.
4. Program the bootloader binary at address **`0x08000000`**.
5. Disconnect the adapter, power the driver. The bootloader finds no valid application and waits in bootloader
   mode (the LED stays off).
6. Flash the firmware release through the bootloader, over UART or CAN, as in
   [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/).
7. `#Info` shows the new release. `#Default`, then calibrate (`#Cal`), set the current limit (`#Ilim`) and
   `#Save`; see [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/).

!!! success "Check"
    `#Info` prints the release you flashed, and a driver powered up while `bl_flash.py list` or Motor GUI's
    *Scan bootloaders* is polling answers in its first two seconds: the bootloader is there. If the firmware does
    not start, see [Updating through the bootloader: when it fails](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/#when-it-fails).

!!! note "Memory layout"
    `0x08000000`–`0x080022FF` bootloader, `0x08002C00` its configuration page (board ID, the application's CRC),
    `0x08003000`–`0x0801FFFF` the application (116 KB). The bootloader keeps a magic value in RAM to hand over
    to the application in about 10 ms on a normal boot.

## The programmer's settings

In ST-LINK Utility, *Target → Settings* with SWD and the default frequency works; *Target → Program & Verify*
with the start address `0x08000000`. The pictures of the old flashing procedure apply to the connection and the
settings dialog:

| Settings | Programming |
|---|---|
| ![ST-LINK settings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/stlink1.webp){ width="420" } | ![ST-LINK program and verify](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/stlink_prog.webp){ width="420" } |

The same adapter uploads a firmware you build yourself, see [Building from source](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/building/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/building/ -->

# Building from source

The firmware is a PlatformIO project for the Arduino core on the STM32F103CB, in the `Spectral BLDC Firmware` folder
of the [firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-Micro-BLDC-controller/tree/Bootloader_main/Spectral%20BLDC%20Firmware)
on the `Bootloader_main` branch.

## Building

1. Install [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and the PlatformIO extension.
2. Clone the repository and check out `Bootloader_main`.
3. Open the `Spectral BLDC Firmware` folder in VS Code; PlatformIO fetches the platform (`ststm32@15.4.1`) and builds
   with the PlatformIO *Build* button or `pio run`. The image is `.pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin`.

The project is linked for the bootloader: `VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000`, the linker script `ldscript_bootloader.ld`,
the upload offset `0x08003000` and a maximum size of 118784 bytes, in `platformio.ini`. A build that exceeds the
size fails to link.

!!! success "Check"
    PlatformIO ends the build with `SUCCESS`, and `.pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin` is there. If it
    fails, the first error above the summary names the cause.

## Uploading

PlatformIO runs on Windows, Linux and macOS alike. On Linux, an upload with the programming adapter also needs
PlatformIO's udev rules (`99-platformio-udev.rules`, in the PlatformIO documentation), and a serial port the
`dialout` group.

- **Through the bootloader**: flash the built `firmware.bin` with `bl_flash.py` or Motor GUI as in
  [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/). This is how a release is installed, and works on any driver with
  the bootloader.
- **With the programming adapter**: *Upload* in PlatformIO uses ST-LINK and writes the image at `0x08003000`. The
  bootloader must already be on the board; the upload does not touch it. The serial monitor (the plug icon) opens
  the UART at 256000 with `send_on_enter`, so you can type commands to the driver from the same window.

![Build, upload and the serial monitor in PlatformIO's status bar.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/VSUPLOAD.png){ width="700" }

## Where things are

| | |
|---|---|
| `src/constants.h` | `FIRMWARE_VERSION`, the CAN command IDs, the EEPROM map, the loop and PWM frequencies |
| `src/common.h` | the controller and PID structures with their defaults |
| `src/communication.cpp` | the UART command handlers |
| `src/communication_CAN.cpp` | the CAN receive switch and the transmit functions |
| `src/SerialPacketParser.cpp` | the UART parser: it splits a line into the command and its argument (up to 107 it also kept the list of names it accepted) |
| `src/motor_control.cpp` | the control loops, the calibration routine, the gripper state machine |
| `src/bootloader_config.cpp` | the vector table offset and the reset into the bootloader |
| `release_guide.md` | how a release is cut: version bump, build, tag, GitHub release with `firmware.json` |

## Making a release

`release_guide.md` in the repository is the procedure: bump `FIRMWARE_VERSION`, build, commit the source change, tag
`V<number>`, create the GitHub release with the image, `firmware.json` and the release notes. This site's
`tools/sync_firmware.py` reads a release by its tag; the version box names the release.

## A firmware for a board without a bootloader

The `main` branch builds a firmware linked at `0x08000000` for boards that have no bootloader. Its last tagged
release is 101; it is not maintained. Install the bootloader instead:
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/).
