<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/ -->

# Troubleshooting

By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/); the
faults of the firmware that are known and not yet fixed, with what to do until they are, in
[Known issues](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/).

## The motor does not move

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A([The motor does not move]) --> B{Does the driver answer?}
    B -- no --> C[The supply and its polarity, the LED;<br>UART: the baud rate, TX and RX;<br>CAN: the node ID, 1 Mbit/s, the termination]
    B -- yes --> D{Calibrated?}
    D -- no --> E[#Cal and #Save]
    D -- yes --> F{An error active? The LED on steadily}
    F -- yes --> G[#Error names it: fix the cause, then #Clear]
    F -- no --> H{A current limit above 0?}
    H -- no --> I[#Ilim to the motor's rated current, #Save]
    H -- yes --> J[Command a setpoint in a closed-loop mode;<br>#Mode and #Info show the state]
```

## The driver does not answer

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| No LED | the supply, DC+ and DC−, the power cable's orientation. If the cable was the wrong way round the driver is destroyed |
| LED on, nothing on the terminal | 256000 baud; TX to RX and RX to TX; the adapter's port; 3.3 V adapter; the line ending CR+LF |
| LED on, nothing on CAN | the node ID; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; termination (about 60 Ω across CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered); the CAN cable's orientation |
| `Unknown command` | the name's spelling and case: `#Kpiq`, not `#kpiq`; an argument with a space in it (`#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2`, not `#WdFb 2000, 0, 1000, 2`) |
| `Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)`, the LED on steadily | the other product's firmware was flashed: a STEPFOC image on a Spectral Micro. Flash the Spectral Micro firmware; the configuration was not touched ([The product lock](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/diagnostics/#the-product-lock)) |
| the LED is off and nothing works after a firmware update | the bootloader has no valid firmware: flash again, see [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/update/) |

## Motor GUI

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| the browser offers no port | a Chromium-based browser (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera); Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial |
| the port is listed but will not open | another program holds it: a terminal, PlatformIO's monitor, the Arduino serial monitor |
| the port opens, nothing appears | the driver's power; TX and RX crossed on a non-Source adapter; the baud rate on a non-Source adapter (256000) |
| *No connection* on CAN | the CANvas adapter's port; the bus termination; the node ID of the driver; 1 Mbit/s |
| the calibration does not start | calibration runs over the serial connection only, not over CAN |
| *Unsaved changes* after a power cycle | the settings were not saved to the driver; Save writes them |
| the firmware update finds no bootloader | power-cycle the driver while the GUI scans, to catch the bootloader's 2 s window. A driver with firmware 101 or older has no bootloader (one that reports 101 may have it: [Drivers that report 101](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/releases/#drivers-that-report-101)): [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/) |

## Calibration

The messages and their causes are in [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/). The ones that
come back most:

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Magnet test: Failed` | magnet too far, axially magnetised, or missing |
| the motor wobbles left and right during calibration | one phase is not connected |
| `Open loop: Failed` | the rotor did not follow the open-loop field, or the pole pairs came out outside 1 to 49: a phase open, the shaft not free, the open-loop voltage (`#Openv`) too low for the motor |
| `Commutation/alignment check failed!` | the motor did not respond to the commutation check: a phase open, `#Iqoffset` too low, a magnet that slips |
| calibration succeeds, the motor then runs badly or in the wrong direction | the magnet slipped on the shaft; glue it and calibrate again |
| after `Calibration success!` the motor turns slowly by itself for about a minute | the encoder table and the anti-cogging that follow a `#Cal`; let them finish, they save everything ([What follows the calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/#what-follows-the-calibration)) |
| the anti-cogging does not switch on (parameter 37 stays 0) | no set is identified for that form; run `#Cogcal save`. After an encoder table measured on its own the set is switched off until it is identified again ([Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/)) |
| calibration succeeds but the LED stays on and `#Error` shows nothing | `#Info` shows `-1`, a value from an older release ([The check at power-up](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/#the-check-at-power-up)): `#Default`, calibrate again |

## The motor

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| crunching or whining at speed | the current limit or the current loop gains too high; lower `#Ilim`, lower `#Cbw` and calibrate again, or lower `#Kpiq` |
| humming, oscillating at rest | `#Kpv` or `#Kpp` too high; see [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/tuning/) |
| weak torque | `#Ilim` low; the supply's current limit; a calibration run at a low supply voltage (the constants are off) |
| the motor is hot | lower `#Ilim`, enable the thermistor; a gimbal motor held against a load at its current limit heats quickly |
| it stops with a Vbus error when decelerating | the supply cannot absorb the returned energy; a different supply, or a brake resistor |
| it stops with a velocity error | the measured speed passed the fixed limit of 20,000,000 ticks/s: an encoder fault or a slipping magnet, rarely a real runaway; `#Vlimit` does not change it |
| it falls behind under a load | the torque limit: raise `#Ilim` within the motor's rating, or a bigger motor |
| it holds position with a sawtooth noise | the position loop gain; the magnet distance |

## Low-quality motors

Motors with visibly bad windings, an uneven back-EMF or a resistance that differs between the phases calibrate
poorly and run rough. The [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/03-technical-data/tested-motors/) are known good.

## The magnet and the encoder

- The distance is 1 mm. "Magnet Good" from the magnet test does not mean the distance is right, only that the
  field is strong enough.
- A magnet touching the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet too far gives a noisy, wrong position.
- The magnet must be diametrically magnetised and centred on the shaft.

## The driver gets hot or shuts down

The MOSFET driver stage shuts down on its own overtemperature or overcurrent and reports a driver error. Lower
the current limit, give the board airflow, check the motor leads for a short. Near 2.8 A the driver needs
cooling.

## After a firmware update

`#Info` shows the new release. If the values look wrong or the LED stays on: `#Default`, `#Cal`, `#Save`. A release note says when an update clears the calibration. After an update to 109, calibrate again (`#Cal`) where the motor can turn freely; on an assembled SSG-48 apply its preset instead. [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/) says why and what else changes.

A Vbus error right after power-up, cleared by `#Clear`, was the supply ramping up; from firmware 109 a low supply is
not checked in the first 500 ms.

## Getting help

[Support](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/support/) says where to ask and what to include; `#Info`'s output is the first thing.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/ -->

# Known issues

The faults in the Spectral Micro firmware that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are. The pages that
describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects them in one place. Which releases work
together is in [Versions and compatibility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/compatibility/).

### Spectral Micro firmware

Seen in: 110.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-3 | The serial number is not read back from the EEPROM at power-up, so `#SERNUM`, Motor GUI and Send_Respond_Device_Info report 1, and every `#Save` writes that 1 over the stored number. | Tell drivers apart by their CAN node ID. To keep a serial number stored, set it with `#SERNUM` before every `#Save`. | [Saving: what is not saved](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/#what-is-not-saved) |
| KI-4 | For anyone reading or changing the source, the start values in `common.h` are not the factory defaults (the gripper flag starts at 1, the pole pairs at 11, `Max_Vbus` at 29500 mV). The EEPROM replaces them at power-up, so a running driver does not show them. | Take the defaults from the Defaults page, which lists what `#Default` writes, or from `Set_Default_config()` in `EEPROM.cpp`. | [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/defaults/) |
| KI-5 | While the E-stop bit of the last Send_gripper_data_pack (or `#Gripstop 1`) is 1, the driver raises the gripper E-stop error again on every control cycle, so Send_Clear_Error or `#Clear` alone does not clear it. | Send a gripper frame with the E-stop bit 0 (or `#Gripstop 0`) first, then clear the error. | [Gripper mode: moving](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/#moving) |
| KI-6 | The answer to a 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack goes out before the driver has acted on the command, so its object detection and error bits are those of the moment before, for example 3 (position reached) from the previous move. | Judge the new move by the answers to later frames, or poll with an empty Send_gripper_data_pack. | [Gripper mode: moving](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/#moving) |
| KI-8 | The action bit in Respond_Gripper_data_pack is a copy of the last command's action bit; the driver never clears it, so it stays 1 after the move has ended. | Tell the end of a move by the object detection, 3 position reached, 1 or 2 stopped on an object. | [Respond_Gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gripper/#respond_gripper_data_pack) |
| KI-9 | Open loop (`#Openloop`) puts the voltage `#Openv` (5000 mV by default) on the phases without a current limit; `#Ilim` does not apply, so a low-resistance motor draws far more than its limit. | Lower `#Openv` before you run a low-resistance motor in open loop, and keep the test short. | [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/) |
| KI-10 | The velocity error trips only above a fixed 20,000,000 ticks/s, about 1220 revolutions per second and far above the speeds the driver can follow; `#Vlimit` does not change it, so it does not catch a motor that runs away. | Watch the speed in your host and send Send_Idle or Send_ESTOP when it is wrong. | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/) |
| KI-11 | Only motion frames and answered status requests reset the watchdog. Setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear) and UART commands do not, so a host that only configures the driver, or a terminal session with a saved watchdog, ends in a watchdog error. | While the watchdog runs, send a status request such as Send_Respond_Encoder_data within every watchdog period. Before you work over UART alone, set the watchdog to 0 and save (`#Par 6,0`, then `#Save`). | [The watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/#the-watchdog) |
| KI-12 | The current a turned motor drives through its shorted phases while the driver brakes in idle (`#Brake 1`) is not limited. | Brake only a motor whose resistance keeps that current under 2.8 A at the speeds it is turned at, and do not let a load drive a braking motor fast. | [Braking in idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/#braking-in-idle) |
| KI-14 | Send_Respond_Device_Info carries the batch date in one byte, its lowest 8 bits, so a host reading it over CAN gets 120 for the 24092024 that `#Default` stores. | Read the batch date with `#Info` over UART, which prints the whole number. | [Send_Respond_Device_Info](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/status/#send_respond_device_info) |
| KI-19 | The encoder table holds a field current of 80 % of the current limit for about 20 s, also in the run that follows every `#Cal`. With a limit above the motor's rating (1000 mA after `#Default`), the run is above the rating too. | Set `#Ilim` for the motor before `#Encal` and before every `#Cal` (calibration puts the limit that was in force back before the runs that follow). | [Encoder table and anti-cogging: running them](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/anti-cogging/#running-them) |

### Release 104

Seen in: the image of the GitHub release V104.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-16 | For anyone who builds or reads the source of release 104, the tag `V104` is not what its image was built from. The image comes from commit `20765c9` on `Bootloader_main`, which adds Send_Voltage_Limit; the tag lacks it. | Check out `20765c9` to see or rebuild the 104 image's source; better, update the board to the current release. | [Releases: the two branches](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/releases/#the-two-branches) |

### Fixed

| | What happened | Fixed in | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-1 | The current limit of Send_Limits over CAN is used as sent, also above the driver's 2800 mA; only `#Ilim` over UART clamps it. | 109: Send_Limits stops the current limit at 2800 mA and ignores a negative value | [Send_Limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_limits) |
| KI-2 | Calibration sets the current limit to 1600 mA and leaves it there, whatever it was before; a `#Save` right after calibration stores the 1600 mA. | 109: calibration puts back the current limit that was in force when it started | [Calibration: current limit and save](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/calibration/#3-set-the-current-limit-and-save) |
| KI-7 | A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or `#Clear` during the gripper calibration stops it without a message and leaves its counters as they were, so the next calibration starts part way through; it may skip the opening or give up early. | 110: a new gripper calibration starts from its first step, also after one that was stopped (a command during the calibration still stops it) | [Gripper mode: calibrating](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/gripper-mode/#calibrating-the-gripper) |
| KI-13 | `#Save` does not keep the idle behaviour: after every power-up the driver coasts in idle again, whatever `#Brake` or Send_Settings set before. | 110: `#Save` keeps the idle behaviour (`#Brake`, Send_Settings, parameter 18) | [Braking in idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/modes/#braking-in-idle) |
| KI-15 | `#Error` prints `FAULT pin is HIGH` while the driver stage reports a fault, which is when that pin is low: the text names the wrong level. | 109: the line reads `FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault` | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/errors/) |

## Something that is not here

Check the [symptom tables](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/08-troubleshooting/) first. If it is still not explained, [Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/support/report-a-problem/)
says what to include so it can be reproduced. A fixed issue stays on this page, under "Fixed", with the release
that fixes it.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/firmware-release-notes/ -->

# Firmware release notes

What changed in each firmware release, from the release notes in the firmware repository, up to the release this site describes.

There is no release 108 for the Spectral Micro: from 109 it shares its version numbers with STEPFOC, and goes
from 107 straight to 109. [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/upgrading/) says what a driver keeps
and what to run when it moves to 109.

## V110 (2026-11-13)

Spectral BLDC firmware **V110** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader. Mostly gripper work: an SSG-48 gripper (a Spectral Micro in gripper mode) now ends its moves cleanly and closes fully at position 255. Everything below is described in the manual: [Spectral Micro docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/); what a driver keeps and what to run after the update: [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/latest/07-firmware/upgrading/).

#### Grippers
- **A move ends cleanly.** On 109 the current took over two seconds to settle after a move: the speed loop's integral was carried into the hold and unwound slowly through friction. Now the integral is dropped on arrival, the last stretch of a move slows down, and the hold has a small dead zone (a quarter of a position count). A few mA are left after a move.
- **A soft start.** A move picks up speed over 0.1 s instead of starting at full speed.
- **Positions 0 and 255 clear the stops, and 255 is fully closed.** On 109 the calibration read the ends while pushing at 500 mA, so 0 and 255 lay inside the stops: a full open or close pressed on the stop, drew the grip current for good and often reported an object. Each end is now read under a light 100 mA push (released to no current, the SSG-48's free-running jaws spring back about 1 mm off the stop); 0 sits 32 ticks inside the open stop and 255 16 ticks from the closed one. On an SSG-48 the jaws stop 0.12 mm short of fully closed at 255, and the calibration repeats within 4 ticks.
- **Object detection** reports an object after the jaws have stood still against it for 50 ms.
- **The gripper pushes with its own current limit.** On 109 every gripper command overwrote the driver's current limit (parameter 16) with its grip current, and a Save config then stored it.
- The gripper calibration can be started again while it runs, ends on a timeout or a stroke under 1000 ticks, and puts the current limit back. The position is rounded to the nearest count (it was cut off).

#### CAN bus
- **Parameters 90-93:** 90 `#Rstint`, 91 the thermistor (`#Term`), 92 gripper mode (`#Gripper`, written only while idle), each 0 or 1 and saved by Save config, so a preset over CAN can set everything (issue #1); 93, read only, the gripper's stroke between positions 0 and 255 in ticks (0 until calibrated).

#### UART
- **`#Estop`:** the E-stop, as CAN has it. The motor is released, a running calibration ends, and the E-stop latches until `#Clear`.
- **`#Close` during a motor calibration** stops the calibration (`Close: the calibration is stopped`). On 109 it switched the mode under the running calibration.

#### Settings and safety
- **Brake or coast when idle (parameter 18) is saved** by Save config. On 109 it was back to its default at every power-up. A driver that never saved it coasts, as before.
- **Watchdog:** a trip while the driver is idle no longer starts the hold or the descend (on 109 it did, for the whole fallback time). A trip while a loop is closed holds as before.

#### Compatibility
- The settings and the motor calibration of 109 are kept. The gripper calibration is kept in RAM, as always: calibrate the gripper after the update.
- Python library **1.22** (`pip install --upgrade Spectral-BLDC`) names parameters 90-93; 1.21 reads them by number. Motor GUI **0.7.0** uses what 110 adds: STOP over UART sends `#Estop`, brake or coast counts as saved, a preset over CAN writes 90-92.
- Bench-tested for this release on an SSG-48 gripper: the moves and the hold, moves of one count, the ends and the closed gap, the soft start, gripping objects, the calibration's repeatability, parameters 90-93, brake or coast over a save and a restart, the driver's current limit through gripper moves, the watchdog while idle and in a closed loop, an aborted gripper calibration. `#Estop` and `#Close` were tried over UART on the STEPFOC, which has the same code. Not tested on the bench: an upgrade from V103 with the ST-Link, and a downgrade.

#### Assets
- `spectral-bldc-firmware-V110.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `eae54f56b4d0eb3677155447a5ce68156bfbda16e81534513ad71cb0dbbbfb21`
- Size: 112984 bytes

Built from commit 38d210d on `Bootloader_main` (`#Info` shows it as `Build: 38D210D`). Includes bootloader entry support (CAN/UART reset-into-bootloader).

## V109 (2026-11-10)

Spectral Micro BLDC firmware **V109** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader. From 109 the Spectral Micro and the STEPFOC share their version numbers, so there is no 108: 109 follows 107. Everything below is described in the manual: [Spectral Micro docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/); what a driver keeps and what to run after the update: [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/latest/07-firmware/upgrading/).

#### Phase B (the main fix)
- In every release up to 107 the gate driver's phase-B enable input was fed by the microcontroller's 8 MHz clock output instead of a steady level, so phase B could drop out: weaker or uneven torque, a calibration that failed with a wrong pole-pair count, or a motor that took a current command and did not move, with no error. 109 drives the pin properly. On the bench: 5 of 5 calibrations and full torque on every test, also over 10 restarts.
- The calibration now reports the true phase resistance and inductance (on the reference gimbal motor about 7.0-7.2 Ω and 1.75-1.9 mH, where 107 reported about 6.4 Ω and 1.25 mH); the old × 1.25 correction is gone.
- **After the update:** a calibration made with 107 keeps working. Calibrate again (`#Cal`) where the motor can turn freely, so the current gains follow the true values. An assembled SSG-48 gripper keeps its calibration: apply Motor GUI's SSG-48 preset instead, with the gripper's CAN ID set first.

#### New features
- **Parameters:** any setting or read-out by number over CAN (commands 36-38) or `#Par` (parameters 1-89). Identity (39) and telemetry (40) frames.
- **Capture, histogram and buffers** (41-43).
- **Watchdog actions:** idle, brake, coast, hold the position, or descend at a capped speed, with a fallback time.
- **Current loop from R, L and one bandwidth** (parameter 49, default 160 Hz; the SSG-48 preset uses 300 Hz). Measured on the bench and on by default: the direct PLL speed estimate at 100 Hz and commutation delay compensation of 234 µs (a speed step overshoots about 18 % instead of 63 %).
- **Encoder table and anti-cogging measured on the driver:** `#Cal` runs the calibration, then both, and saves; `#Calonly` is the calibration alone.
- **Sound through the motor:** tones, a queue of notes and samples (CAN 44 and 45, `#Tone`).
- **Identification:** `#Info` and parameters 84-87 report the build (git commit), the board ID and a calibration ID. Parameters 88 and 89 are an experimental current-sampling diagnostic, off by default.
- **Settings in blocks with their own checksums;** a reset keeps the CAN ID; a product lock refuses a STEPFOC image on a Spectral board.

#### Calibration
- Both current sensors are averaged; pole pairs 1-49; a rotor that does not follow the open-loop field ends with `Open loop: Failed` and two hint lines; an inductance that gives no gains fails the calibration instead of hanging.
- Kt and KV are measured in four spins alternating direction; a warning only when two same-direction spins differ by more than 5 %.
- The gate driver stays awake for the whole calibration. A failed calibration switches the bridge off at once and enables all three phases again. An E-stop ends a calibration, and `#Cal` is refused while one is latched. Calibrating many times without a power cycle no longer uses up memory.

#### Safety
- The control loop keeps the gate driver awake in every driving mode: a command arriving at the wrong moment could leave it asleep, with no torque and no error, until the next idle.
- Limits: a negative or not-a-number value is ignored by the legacy CAN frames (limits, gains, Kt, voltage limit 0-60000 mV); `#Ilim` and `#Vlimit` take the magnitude; the current of a gripper move stays within 0-2800 mA; `#PP` and parameter 78 take 1-49 pole pairs, only while idle (50 and more would read as a STEPFOC calibration at the next start). PWM duties stay between 0 and 100 %.
- The current-sense zero waits for the motor supply: started on USB before the supply, the driver used a zero about 100 mA off. It now says so in `#Info` and measures the zero by itself once the supply is there.
- `#Error` says `FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault` (the text said HIGH). No undervoltage error while the supply ramps up at power-up.

#### CAN bus
- A gripper poll right after a new move command no longer cancels it as new: object detection reports contact again (it read "at position" while pressing on an object). The same in every release before 109.
- The current and PD frames set their setpoint and mode together. Length codes above 8 are read as 8; extended (29-bit) frames are ignored.
- Watchdog: setting its time or a save starts a fresh window; a negative time means off; hold and descend no longer use the last moving loop's delay compensation.

#### Bug fixes
- After `#Cal`, a host that takes the driver within 3 s drops the encoder-table and anti-cogging runs. `#Encal` and `#Cogcal` start only on their own words. While such a run turns the motor, a capture is not armed and the histogram is not changed.
- A storage block whose check fails is read up to three times before its defaults are used. `#Info` says the anti-cogging is saved only while what is in RAM equals what is stored.
- The sound queue and sample buffer no longer replay old content after a stop; a pitch the driver cannot play answers `Tone: not played`.

#### Compatibility
- Python library **1.21 or newer** (`pip install --upgrade Spectral-BLDC`), Motor GUI **0.5.0**.
- Bench-tested for this release: calibration, current mode, restarts, the E-stop, the encoder table and anti-cogging, and the SSG-48 gripper on its 107 calibration. Not tested on the bench: an upgrade from V103 with the ST-Link, a downgrade, and on the Spectral Micro the watchdog actions, the capture and the sound (the same code passed on the STEPFOC).

#### Assets
- `spectral-bldc-firmware-V109.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `96945eec70be12f0e74c6add5fd9fafd4054677e4ebf29d0380062c77a4f6d87`
- Size: 112420 bytes

Built from commit b5cedd5 on `Bootloader_main` (`#Info` shows it as `Build: B5CEDD5`). Includes bootloader entry support (CAN/UART reset-into-bootloader).

## V107 (2026-08-26)

Spectral BLDC firmware **V107** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

#### CAN bus
- Fixed `IN_DATA_PACK_PD` writing the commanded speed into `Feedforward_speed` instead of `Velocity_setpoint` — PD mode's KD (velocity-damping) term was being evaluated against a stale/zero setpoint, so it silently ignored the commanded speed.
- Added a generic mask+value settings command (`IN_SETTINGS`) for CAN-unreachable boolean settings, starting with idle-mode brake/coast selection.

#### Usability
- Idle mode can now be set to brake (driver stays enabled, phases held shorted via a zero-voltage PWM vector) or coast (Hi-Z, previous/default behavior), via `IN_SETTINGS` over CAN or `#Brake <0|1>` over UART.

#### Calibration
- Fixed `#Cal` spuriously failing with "Commutation/alignment check failed!" on some individual motor units. The pre-check that confirms the motor responds to a current command was driving a fixed voltage at the raw (uncalibrated) encoder angle; whether that produced torque depended on each unit's random magnet-to-encoder mounting angle. It now retries once at a 90-degree angle bias before failing.

#### Assets
- `spectral-bldc-firmware-V107.bin` — application firmware image (flash at `0x08003000`, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

#### Integrity
- SHA-256: `2ca1f2e3ad3ee7848cf47d8733b084be2daa87fc2e49f954dd41c76405d48ada`
- Size: 95404 bytes

Built from commit `2e7febc` on `Bootloader_main`.

## V106 (2026-07-06)

Spectral BLDC firmware **V106** — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

**CAN bus**
- The controller now drains up to 8 CAN messages per pass instead of just 1, so short bursts (multiple commands sent back-to-back, or a busy multi-node bus) no longer silently drop messages once the 3-deep hardware FIFO fills.
- A CAN peripheral that fails to initialize no longer bricks the board — UART stays fully usable, only the CAN bus is skipped.

**Safety**
- Added a hardware watchdog (100ms). If the control loop ever stops running, the board resets instead of leaving the motor driven at a stale duty cycle.
- Fixed a bug where `Torque_mode` could silently overwrite your commanded Iq setpoint when clamping to the current limit — reading it back after clamping now shows what you actually asked for, and raising the current limit afterward immediately restores the original commanded torque instead of requiring the command to be resent.
- Fixed undefined behavior in a serial-protocol integer conversion (`fourBytesToInt`).
- Synced default configuration values that had drifted between two locations in the code, so a fresh `#Default` and a freshly-flashed board's built-in defaults now agree.

**EEPROM / configuration integrity**
- Added CRC validation over the saved configuration, split into two independent halves: calibration data (resistance, inductance, Kt/KV, angle offset, current-loop gains, etc.) and settings (PID tuning, limits, watchdog config, CAN ID, etc.).
- This means a corrupted save (e.g. from a power loss mid-write) is detected and safely defaulted instead of silently running with garbage values — and critically, a future firmware update that only adds a new setting can no longer wipe your calibration, since the two are validated independently.
- Boards upgrading from older, pre-CRC firmware keep their existing calibration automatically — no need to recalibrate after this update.
- A few unused slots were reserved in the calibration block for upcoming features (e.g. magnet alignment), so those can be added later without another migration.

**Performance**
- PWM output no longer re-resolves which timer/channel it's writing to on every single call (it was doing this 4x per control tick) — resolved once and cached, freeing up ISR headroom.
- Velocity calculation switched from a floating-point divide to an integer multiply.

**Usability**
- New `#Help` command — prints a summary of the available commands.
- Serial now responds with `"Unknown command"` for unrecognized input instead of silently ignoring it.
- Calibration now prints progress during the angle-offset search (previously up to ~40 seconds of silence that could look like the board had hung).
- `#Info` now always reports live ISR execution time, useful for checking control-loop headroom on the bench.
- Fixed a leftover calibration-failure message that incorrectly suggested swapping motor phases — that failure mode no longer exists (reversed wiring has been auto-detected/compensated in software since V105); the message now accurately describes what actually happened (a commutation/current-response check, not a wiring-direction problem).

**Assets**
- `spectral-bldc-firmware-V106.bin` — application firmware image (flash at 0x08003000, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

**Integrity**
- SHA-256: `edb06ca112a7d24b0581e0b157a4524928067a46f8dc850ce22df8128092a758`
- Size: 94908 bytes

Built from commit `e1f8611` on `Bootloader_main`.

## V105 (2026-07-05)

Spectral BLDC firmware **V105** — reversed-wiring auto-calibration

`#Cal` now auto-detects reversed motor phase wiring during the open-loop spin and compensates it in software as a phase B<->C reflection, instead of failing and telling you to physically swap phases. Angle-offset calibration is now found automatically as part of `#Cal` itself (deterministic rotor-lock + verify + symmetry-sweep), so the standalone `#Calangle` command has been removed. `#Info` now reports the true firmware version instead of a stale EEPROM value. Existing calibrated units are unaffected and do not need `#Default`.

**Assets**
- `spectral-bldc-firmware-V105.bin` — application firmware image (flash at 0x08003000, target STM32F103CB).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256 for download verification by the web flasher.

**Integrity**
- SHA-256: `0bd80ea038b8497fca8ab6a613b083d28e3473b360fa152b512b8ab0304dedb5`
- Size: 91732 bytes

Built from commit `b7dded3` on `Bootloader_main`. Includes reversed-wiring auto-calibration (`commutation_dir` detection + phase B<->C reflection) and deterministic rotor-lock angle-offset calibration.

## V104 (2026-06-19)

Spectral BLDC firmware **V104** — bootloader build.

#### Assets
- `spectral-bldc-firmware-V104.bin` — firmware image (90,968 bytes).
- `firmware.json` — manifest with version, size, and SHA-256.

Built from commit 20765c9 on `Bootloader_main`. Includes CAN Vlim command and bootloader support.

# Hardware revisions

What changed in each revision of the Spectral Micro board, and which firmware and which revision of this manual go
with it. The board reports its hardware revision in `#Info` (`Hardware version`) and in Send_Respond_Device_Info;
the silkscreen on the bottom of the board carries the board's name and date.

| Revision | Marked | Changes | Firmware | Manual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v2.0 | Spectral motor controller micro v2.0, 10.1.2024 | the production board | 101 and newer; 104 and newer run on the bootloader | this manual |

A board that runs firmware 101 or older has no bootloader; [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/bootloader/)
brings it to the current firmware.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/appendix/theory/ -->

# Theory corner

The control concepts behind the driver's modes, for readers who want to know why a setting does what it does.
Nothing here is needed to use the driver; the chapters say what to type.

## Field-oriented control of a brushless motor

A brushless motor has three stator windings and a rotor of permanent magnets with $p$ pole pairs: one mechanical
revolution is $p$ electrical cycles, 11 for a typical 5208 gimbal motor.

The torque the rotor receives depends on the angle between the stator field and the rotor field, the *load angle*; it
is largest when the stator field stands a quarter of an electrical cycle ahead of the rotor and zero when the two are
aligned.

A hobby ESC does not measure the rotor angle: it steps the field around in six fixed states and infers the rotor's
position from the back-EMF of the winding it is not driving, which works at speed and fails at standstill. That is why
an ESC cannot hold a position or produce a controlled torque at low speed.

Field-oriented control (FOC) measures the rotor angle instead. The encoder on the motor shaft gives the mechanical
angle $\theta$; with the pole pairs $p$ and the angle offset $\theta_0$ found by calibration, the electrical angle
is $\theta_e = p\,\theta + \theta_0$.

The three phase currents, which sum to zero, are reduced to two (the Clarke transform) and then expressed in the
rotor's frame of reference (the Park transform):

$$
I_\alpha = I_U,\qquad I_\beta = \frac{I_U + 2\,I_V}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

$$
I_d = I_\alpha \cos\theta_e + I_\beta \sin\theta_e,\qquad
I_q = -I_\alpha \sin\theta_e + I_\beta \cos\theta_e
$$

$I_q$, the *quadrature* current, is the part of the current that stands at right angles to the rotor field and
produces torque: $\tau = K_t\, I_q$. $I_d$, the *direct* current, is aligned with the field and produces none. Two
PI controllers regulate $I_q$ to the torque demand and $I_d$ to zero by choosing the voltages $U_q$ and $U_d$.

The inverse transforms turn those into three phase voltages, applied by PWM at 25 kHz with space-vector modulation,
which gets about 15 % more phase voltage out of the supply than a plain sine would. The loop runs at 5 kHz.

The consequences are what makes a FOC drive behave like a servo:

- the current is only what the torque needs, so the motor runs cool and quiet;
- the field is always placed where it produces the most torque per ampere;
- the motor produces its full torque at standstill and holds a position;
- the torque is known from the current, which is what makes impedance control and force-limited motion possible.

Calibration supplies the constants this needs. The resistance $R$ and inductance $L$ of a winding are measured.
The current loop gains follow from them and the chosen bandwidth $\omega_c = 2\pi f_c$ (`#Cbw`):
$K_p = L\,\omega_c$ and $K_i = R\,\omega_c$ cancel the winding's electrical time constant and give a first-order
response at $f_c$.

The driver stores them in the form its 5 kHz loop uses: `Kpiq` is close to $L\,\omega_c$, and `Kiiq` is
$R\,\omega_c T$, with $T$ the 200 µs control period. The pole pairs come from an open-loop spin: the field is turned a
known number of electrical cycles and the encoder says how far the rotor went.

The angle offset is found by driving a current along the $d$ axis and reading where the rotor settles. The velocity
constant $K_V$ comes from the back-EMF the spinning motor generates, and the torque constant follows from it: in SI
units $K_t = 1/K_V$. The firmware computes $K_t = 8.27/K_V$ Nm/A, with $K_V$ in rpm/V.

## The cascade of loops

Position, velocity and current are controlled by three loops nested inside one another:

$$
\text{position loop: } \omega_d = K_{pp}\,(\theta_d - \theta)
\qquad
\text{velocity loop: } I_{q,d} = K_{pv}\,(\omega_d - \omega) + K_{iv}\!\int(\omega_d - \omega)\,dt
\qquad
\text{current loop: } U_q = \text{PI}(I_{q,d} - I_q)
$$

The position loop is proportional: its output is a speed demand, limited by the velocity limit. The velocity loop
is a PI controller: its output is a current demand, limited by the current limit; the integral term removes the
steady-state error a load would otherwise leave. The current loop is the innermost and fastest.

Each loop must be slower than the one inside it, by a factor of five to ten, for the inner loop to look like an
ideal actuator to the outer one.

That is why the loops are tuned from the inside out, and why a current loop bandwidth of 160 Hz (the default from
firmware 109) leaves room for a velocity loop of a few tens of hertz and a position loop below that.

A command picks where the cascade is entered: a current setpoint uses the current loop alone, a speed setpoint
the two inner loops, a position setpoint all three.

The *feedforward* terms the CAN motion frames carry are added to the demands rather than computed from an error: a
speed feedforward is added to the position loop's output, a current feedforward to the velocity loop's output.

A host that knows the trajectory can command it directly and leave the loops to correct what is left, which gives a
faster, smoother response than letting the loops produce the whole demand from the error.

An integrator accumulates error over time, and keeps accumulating while the output is at its limit; the overshoot
this causes when the limit is released is *windup*. The velocity loop's integrator is clamped to the current
limit, and `#Rstint` resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which suits a host that sends one setpoint
after another in large steps.

## Impedance control

Impedance control does not prescribe a motion or a force. It prescribes the *relation* between the two: how much
force the motor produces when it is displaced from its setpoint and how fast. The driver's PD mode implements a
spring and a damper around the setpoint:

$$
\tau = K_P\,(\theta_d - \theta) + K_D\,(\dot\theta_d - \dot\theta) + K_t\, I_{ff}
$$

with the stiffness $K_P$ in Nm/rad, the damping $K_D$ in Nm·s/rad, and a current feedforward $I_{ff}$ for a known
load such as gravity. The torque is produced by the current loop ($I_q = \tau / K_t$), which is what makes FOC a
prerequisite: a drive without the rotor angle cannot produce a commanded torque at low speed.

The driver computes the same loop in its own units. Its `KP` is in mA per encoder tick and its `KD` in mA per
tick/s (0.14 and 0.0028 by default), and the result is a current in mA.

The stiffness in Nm/rad is `KP` × $K_t$ × 2.608, and the damping in Nm·s/rad is `KD` × $K_t$ × 2.608 (16384 ticks per
turn, 1000 mA per A).

Pushed off its setpoint by an external force $F$, the motor yields by $\Delta\theta = \tau_{ext}/K_P$ and pushes
back with that force; let go, it returns, with the damper settling the motion. A small $K_P$ makes a soft joint,
a large one a stiff joint; $K_D$ without $K_P$ is a pure damper.

The setpoint can move, in which case the virtual spring drags the rotor along a trajectory with a bounded force — the
property legged robots, hand-guided arms and anything that touches people or an uncertain environment need.

The impedance loop is also what a position loop is *not*: the position loop's integral action removes any steady-state
deflection and so makes the joint as stiff as the current limit allows, which is the right thing for a machine tool
and the wrong thing for a leg.

The full impedance model includes an inertia term, $M\ddot\theta$; the driver, like most joint controllers, leaves
it out, so the apparent inertia is the motor's own.

## Admittance control

Admittance is the inverse relation: the controller measures the force and commands a motion,

$$
\dot\theta_d = \frac{\tau_{ext} - K\,(\theta - \theta_0)}{B}
$$

on top of a stiff position controller. It is the natural form for a machine that has a force sensor and a position
loop that cannot be made soft, such as an industrial arm; impedance control is the natural form for a machine whose
actuator is a torque source, such as a FOC motor.

The driver has no force sensor and implements impedance; a host that wants admittance behaviour can estimate the
external torque from $K_t I_q$ minus the known load and command positions accordingly, with the limits of that
estimate (friction, cogging, the current loop's accuracy).

## Compliance and stiffness

Stiffness $K$ is the force per unit of displacement; compliance is its inverse, $C = 1/K$, the displacement per
unit of force. *Passive* compliance is in the mechanism — a spring, a flexible finger, a belt; *active* compliance
is in the controller — the impedance loop above.

The driver offers three points on that scale: the position mode, stiff up to the current limit; the PD mode, as stiff
as $K_P$; and the current mode, which is no stiffness at all, a torque source the host shapes as it likes.

The current limit `#Ilim` is a force limit in every mode: the largest torque the motor will produce before it
yields, whatever the loops ask. Set it for the motor's rating, and for the mechanism's.

## Which mode

| Mode | Behaviour under an external force | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Position | holds the position up to the current limit, then yields | positioning, machines, anything that must not deflect |
| Velocity | holds the speed up to the current limit | wheels, conveyors, spindles |
| PD (impedance) | deflects in proportion to the force, returns when released | legs, arms that touch things or people, hand guiding, teleoperation |
| Current (torque) | produces the commanded torque, moves as the load dictates | a host that closes its own loop, gravity compensation, force-limited pressing |

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/terminology/ -->

# Glossary

**Activated**
:   Two flags with the same name. The controller's flag is set by `#Activate` and reported in
    Send_Respond_State_of_Errors; nothing else uses it. The gripper's activate bit is set by `#Gripact`, `#Grippos`
    and Send_gripper_data_pack; in gripper mode a move is carried out only while it is set.

**Angle offset** (theta offset)
:   The angle between the encoder's zero and the motor's electrical zero, found by calibration and stored. The
    driver needs it to place the current vector relative to the rotor.

**Anti-cogging**
:   A current added to the current setpoint, a function of the electrical angle, that cancels the motor's own
    torque ripple (the pull of its magnets towards the stator's teeth and the ripple of current-sensing errors).
    Identified on the driver (`#Cogcal`, parameter 43; firmware 109 and newer).

**Back-EMF**
:   The voltage a turning motor generates in its own windings, proportional to speed. It opposes the supply, limits
    the top speed at a given voltage, and is what calibration measures to find KV, Kt and the flux linkage.

**Board ID**
:   The bootloader's own address, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. The firmware sets it to the CAN node
    ID when the configuration is saved. The `Board ID` line of `#Info` (parameter 86, firmware 109 and newer) is
    another thing: 8 hex digits from the chip's unique number, which never change.

**Bootloader**
:   The program in the first 12 KB of the driver's flash on boards that run firmware 104 or newer. It starts the
    firmware, and loads a new firmware over UART or CAN. See [The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/07-firmware/the-bootloader/).

**Calibration**
:   The routine (`#Cal`) that checks the magnet and the supply, measures the motor's resistance and inductance,
    computes the current loop gains, spins the motor in open loop to find the pole pairs and the phase order, aligns
    the encoder to the rotor field and measures Kt, KV and the flux linkage. Its result is kept with `#Save`.

**CAN ID** (node ID)
:   The address of the driver on the CAN bus, 0 to 13 (the field holds 0 to 15, but the bootloader reserves 14 and
    15). It occupies bits 10 to 7 of the 11-bit CAN frame identifier; the command ID occupies bits 6 to 1 and the
    error bit is bit 0.

**CANvas**
:   Source Robotics' USB-to-CAN adapter. It appears as a serial port and speaks slcan, which `python-can` and Motor
    GUI use.

**Clarke and Park transforms**
:   The two steps that turn the three phase currents into the two components FOC regulates: Clarke reduces the three
    phases to two axes fixed to the stator, Park turns those into the frame that rotates with the rotor (the d-q
    frame).

**Command ID**
:   The number, 0 to 63, in bits 6 to 1 of a CAN frame identifier that says which message the frame carries. The
    API reference lists every command ID.

**Commutation**
:   Placing the stator current so that it produces torque at the rotor's present angle. FOC does it continuously
    from the encoder angle and the angle offset; a hobby ESC does it in six steps from the back-EMF, which fails at
    standstill.

**Commutation delay compensation** (parameter 64)
:   Turning the output voltage forward by the angle the rotor covers between the angle reading and the moment the
    voltage reaches the motor. 234 µs on the Spectral Micro by default.

**Control mode**
:   What the driver is doing with the motor: idle, position, velocity, current, PD (impedance), voltage torque, open
    loop, gripper, or calibration. A command that carries a setpoint puts the driver in the matching mode.

**Current loop bandwidth** (`#Cbw`, parameter 49)
:   How fast the current loop follows a change of its setpoint, in Hz. The current loop gains follow from it and
    the motor's resistance and inductance: Kpiq ≈ ω·L, Kiiq = ω·R·T (T the 200 µs control period). 160 Hz by default from firmware 109 (500 Hz before).

**Current-sense zero**
:   The reading of a current sensor with no current flowing. From firmware 109 the driver measures it at every
    start-up and subtracts it.

**Daisy chain**
:   Several drivers on one CAN bus and one supply, each driver's second CAN and power connector feeding the next.

**d-q frame**
:   The rotating frame of reference FOC works in: the q axis is at right angles to the rotor field and the current on
    it (Iq) produces torque; the d axis is along the field and its current (Id) produces none, so it is held at 0.

**Diametrical magnet**
:   A disc magnet whose poles are across its diameter, so the field turns with the shaft. The encoder needs this
    kind; an axially magnetised disc looks the same and does not work.

**EEPROM**
:   The non-volatile memory on the driver that holds the configuration and the calibration. `#Save` writes it,
    `#Default` restores the factory values.

**Encoder table**
:   A correction of the encoder's small angle error around the turn, measured on the driver (`#Encal`, parameter
    52) and saved with the configuration (firmware 109 and newer).

**Encoder ticks**
:   The unit of position: the 14-bit magnetic encoder gives 16384 ticks per revolution of the motor shaft, counted
    over as many revolutions as the motor makes. Speed is in ticks per second.

**Error bit**
:   Bit 0 of every CAN frame identifier the driver sends: 1 while any error is active.

**Feedforward**
:   A term added to a loop's output from what is known in advance rather than from the error: the motion frames
    carry a speed and a current feedforward so a host that knows the trajectory can command it directly, leaving
    the loops to correct the rest.

**Field-oriented control** (FOC)
:   Controlling a motor by regulating the stator current as a vector in the rotor's frame, from a measurement of the
    rotor angle. The three phase currents are reduced to a torque-producing and a field-producing component, each
    regulated by its own loop, which gives smooth torque at any speed down to standstill, a known position, and
    the most torque per ampere.

**Firmware release**
:   One build of the firmware, numbered 101, 104, 105, … and tagged `v101`, `V104`, `V105`, … in the firmware
    repository. `#Info` prints the release a driver runs. This documentation describes one release; the version
    selector switches between them.

**Flux linkage**
:   The rotor's magnetic flux as seen by a winding, in weber; found by calibration from the back-EMF, together with
    KV and Kt.

**Gimbal motor**
:   A brushless motor wound with many turns of thin wire for low speed and smooth torque at low current, originally
    for camera gimbals: a phase resistance of a few ohms to a few tens of ohms, and many pole pairs. The kind of
    motor the Spectral Micro is made for.

**Gripper mode**
:   The driver running a gripper (`#Gripper 1`): jaw positions from 0 (open) to 255 (closed), a speed, a current
    limit that becomes the grip force, and object detection.

**Heartbeat**
:   A frame (Respond_Heartbeat) the driver sends at a set interval so the host knows it is alive. Off by default.

**Iq, Id**
:   The two components of the motor current in the d-q frame: Iq produces torque, Id is normally held at 0. The
    current mode's setpoint and limit are Iq values.

**Impedance (PD) mode**
:   The control mode in which the driver behaves like a spring and a damper around a position setpoint, with the
    stiffness `KP` and the damping `KD`, plus a current feedforward.

**Kt, KV**
:   The motor's torque constant (torque per ampere) and velocity constant (speed per volt), found by calibration.
    Kt turns a current into an estimated torque; KV gives the top speed at a supply voltage.

**Motor GUI**
:   Source Robotics' browser tool for the driver: setup, calibration, tuning, plots and firmware updates over a
    serial or CAN adapter.

**Open loop**
:   Turning the stator field at a set electrical speed without the encoder in the loop, so that the rotor follows it
    like a stepper: `#Openloop`, and the open-loop spin of the calibration that finds the pole pairs.

**Parameter**
:   A setting reached by its number through Send_Parameter and Send_Get_Parameter (CAN 36 to 38) or `#Par`
    (firmware 109 and newer). The numbers are permanent.

**Phase order**
:   The order in which the motor's three phases are connected to U, V and W. Firmware 105 and newer learns it during
    calibration and compensates it; firmware 101 asks for two wires to be swapped when it is reversed.

**PIN** (ADDITIONAL)
:   The spare pin of the driver, on the three-pad header next to the UART connector, usable as an analog input or a
    digital input/output. The firmware's name for it is ADDITIONAL.

**PLL (speed estimate)**
:   A phase-locked loop that follows the encoder count and gives the speed with less lag than a moving average
    (parameter 50, firmware 109 and newer; the direct PLL at 100 Hz is the default).

**Pole pairs**
:   The number of electrical cycles per mechanical revolution, half the number of rotor magnets: 7 for a typical
    2804 gimbal motor, 11 for a 5208, 14 for an 8108. Calibration finds it; `#PP` sets it by hand.

**Product lock**
:   The stamp in the EEPROM of the product that calibrated a board. A firmware that finds the other product's
    stamp drives nothing (firmware 109 and newer).

**Remote frame**
:   A CAN frame with the RTR bit set and no data: a request. The host asks for data with a remote frame under a
    command ID, and the driver answers with a data frame under the same ID.

**Sound** (`#Tone`, CAN 44 and 45)
:   Tones, a queue of notes and recorded samples the driver adds to its output voltage while it holds or moves, so
    the motor plays them (firmware 109 and newer).

**STEPFOC**
:   Source Robotics' stepper driver, the Spectral Micro's sister: similar hardware and firmware and practically
    the same commands, for two-phase stepper motors.

**Termination**
:   The 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node of a CAN bus need. The switch on the driver turns it on.

**Tool id** (`#Tool`, parameter 1)
:   What a drive is built into: 0 none, 1 SSG-48, 11 to 33 an MSG, 200 to 254 a customer's tool.

**Vbus**
:   The supply voltage at the driver, measured and printed in mV. Outside the limits the driver raises a Vbus
    error.

**Watchdog**
:   A timer the driver resets with every motion command and status request it receives over CAN. When it is set
    (Send_Watchdog) and runs out, the driver reports a watchdog error and stops; from firmware 109 it holds,
    brakes, coasts or descends as the watchdog's action says.

# API reference

Every CAN message and every UART command of the firmware release this site describes, the factory defaults of
its settings and which of them are saved, the error flags, and the map from the Python library's calls to the
messages they send.

## Where the facts come from

The command IDs, the frame lengths the firmware accepts, the responses it sends, the list of UART commands with
their kind (Set/Get, Get or action), their argument type, the mode each enters and what it prints, the parameter
numbers, and the defaults are read from the firmware's source at its release tag by `tools/sync_firmware.py` in
the documentation repository, and the pages are built from that at every build. The descriptions, units and byte layouts are
written by hand, and the build fails when they name a command the firmware does not have, or miss one it has, or
when a byte layout does not fit the frame. The firmware version is in the version box on the
[landing page](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/).

## Conventions

- **Bytes** are numbered from 0, the first byte on the bus (`data[0]`). Multi-byte values are **big-endian**: the
  most significant byte first. Floats are IEEE 754 single precision in 4 bytes.
- **Bits** inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit: bit 7 is the first flag the firmware packs
  into the byte, bit 0 the last.
- **Encoder ticks**: 16384 per revolution; speeds in ticks per second; currents in mA; voltages in mV.
- UART command names are **case-sensitive** and spelled exactly as the firmware compares them.

## In the API reference

- [CAN protocol](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/): the identifier, the three kinds of message, every message by group, and every
  [parameter](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/)
- [UART commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/): the syntax and every command by group
- [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/defaults/)
- [Errors and LED states](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/errors/)
- [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/python/): library call → message

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can-tools/ -->

# CAN frame tool and downloads

Build or inspect a frame using the command definitions of this manual's firmware release. All calculations
run in your browser; the tool does not connect to an adapter or send commands to hardware.

## Downloads

[Command definitions (JSON)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/can/protocol-V110.json) · [Position DBC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/can/protocol-V110-position.dbc) · [Velocity DBC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/can/protocol-V110-velocity.dbc) · [Current DBC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/can/protocol-V110-current.dbc)

The JSON includes the firmware tag, source commit, message IDs, every documented layout and its bit order.
The DBC files cover **nodes 0 to 13**, with both the clean and fault-bit identifiers of driver replies.
Reserved commands are omitted. Values use the firmware's native units: ticks, ticks/s, mA and the units in
the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/).

Choose the DBC for the `Send_data_pack_1` layout your host sends:

| File | Command layout |
|---|---|
| Position DBC | 8 bytes: position, speed feedforward, current feedforward |
| Velocity DBC | 5 bytes: speed, current feedforward |
| Current DBC | 2 bytes: current |

The three layouts share a CAN identifier. DBC cannot select a layout from the frame's length, so load the
matching file; the browser decoder below handles all three lengths. Other message layouts are the same in
each download.

An RTR request uses the same identifier as its data reply. DBC describes the **data reply**; it does not
represent the request's RTR flag or the empty gripper status poll. Both are supported by the browser tool.

The gripper's two object-detection bits have an unusual order: bit 5 is the low bit, bit 4 the high bit.
The DBC signal `gripper_object_detection_raw` retains the wire value and supplies text labels (raw 2 =
object while closing, raw 1 = object while opening). The browser decoder converts that pair to the firmware's
numeric status (1 = closing, 2 = opening).

## Try a frame

The example `0x07A`, data `C8 1E 01 2C C0`, is a command to gripper node 0: position 200, speed 30,
current 300 mA, activate and action set, E-stop and release direction clear. These are an illustration of the
encoding; the device's current and motion limits still apply. Select another message above the fields to build
one of its documented forms. To inspect a reply, enter its identifier and data bytes below.

<div class="can-tool" data-schema="../../assets/can/protocol-V110.json" markdown="0">
  <p class="can-tool__status" role="status">Loading the firmware's command definitions…</p>
  <fieldset><legend>Build a frame</legend>
    <label for="ct-node">Node ID (0–13)</label><input id="ct-node" name="node" type="number" min="0" max="13" step="1" value="0">
    <label for="ct-command">Message and layout</label><select id="ct-command" name="command"></select>
    <label><input name="error" type="checkbox"> Driver reply has an active fault (error bit 1)</label>
    <div class="can-tool__fields"></div>
    <button type="button" name="build" class="md-button md-button--primary">Build frame</button>
    <pre class="can-tool__built" aria-live="polite"></pre>
    <button type="button" name="use" class="md-button">Use this frame in the decoder</button>
  </fieldset>
  <fieldset><legend>Decode a frame</legend>
    <label for="ct-id">CAN identifier (hex)</label><input id="ct-id" name="identifier" type="text" value="0x07A" spellcheck="false">
    <label for="ct-data">Data bytes (hex, up to eight)</label><input id="ct-data" name="data" type="text" value="C8 1E 01 2C C0" spellcheck="false">
    <label><input name="remote" type="checkbox"> Remote request (RTR; no payload)</label>
    <button type="button" name="decode" class="md-button md-button--primary">Decode frame</button>
    <div class="can-tool__decoded" aria-live="polite"></div>
  </fieldset>
  <noscript>Enable JavaScript for the frame tool, or use the reference tables and downloads above.</noscript>
</div>

!!! success "Check"
    The example decodes to the values above. Change the identifier to `0x1FA` to see the same command
    addressed to node 3. An invalid length or out-of-range field produces an explanation instead of a frame.

For wiring, termination, host timing and recovery, use [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/can/). To look up a
message's purpose and accepted lengths, use the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/ -->

# CAN protocol

CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. The identifier carries the node ID (bits 10 to 7, 0 to 15), the command ID
(bits 6 to 1, 0 to 63) and, in frames from the driver, the error bit (bit 0). [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/can/)
explains how the pieces are used; this page lists them.

Three kinds of message:

- **Send_…** — the host sends data to the driver. A few are answered (the motion commands with
  Respond_data_pack_1, the gripper command with Respond_Gripper_data_pack); most are not.
- **Send_Respond_…** — the host asks for data with a **remote frame** (RTR bit set, no data) under the command ID;
  the driver answers with a data frame under the same command ID.
- **Respond_…** — frames only the driver sends.

Multi-byte values are big-endian (data[0] first); floats are IEEE 754 single precision; bits inside a byte are
numbered from the most significant bit (bit 7 first).

## By group

- [Motion](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/motion/): the motion commands and their answers
- [Gains and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gains-and-limits/): the loop gains, the limits, Kt
- [Status requests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/status/): temperature, voltage, device info, errors, current, encoder, Kt, identity,
  telemetry, the heartbeat
- [System](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/): node ID, E-stop, idle, save, reset, clear, watchdog, heartbeat setup, settings
- [Parameters and buffers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/): the parameters behind Send_Parameter and Send_Get_Parameter, every one
  of them, and the buffers: capture, histogram, anti-cogging, encoder table
- [Sound](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/sound/): tones, the queue and samples through the motor
- [Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gripper/): the gripper command, calibration and the gripper state

## The Python library

Every message the host can send has a method of the same name in `Spectral_BLDC.SpectralCAN`, listed in
[Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/python/).

## Tools and downloads

[Build or decode a CAN frame, and download this firmware's JSON and DBC definitions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can-tools/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/motion/ -->

# Motion

The commands that move the motor and the frames that come back.

### Send_data_pack_1

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 2</span><span class="fact">host → driver</span><span class="fact">2 or 5 or 8 bytes</span><span class="fact">Python: `Send_data_pack_1()`</span></div>

The motion command. Its length decides the control mode the driver enters: 8 bytes command a position with a speed and a current feedforward, 5 bytes a speed with a current feedforward, 2 bytes a current. Send 0 for a feedforward you do not use. A frame of any other length is ignored (the driver flags it as a wrong data length) but still answered.

**8 bytes** — position setpoint with speed and current feedforward (position mode)

<div class="ref-table fields" markdown>

| Byte | Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2 | Position setpoint | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks |
| 3-5 | Speed feedforward | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks/s |
| 6-7 | Current feedforward | signed 16-bit | mA |

</div>

**5 bytes** — speed setpoint with current feedforward (velocity mode)

<div class="ref-table fields" markdown>

| Byte | Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2 | Speed setpoint | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks/s |
| 3-4 | Current feedforward | signed 16-bit | mA |

</div>

**2 bytes** — current setpoint (current mode)

<div class="ref-table fields" markdown>

| Byte | Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-1 | Current setpoint | signed 16-bit | mA |

</div>

The driver answers with **Respond_data_pack_1**.

Every form resets the watchdog. With `Rstint` set, the integral accumulators are cleared on each new setpoint. From firmware 109 a position or speed frame that follows another mode (idle, current, PD, a watchdog trip) starts the velocity integral from zero, so a release from a wound-up mode does not kick; one that follows position or velocity mode keeps it. The new setpoint, the mode change and the driver's wake-up reach the control loop together, so the first frame after Idle is followed.

---

### Send_data_pack_PD

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 4</span><span class="fact">host → driver</span><span class="fact">8 bytes</span><span class="fact">Python: `Send_data_pack_PD()`</span></div>

Puts the driver in impedance (PD) mode and sets the position, speed and current feedforward of the PD loop, whose gains are KP and KD (Send_PD_Gains).

**8 bytes**

<div class="ref-table fields" markdown>

| Byte | Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2 | Position setpoint | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks |
| 3-5 | Speed setpoint | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks/s |
| 6-7 | Current feedforward | signed 16-bit | mA |

</div>

The driver answers with **Respond_data_pack_1**.

Firmware 106 and older wrote the speed into the feedforward instead of the PD loop's speed setpoint, so the speed term had no effect; 107 fixed it.

---

### Respond_data_pack_1

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 3</span><span class="fact">driver → host</span><span class="fact">8 bytes</span></div>

The driver's answer to Send_data_pack_1 and Send_data_pack_PD: where the motor is, how fast it turns and the current it draws. The Python library stores them as `position`, `speed` and `current`.

**The frame** (8 bytes)

<div class="ref-table fields" markdown>

| Byte | Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2 | position | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks |
| 3-5 | speed | signed 24-bit | encoder ticks/s |
| 6-7 | current | signed 16-bit | Iq in mA |

</div>

---

### Send_data_pack_2

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 6</span><span class="fact">host → driver</span><span class="fact">not implemented</span></div>

Reserved. The firmware has no handler for this ID and the Python library's call does nothing.

---

### Send_data_pack_3

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 8</span><span class="fact">host → driver</span><span class="fact">not implemented</span></div>

Reserved. The firmware has no handler for this ID and the Python library's call does nothing.

---

### Respond_data_pack_2

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 5</span><span class="fact">driver → host</span><span class="fact">0 bytes</span></div>

Reserved; the driver never sends it.

---

### Respond_data_pack_3

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 7</span><span class="fact">driver → host</span><span class="fact">0 bytes</span></div>

Reserved; the driver never sends it.

---

### Send_Iq

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">ID 21</span><span class="fact">host → driver</span><span class="fact">not implemented</span></div>

Reserved; the firmware has no handler for this ID. Use the 2-byte form of Send_data_pack_1 for a current setpoint.
