<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/motion/ -->

# Motion

<div class="cmd-index" markdown>[`#Iq`](#iq) [`#Id`](#id) [`#V`](#v) [`#P`](#p) [`#PD`](#pd) [`#PDV`](#pdv) [`#PDI`](#pdi) [`#Uq`](#uq) [`#Ud`](#ud) [`#Openloop`](#openloop) [`#Idle`](#idle) [`#Estop`](#estop) [`#Brake`](#brake) [`#Close`](#close)</div>

### `#Iq` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: current setpoint in mA</span><span class="fact">Enters **current** mode</span></div>

Current (torque) control with the given Iq setpoint.

**Response:** the measured Iq in mA

---

### `#Id` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: current setpoint in mA</span></div>

Sets the Id setpoint; normally left at 0. Also parameter 58.

**Response:** the measured Id in mA

---

### `#V` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: speed setpoint in encoder ticks/s</span><span class="fact">Enters **velocity** mode</span></div>

Velocity control with the given speed.

**Response:** the measured speed in ticks/s

---

### `#P` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: position setpoint in encoder ticks</span><span class="fact">Enters **position** mode</span></div>

Position control to the given position.

**Response:** the measured position in ticks

---

### `#PD` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: position setpoint in encoder ticks</span><span class="fact">Enters **PD** mode</span></div>

Impedance (PD) control around the given position with the gains KP and KD.

**Response:** the measured position in ticks

---

### `#PDV` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: speed setpoint in encoder ticks/s</span></div>

The speed setpoint of the PD loop.

**Response:** the PD speed setpoint

---

### `#PDI` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: current feedforward in mA</span></div>

The current feedforward of the PD loop.

**Response:** the PD current feedforward

---

### `#Uq` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span><span class="fact">Enters **voltage torque** mode</span></div>

Voltage-torque mode with the given q-axis voltage (no current loop).

**Response:** the Uq setpoint in mV

---

### `#Ud` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span></div>

The d-axis voltage used in voltage-torque mode; does not change the mode.

**Response:** the Ud setpoint in mV

---

### `#Openloop` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: electrical speed in rad/s</span><span class="fact">Enters **open loop** mode</span></div>

Turns the stator field at the given electrical speed without the encoder in the loop, with the voltage set by Openv. Without a number it still starts the motor, at the stored speed: `#Openloop` alone is not a query. The speed is the same setting as `#Opens`.

**Response:** the open-loop speed

---

### `#Idle` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact">Enters **idle** mode</span></div>

Goes to idle; the motor coasts or brakes as set by Brake.

**Response:** `Idle`

---

### `#Estop` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

The E-stop, as Send_ESTOP over CAN: it raises the E-stop error, the driver disables the motor, which coasts, and a calibration, gripper calibration or encoder-table or anti-cogging run that is running ends. The error stays until Clear. Added in firmware 110.

**Response:** `E-stop`

---

### `#Brake` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

What the motor does in idle: 1 brakes (the phases are shorted through the driver), 0 coasts (the phases are open, the default). Takes effect once the driver is idle, so send Idle first. From firmware 110 Save keeps it; on 109 the driver coasted again after a power cycle. Also parameter 18. An error always disables the motor, which then coasts. The braking current is not limited, see Control modes. Added in firmware 107.

**Response:** the setting

---

### `#Close` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact">Enters **idle** mode</span></div>

Leaves open loop and goes back to closed-loop idle. From firmware 110, while a calibration (Cal, Calonly) runs, it stops the calibration instead: it ends as a failed one (`Calibration failed!`), with the motor released and the driver not calibrated until it calibrates again. Firmware 109 switched the mode under the running calibration.

**Response:** nothing; `Close: the calibration is stopped` during a calibration (firmware 110)

---


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/gains/ -->

# Gains and limits

<div class="cmd-index" markdown>[`#Kpp`](#kpp) [`#Kpv`](#kpv) [`#Kiv`](#kiv) [`#Kpiq`](#kpiq) [`#Kiiq`](#kiiq) [`#Kpid`](#kpid) [`#Kiid`](#kiid) [`#KP`](#kp) [`#KD`](#kd) [`#Vlimit`](#vlimit) [`#Ilim`](#ilim) [`#Vlim`](#vlim) [`#Rstint`](#rstint) [`#Cbw`](#cbw)</div>

### `#Kpp` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Kp of the position loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kpv` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Kp of the velocity loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kiv` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Ki of the velocity loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kpiq` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Kp of the Iq current loop; also sets Kpid.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kiiq` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Ki of the Iq current loop; also sets Kiid.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kpid` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Kp of the Id current loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kiid` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

Ki of the Id current loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#KP` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

KP of the impedance (PD) loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#KD` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: gain</span></div>

KD of the impedance (PD) loop.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Vlimit` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: speed in encoder ticks/s</span></div>

The speed limit: the speed the position loop may command, and the largest velocity setpoint. (The velocity integrator is clamped to the current limit.) The magnitude of a negative number is taken.

**Response:** the current limit

---

### `#Ilim` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: current in mA</span></div>

The Iq current limit. Set it to the rated phase current of your motor; the firmware clamps it to 2800 mA and takes the magnitude of a negative number.

**Response:** the current limit

---

### `#Vlim` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span></div>

The voltage limit of the current loops (Ud and Uq); 0 means use the supply voltage.

**Response:** the current limit in mV

---

### `#Rstint` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

Whether the integral accumulators are reset on every new setpoint. From firmware 110 also parameter 90.

**Response:** the setting

---

### `#Cbw` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: bandwidth in Hz, 10 to 500</span></div>

The current loop bandwidth. From firmware 109 setting it computes Kpiq and Kiiq at once from R and L, the way calibration does, and prints them (the same as parameter 49); a value outside 10-500, or with R or L at 0, changes nothing. Not saved: 160 Hz after a power cycle, but the gains it set are kept by Save.

**Response:** the bandwidth, then `Kp_iq = …, Ki_iq = …`

---


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/calibration/ -->

# Calibration and motor parameters

<div class="cmd-index" markdown>[`#Cal`](#cal) [`#Calonly`](#calonly) [`#Encal`](#encal) [`#Cogcal`](#cogcal) [`#R`](#r) [`#L`](#l) [`#PP`](#pp) [`#Kt`](#kt) [`#KV`](#kv) [`#Flux`](#flux) [`#Offset`](#offset) [`#Iqoffset`](#iqoffset) [`#Magnet`](#magnet) [`#Dir`](#dir) [`#Phase`](#phase) [`#Resv`](#resv) [`#Calpwr`](#calpwr) [`#Openv`](#openv) [`#Opens`](#opens) [`#Vp`](#vp) [`#Calibrated`](#calibrated)</div>

### `#Cal` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact">Enters **idle** mode</span></div>

Runs the calibration routine (see Calibration): it measures R and L, finds the pole pairs, the phase order and the angle offset, and measures Kt, KV and the flux linkage. It uses its own 1600 mA current limit for its steps; from firmware 109 it puts the limit that was in force back when it ends. From firmware 109, when it succeeds, the encoder table and then the anti-cogging follow by themselves, and everything is saved (about a minute; keep the shaft free).

**Response:** the calibration log

---

### `#Calonly` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact">Enters **idle** mode</span></div>

The calibration alone: like Cal, but nothing follows it. Save afterwards with Save. Added in firmware 109.

**Response:** the calibration log

---

### `#Encal` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> nothing, or save, all, stop, on, off, state</span></div>

The encoder table (see Encoder table and anti-cogging). Alone it measures the table and uses it: the field turns the rotor open loop one shaft turn each way at 2048 ticks/s, about 20 s, with the shaft free. `save` also saves; `all` then identifies the anti-cogging and saves both; `stop` aborts; `on` and `off` switch the correction (on only with a measured table, and not while a run turns the motor); `state` or any other word only prints. The same as parameters 52 and 53. Added in firmware 109; not yet tested on a Spectral Micro.

**Response:** `Encoder table: <state>`, then the table's error in degrees

---

### `#Cogcal` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> nothing, or save, trim, stop, state</span></div>

The anti-cogging identification on the drive (see Encoder table and anti-cogging): one motor turn forward and one back in velocity mode at parameter 44's speed (1500 ticks/s, about 22 s), the shaft free to turn. `save` also saves; `stop` aborts, also the encoder part of a combined run; `state` or any other word only prints. `trim` identifies like the plain command on the Spectral Micro: its firmware skips the current-sense trim. Added in firmware 109; not yet tested on a Spectral Micro.

**Response:** `Anti-cogging identification: <state>`, the speed and the identified cogging in mA rms, and the harmonics when done

---

### `#R` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: resistance in Ω</span></div>

The phase resistance of the motor, measured by Cal; it can also be set by hand. Also parameter 76, in mΩ.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#L` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: inductance in H</span></div>

The phase inductance of the motor, measured by Cal; it can also be set by hand. Also parameter 77, in µH.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#PP` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: pole pairs</span></div>

The motor's pole pairs, found by Cal; they can also be set by hand. Also parameter 78: 1-49, only while idle (50 and more would read as a STEPFOC calibration); from 109 `#PP` answers `PP: not taken (1-49, and only while idle)` otherwise.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Kt` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: Nm/A</span></div>

The torque constant, found by calibration.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#KV` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: rpm/V</span></div>

The velocity constant, found by calibration.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Flux` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: Wb</span></div>

The flux linkage, found by calibration. Works over UART from firmware 109; the parser of 107 and older accepted only the lowercase `#flux`, which had no handler.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Offset` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: angle in rad</span></div>

The angle offset between encoder zero and electrical zero, found by calibration.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Iqoffset` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: current in mA</span></div>

The current used by the angle-offset search and the commutation check of Cal, 300 mA by default. Not saved.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Magnet` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Reads the encoder's magnet status.

**Response:** `Magnet Good` or `Magnet Bad`

---

### `#Dir` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

The base direction of the encoder and phase mapping. Calibration always sets it to 1 (0 after `#Default`); the direction it finds is the commutation direction, which `#Info` prints.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Phase` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the phase order found by calibration.

**Response:** `Phase order is: N`

---

### `#Resv` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span></div>

The voltage the resistance test of Cal starts at; it rises until the power reaches Calpwr. Not saved.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Calpwr` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: power in W</span></div>

The power the resistance and inductance tests of Cal may dissipate in the motor. Not saved.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Openv` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span></div>

The voltage of the open-loop spin, in calibration and with Openloop. Not saved.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Opens` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> float: electrical speed in rad/s</span></div>

The speed of the open-loop spin in calibration; the same setting as the speed of `#Openloop`.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Vp` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span></div>

The voltage of the phase-order search in calibration. Not saved.

**Response:** the current value

---

### `#Calibrated` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

The calibrated flag. `#Calibrated 1` clears a calibration error without calibrating; the motor may still be uncalibrated.

**Response:** the flag

---


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/utility/ -->

# Status and utility

<div class="cmd-index" markdown>[`#Save`](#save) [`#Reset`](#reset) [`#Default`](#default) [`#Pullconfig`](#pullconfig) [`#Info`](#info) [`#Tone`](#tone) [`#Par`](#par) [`#Tool`](#tool) [`#WdFb`](#wdfb) [`#Product`](#product) [`#Param`](#param) [`#Help`](#help) [`#Error`](#error) [`#Clear`](#clear) [`#Mode`](#mode) [`#Vbus`](#vbus) [`#Vmax`](#vmax) [`#Temp`](#temp) [`#Term`](#term) [`#Tlim`](#tlim) [`#Iabc`](#iabc) [`#PWM`](#pwm) [`#LED`](#led) [`#CANID`](#canid) [`#SERNUM`](#sernum) [`#Activate`](#activate) [`#Cyc`](#cyc) [`#Cyca`](#cyca)</div>

### `#Save` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

Writes the configuration to the EEPROM. Do it after calibration and after tuning.

**Response:** `Save`

---

### `#Reset` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

Resets the driver. From firmware 104 the reset lands in the bootloader, which waits 2 s for a flashing host and then starts the firmware again.

**Response:** nothing

---

### `#Default` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

Writes the factory defaults to the EEPROM and loads them: the calibration is erased (Not calibrated), the gripper flag, heartbeat and watchdog are cleared, the hardware version and batch date are set to 1 and 24092024, and 1111 is stored as the serial number; from firmware 109 also the tool id (0), the watchdog fallback, and the anti-cogging set, the encoder table, its trims and parameter 56 (cleared). From firmware 109 the CAN node ID is kept (0 only when no valid one is stored). Note the values first.

**Response:** `Loaded default config!`

---

### `#Pullconfig` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the whole configuration on one line, for Motor GUI.

**Response:** the configuration

---

### `#Info` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

Prints the driver's identity and the motor: hardware version, batch date, firmware version, ISR time, CAN ID, calibrated or not, temperature, Vbus, Dir, phase order, commutation direction, the speeds of the calibration spin, pole pairs, R, L, Kt and KV. From firmware 109 also the build (`Build:`, the git commit, with `+` when built with uncommitted changes), the `Board ID` (this board, from the chip's unique number; not the bootloader's board ID), the `Calibration ID` (new at every successful calibration), the CAN receive overruns and dropped transmits, the product, the current-sense zeros, the tool id, the watchdog and its fallback, settings block 2, the anti-cogging, and at the end the `In force:` section (see Status and diagnostics). The serial number is `#SERNUM`, the gains `#Param`, the errors `#Error`.

**Response:** the report

---

### `#Tone` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> f,mA[,ms], or off</span><span class="fact">Enters **position** mode</span></div>

A tone through the motor (see Sound): `#Tone 440,250,1000` plays 440 Hz at a loudness of 250 mA for 1000 ms, on the axis parameter 82 picks. mA left out: 200; ms left out: 500; ms 0: until `#Tone off`. 20 Hz up to below 2500 Hz. It plays only while the driver holds or moves; from idle a calibrated driver first holds the position it is at (`#Idle` releases it). `#Tone` alone or `#Tone off` stops all sound. Added in firmware 109.

**Response:** `Tone 440 Hz, 250 mA, 1000 ms`; from idle first `Holding the position while it plays (#Idle releases it)`; `Tone: not played (…)` when it cannot; `Tone off`

---

### `#Par` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: n, or n,value</span></div>

Any parameter by its number (see Parameters and buffers): alone it lists every parameter, `#Par 1` reads one, `#Par 1,200` sets it (no spaces); a gain or limit (8-16, 20) takes a decimal, e.g. `#Par 9,0.02` sets Kpv. Added in firmware 109.

**Response:** `P<n> = <value>`; `refused: out of range, read only, not now, or unknown` when the driver did not take it; `P<n> unknown`

---

### `#Tool` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 to 255</span></div>

The tool id: what the drive is built into, 0 none, 1 SSG-48, 11-33 MSG (tens = rail 1/2/3 = 100/150/200 mm, units = stepper 1/2/3 = 21.5/40/60 mm), 200-254 your own. The same as parameter 1. Kept by Save. Added in firmware 109.

**Response:** `Tool ID: N`, or `Invalid tool id (0-255)`

---

### `#WdFb` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int list: time_ms,current_mA,speed_ticks_s,after_action</span></div>

The watchdog fallback, four numbers at once without spaces, e.g. `#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2`: how long hold or descend runs, descend's current and speed cap, and what follows (0 legacy, 2 brake, 3 coast). The same as parameters 2 to 5, clamped the same way; fewer than four numbers change nothing. Kept by Save. Added in firmware 109.

**Response:** `Watchdog fallback: … ms, … mA, … ticks/s, then …`

---

### `#Product` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> nothing, or claim, clear</span></div>

The product lock: prints this firmware and the board's stamp. `claim` stamps the board as this product (a repaired board, a motor the stamp rule misjudges), `clear` removes the stamp; power-cycle after either. Over UART only. Added in firmware 109.

**Response:** `Firmware: Spectral Micro; board stamp: …`

---

### `#Param` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints every gain of every loop.

**Response:** the gains

---

### `#Help` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

Prints a short command reference. Added in firmware 106.

**Response:** the reference

---

### `#Error` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints which errors are active.

**Response:** `No errors!` or `In error state!`, then one line per active error (see Errors and LED states), and `FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault` while the driver stage's fault pin is active

---

### `#Clear` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact">Enters **idle** mode</span></div>

Clears the errors and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; a calibration error is cleared only by calibrating (or `#Calibrated 1`).

**Response:** `Clear errors`

---

### `#Mode` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the control mode. In voltage-torque mode (`#Uq`) it prints nothing.

**Response:** `Idle mode`, `Position control`, `Speed control`, `Current control`, `PD control`, `Open loop`, `Gripper mode`, `Gripper calib mode`

---

### `#Vbus` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the supply voltage.

**Response:** mV

---

### `#Vmax` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: voltage in mV</span></div>

The supply voltage above which a Vbus error is raised: 29000 mV after `#Default`.

**Response:** `Vmax in mV: N`

---

### `#Temp` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the thermistor temperature.

**Response:** °C, or `Temp Off` while the thermistor is disabled

---

### `#Term` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

Enables the thermistor measurement and the temperature error (off by default). From firmware 110 also parameter 91.

**Response:** the setting

---

### `#Tlim` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: temperature in °C</span></div>

The temperature at which the temperature error is raised; 75 by default.

**Response:** `Temp limit N`

---

### `#Iabc` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the phase currents.

**Response:** `Ia`, `Ib`, `Ic` in mA

---

### `#PWM` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the PWM duty values.

**Response:** the duties

---

### `#LED` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

Turns the status LED on or off.

**Response:** the LED state

---

### `#CANID` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 to 13</span></div>

The CAN node ID. Use 0 to 13: the firmware accepts 14 and 15, but the bootloader reserves them and a driver on one of those cannot be updated over CAN. Kept over a power cycle after Save, which also copies it into the bootloader's board ID; from firmware 109 Default and a settings reset keep it too.

**Response:** the ID, or `Invalid CAN ID`

---

### `#SERNUM` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: number</span></div>

The serial number. Save writes it to the EEPROM, but the firmware does not read it back at power-up: after a power cycle the driver reports 1.

**Response:** `Serial number is: N`

---

### `#Activate` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span></div>

Sets the controller's activated flag (bit 6 of byte 1 of Send_Respond_State_of_Errors). It is not the gripper's activate bit, which `#Gripact` and Send_gripper_data_pack set.

**Response:** `Controller activated`

---

### `#Cyc` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: interval in ms (0 = off)</span></div>

Sends position, speed and Iq on its own every interval: `$ <position> <speed> <Iq>`; for BetterSerialPlotter.

**Response:** `Cyclic disabled` for `#Cyc` without a number; `#Cyc 0` stops the output without an answer

---

### `#Cyca` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: interval in ms (0 = off)</span></div>

Like Cyc, in the Arduino plotter format `Position:x,Speed:y,Iq:z`.

**Response:** `Cyclic disabled` for `#Cyca` without a number; `#Cyca 0` stops the output without an answer

---


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/uart/gripper/ -->

# Gripper

<div class="cmd-index" markdown>[`#Gripper`](#gripper) [`#Gripcal`](#gripcal) [`#Grippos`](#grippos) [`#Gripvel`](#gripvel) [`#Gripcur`](#gripcur) [`#Gripact`](#gripact) [`#Gripstop`](#gripstop) [`#Gripinfo`](#gripinfo)</div>

### `#Gripper` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

Whether this driver is a gripper. Save it; `#Default` clears it. From firmware 110 also parameter 92, which takes a write only while the driver is idle.

**Response:** the flag

---

### `#Gripcal` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Action</span><span class="fact">Enters **gripper calibration** mode</span></div>

Starts the gripper calibration (the jaws find their end stops). From firmware 110 each end is read under a light 100 mA push after the 500 mA one, and 0 and 255 lie a few ticks inside the two ends; the gripper stays uncalibrated when the ends lie less than 1000 ticks apart, and Gripcal during a calibration starts it again from its first step. Parameter 93 then gives the stroke in ticks.

**Response:** `Gripper calibration!`

---

### `#Grippos` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 (open) to 255 (closed)</span><span class="fact">Enters **gripper** mode</span></div>

The position setpoint; also activates the gripper, sets the action bit and goes to gripper mode.

**Response:** the current position

---

### `#Gripvel` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 to 255</span></div>

The speed setpoint of gripper moves.

**Response:** the setpoint

---

### `#Gripcur` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: current in mA</span></div>

The current limit of gripper moves. From firmware 109 a gripper move uses its magnitude and stops at 2800 mA; see the gripper manual for the safe range. From firmware 110 it is the gripper's own limit: the driver's current limit (Ilim) stays as set.

**Response:** the setpoint

---

### `#Gripact` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

The activate bit.

**Response:** the bit

---

### `#Gripstop` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Set/Get</span><span class="fact"><span class="k">Argument</span> int: 0 or 1</span></div>

The gripper E-stop bit.

**Response:** the bit

---

### `#Gripinfo` 

<div class="cmd-facts" markdown><span class="fact">Get</span></div>

Prints the gripper state: whether the driver is a gripper, calibrated, activated, the position, speed and current setpoints, the E-stop, action and object-detection status, and the end stops.

**Response:** the report

---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/defaults/ -->

# Defaults

The settings of the firmware, read from its source at the release this site describes. The table leaves out
the firmware's internal state (counters, flags, scratch variables).

- **Start value** is the value in the firmware's structures (`common.h`). At power-up the firmware loads the saved
  settings from the EEPROM over it, so for a setting that `#Save` keeps the start value only shows until the EEPROM
  is read.
- **After `#Default`** is what the driver runs with after `#Default`, which writes the factory values to the EEPROM
  and loads them. A fresh board, and a board whose saved configuration fails its check at power-up, gets the same
  values.
- **Kept by `#Save`** says whether the setting survives a power cycle. *No* means the driver starts with the start
  value again after every power-up.

`#Default` also erases the calibration; from firmware 109 it keeps a valid stored CAN node ID (`existing_id` in
the table; 0 when none is stored); see [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/05-setup/saving/). A name after a value,
such as `160 (CURRENT_BANDWIDTH_DEFAULT)`, is the constant in `constants.h` the value comes from. The settings of
firmware 109 that are parameters, the anti-cogging and the encoder table among them, are in the
[parameter table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#every-parameter) with their defaults.

<div class="ref-table defaults" markdown>

| Variable and firmware comment | Start value | After `#Default` | Kept by `#Save` |

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/errors/ -->

# Errors and LED states

## The LED

| Pattern | State |
|---|---|
| three short flashes, a pause | normal operation: calibrated, no error |
| fast flashing, about 10 times a second | calibration running |
| blinking for about 2 s after power-up | the bootloader waits for a host before it starts the firmware |
| on, steady | error mode, or not calibrated |
| off | no power, or `#LED 0` |

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Fast flashing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |

## The error flags

The flags as the firmware keeps them, the line `#Error` prints for each, and where each sits in the two bytes of
Send_Respond_State_of_Errors (bits numbered from the most significant).

| Flag | `#Error` prints | Byte, bit | Raised when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Error` | `In error state!` | 0, 7 | any of the flags below is set (also the error bit of every CAN identifier) |
| `temperature_error` | `Temp error` | 0, 6 | the thermistor reads above `#Tlim` or below −20 °C (with `#Term 1`) |
| `encoder_error` | `Encoder error` | 0, 5 | the magnet is not detected or the reading fails its check |
| `Vbus_error` | `Vbus error` | 0, 4 | the supply is below 9 V or above `#Vmax` (29 V after `#Default`); from firmware 109 a low supply is not checked in the first 500 ms after power-up |
| `Driver_error` | `Drv error` | 0, 3 | the MOSFET driver reported a fault on its fault pin: undervoltage, thermal shutdown or overcurrent. `#Error` also prints `FAULT pin is LOW: the gate driver reports a fault` while the fault output is still active |
| `Velocity_error` | `Velocity error` | 0, 2 | the measured speed exceeds 20,000,000 ticks/s (about 1220 revolutions per second), a fixed limit: a runaway or an encoder fault, not `#Vlimit` |
| `Current_error` | `Current error` | 0, 1 | never in this firmware; reserved |
| `ESTOP_error` | `Received ESTOP command` | 0, 0 | Send_ESTOP was received, or from firmware 110 `#Estop` over UART |
| `Calibrated` (0) | `Not calibrated` | 1, 7 (1 = calibrated) | the motor has not been calibrated |
| `Activated` | — | 1, 6 | the activated flag, not an error |
| `Watchdog_error` | `Watchdog error` | 1, 5 | the watchdog time passed without a motion command or an answered request over CAN |
| `wrong_product` | `Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)` | 1, 4 | from firmware 109: the firmware found the other product's stamp, or a calibration its product cannot make, at start-up; it drives nothing |

Gripper mode has its own flags in Respond_Gripper_data_pack: a temperature error (the driver's temperature
error), a timeout error (the driver's watchdog error: the CAN watchdog ran out) and an E-stop error; see the
[Gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gripper/) reference.

## Clearing

`#Clear` and Send_Clear_Error clear every flag except `Calibrated` and go to idle; a flag whose cause persists is
set again at once. While any flag is set the driver disables the motor, which coasts whatever `#Brake` says. The watchdog, E-stop and velocity errors clear and stay clear; the Vbus, encoder, driver and
temperature errors come back until the cause is gone. Calibration clears the calibration error. A wrong product
stays until the right firmware is flashed. Clearing a watchdog error also ends a watchdog hold or descend.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/python/ -->

# Python library

The `Spectral-BLDC` package ([Spectral-BLDC-Python](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python),
`pip install Spectral-BLDC`) has one method per CAN message in `Spectral_BLDC.SpectralCAN`, and
`Spectral_BLDC.CanCommunication` for the bus. [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/python/) shows how they are used.

| `Send_data_pack_PD()` | [Send_data_pack_PD](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/motion/#send_data_pack_pd) (ID 4)<br><span class="meta">Motion</span> | Respond_data_pack_1 |
| `Send_PD_Gains()` | [Send_PD_Gains](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_pd_gains) (ID 16)<br><span class="meta">Gains and limits</span> | — |

| `Send_CAN_ID()` | [Send_CAN_ID](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_can_id) (ID 11)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_ESTOP()` | [Send_ESTOP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_estop) (ID 0)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Idle()` | [Send_Idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_idle) (ID 12)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Save_config()` | [Send_Save_config](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_save_config) (ID 13)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Reset()` | [Send_Reset](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_reset) (ID 14)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Clear_Error()` | [Send_Clear_Error](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_clear_error) (ID 1)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Watchdog()` | [Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_watchdog) (ID 15)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Heartbeat_Setup()` | [Send_Heartbeat_Setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_heartbeat_setup) (ID 30)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Settings()` | [Send_Settings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/system/#send_settings) (ID 35)<br><span class="meta">System</span> | — |
| `Send_Parameter()` | [Send_Parameter](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#send_parameter) (ID 36)<br><span class="meta">Parameters and buffers</span> | — |
| `Send_Get_Parameter()` | [Send_Get_Parameter](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#send_get_parameter) (ID 37)<br><span class="meta">Parameters and buffers</span> | Respond_Parameter |
| `Send_Buffer_Read()` | [Send_Buffer_Read](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#send_buffer_read) (ID 41)<br><span class="meta">Parameters and buffers</span> | — |
| `Send_Cogging_Harmonic(), Send_Cogging_Table()` | [Send_Buffer_Write](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/parameters/#send_buffer_write) (ID 43)<br><span class="meta">Parameters and buffers</span> | — |
| `Send_Sound()` | [Send_Sound](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/sound/#send_sound) (ID 44)<br><span class="meta">Sound</span> | — |
| `Send_Samples()` | [Send_Sound_Samples](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/sound/#send_sound_samples) (ID 45)<br><span class="meta">Sound</span> | — |
| `Send_gripper_data_pack()` | [Send_gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_data_pack) (ID 61)<br><span class="meta">Gripper</span> | Respond_Gripper_data_pack |
| `Send_gripper_calibrate()` | [Send_gripper_calibrate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_calibrate) (ID 62)<br><span class="meta">Gripper</span> | — |

</div>

The calls for the messages added in firmware 109 (Send_Parameter, Send_Get_Parameter, Send_Respond_Identity,
Send_Respond_Telemetry, Send_Buffer_Read, Send_Cogging_Harmonic, Send_Cogging_Table, Send_Sound, Send_Samples),
Send_Settings and Send_Brake_Coast for the idle behaviour, and the actions 'Coast' and
'Descend' of Send_Watchdog, come with library 1.21. It also adds calls built on the
parameters, among them Send_Watchdog_Fallback, Send_Tool_ID, Send_Cogging_Mode, Send_Capture_Setup,
Send_Capture_Trigger, Send_Histogram, Send_Cogging_Calibrate and Send_Encoder_Calibrate; the sound calls Send_Tone,
Send_Sound_Stop, Send_Sound_Event, Send_Sound_Play, Send_Sound_Clear, Send_Samples_Play and Send_Samples_Stop on top
of Send_Sound and Send_Samples; and the module `Spectral_BLDC.music` (note names, ringtone melodies, MIDI and WAV
files as queue events and samples, see [Sound](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/06-operation/sound/)).

The same release adds `Spectral_BLDC.helpers`, blocking functions that send a request and wait for the answer:
`get_parameter` and `set_parameter` (which reads the value back), `read_identity`, `read_telemetry`, `features`,
`read_buffer`, `capture`, `wait_for_state` (for the encoder table, the anti-cogging and other runs), and
`play_events` and `stream_samples` for sound. They are for setting up and diagnostics, not for the inside of a fast
control loop. The library's `examples` folder shows them at work: `parameters_and_status.py`, `capture.py`,
`calibration_features.py`, `watchdog.py` and `sound.py`.

The same release is stricter about what it sends and reads:

- `Send_Parameter` takes the value itself. Parameters 8 to 16 and 20 are sent as floats
  (`Send_Parameter(16, 1500)` is 1500 mA); every other parameter takes a whole number, and anything else raises
  `ValueError`.
- A position or a speed that does not fit 24 bits, or a current that does not fit 16 bits, raises `ValueError`;
  1.20 wrapped it round. `Send_Voltage_Limit` raises `ValueError` outside 0 to 60000 mV.
- A node ID must be 0 to 15.
- `UnpackData` ignores frames from other nodes, remote frames and extended frames.
- Parameters 79, 80 and 84 to 87 read as unsigned numbers.
- A send that fails returns `False` and is logged once.

## Receiving

`CanCommunication.receive_can_messages(timeout)` returns `(message, ids)`: the raw `python-can` message and a tuple
`ids` with `node_id`, `command_id` and `error_bit` from the identifier, or `(None, None)` after the timeout.
`SpectralCAN.UnpackData(message, ids)` decodes the message into the object's attributes:

| Message | Attributes |
|---|---|
| Respond_data_pack_1 | `position`, `speed`, `current` |
| Send_Respond_Encoder_data | `position`, `speed` |
| Send_Respond_Iq_data | `current` |
| Send_Respond_Temperature | `temperature` |
| Send_Respond_Voltage | `voltage` |
| Send_Respond_Device_Info | `HARDWARE_VERSION`, `BATCH_DATE`, `SOFTWARE_VERSION`, `SERIAL_NUMBER` |
| Send_Respond_State_of_Errors | `error`, `temperature_error`, `encoder_error`, `vbus_error`, `driver_error`, `velocity_error`, `current_error`, `estop_error`, `calibrated`, `activated`, `watchdog_error`; from 1.21 also `wrong_product` |
| Send_Respond_Identity (1.21 and newer) | `product_id`, `product_name`, `tool_id`, `firmware_version`, `identity_hardware_version`, `pole_pairs`, `identity_calibrated`, `identity_flags` |
| Send_Respond_Telemetry (1.21 and newer) | `temperature`, `voltage`, the error flags as above, `current` |
| Respond_Parameter (1.21 and newer) | `parameters[number]` (floats for 8-16 and 20), `unknown_parameter`; `tool_id` and `watchdog_fallback` when those parameters come in |
| Respond_Buffer_Data (1.21 and newer) | `capture[index]`, `histogram[bin]`, `cogging_harmonics[slot]`, `cogging_table[index]`, `encoder_table[index]` |
| Send_Respond_Kt | `Kt` |
| Respond_Gripper_data_pack | `gripper_position`, `gripper_current`, `gripper_activated`, `gripper_action_status`, `gripper_object_detection`, `gripper_temperature_error`, `gripper_timeout_error`, `gripper_estop_error`, `gripper_calibrated` |

!!! note "Object detection in the library"
    Library 1.20 and older assemble `gripper_object_detection` with the two bits swapped relative to the
    firmware, so they report 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object detected while opening) and 2 where it sends 1
    (object detected while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. 1.21 and newer read them right.

# Guides

Worked examples with code, from a first Python program to a mobile robot, a leg, a gravity-compensated arm and two
motors coupled over a network, and the SimpleFOC library as an alternative firmware. The CAN commands and the Python
library are the same on STEPFOC, so the code runs there unchanged.

- [Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/python/): read a driver's position and speed over CAN
- [Mobile robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/mobile-robot/): two wheels driven from a game controller
- [Quadruped leg](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/quadruped/): the kinematics and control of a two-motor leg
- [Gravity compensation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/gravity-compensation/): hold a link against gravity with a current feedforward
- [Bilateral teleoperation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/bilateral-teleoperation/): two motors that follow each other, with force feedback
- [SimpleFOC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/simplefoc/): running the SimpleFOC library on the Spectral Micro instead of the Spectral firmware

More examples are in the [Spectral-BLDC-Python examples](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/python/ -->

# Python guide

More examples are in the [Spectral-BLDC-Python examples folder](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples).

## Examples

``` py title="Get_encoder_data.py"
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# Init comms channel 
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
# Init motor object
Motor1 = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1)

while True:

    # Send this msg to the motor controller, it will respond with position and speed data
    Motor1.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()

    # Get CAN msg, timeout tells us to continue if there is no msg after in this case 0.2 s
    message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.2) 

    # If there was a msg unpack it
    if message is not None:
        print(f"Message is: {message}")
        print(f"Node ID is : {UnpackedMessageID.node_id}")
        print(f"Message ID is: {UnpackedMessageID.command_id}")
        print(f"Error bit is: {UnpackedMessageID.error_bit}")
        print(f"Message length is: {message.dlc}")
        print(f"Is is remote frame: {message.is_remote_frame}")
        print(f"Timestamp is: {message.timestamp}")
        
        # Here we unpack the data from the packet
        Motor1.UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
        # We are interested in position and speed data that was requested by calling Send_Respond_Encoder_data
        print(f"Motor position is: {Motor1.position}")
        print(f"Motor speed is: {Motor1.speed}")

    else:
        print("No message after timeout period!")
    print("")
    time.sleep(1 )
```

# Mobile robot guide

## Intro
This guide is a really simple example on how you can control mobile robot based on **spectral micro BLDC drives** using xbox controller! <br />

**By following this guide you will be able to make something like this: [Link!](https://youtu.be/LGMLyr4dZZ0)**

!!! tip "Python API"
    This guide leverages [Spectral BLDC python API](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main)

What you will need to create a simple mobile robot is:

* 2 x spectral micro BLDC - used for 2 wheels 
* Wires to connect everything up: [CAN wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [Power wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable)
* 2 x BLDC motors
* 1 x [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter)
* 1 x Drill battery adapter: [Example](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_DExmYtl) - This is great way to power your BLDC motors with cheap and affordable batteries
* A Laptop or raspberry pi
* Xbox controller

!!! note "Building the robot"
    In this guide we only recommend you the hardware you can use to build the robot you designed. We do not offer already made designs you can build!

## Setup

![Two drivers powered from a drill battery, each with a gimbal motor, on one CAN bus with the CAN adapter and a laptop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/AMR_setup.webp)

The setup will be the same for any kind of mobile robot. You will need to follow the  diagram above to wire everything up.

* First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using. 
* After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
* Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
* Connect the power to both drivers. You can daisy chain it or use 2 separate wires.
* You will also need to connect your xbox controller to the PC/laptop via Bluetooth.

The code below is really simple example that drives the robot using the left joystick of the controller. It sets
a watchdog on both drivers, so the wheels stop if the program or the laptop stops; clear the watchdog error
(`#Clear` or Send_Clear_Error) before the next run, as the code does at its start.

``` py title="Spectral_mobile_robot_xbox.py"
from inputs import get_gamepad
import math
import threading
import time
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM3', bitrate=1000000)
Motor = []

# We are using 2 motors with IDs 0 and 1
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

# Stop the wheels when this program stops sending: a watchdog of 500 ms on each driver.
# Every Send_data_pack_1 below resets it; if none arrives for 500 ms, the driver stops the motor.
for m in Motor:
    m.Send_Clear_Error()
    m.Send_Watchdog(500)

timeout_setting = 0.00005

MAX_JOY_VAL = math.pow(2, 15)
DEADBAND_THRESHOLD = 0.1

# Read xbox controller and output left joystick x and y positions
def read_left_joystick():
    left_joystick_x = 0
    left_joystick_y = 0
    
    def monitor_left_joystick():
        nonlocal left_joystick_x, left_joystick_y
        while True:
            events = get_gamepad()
            for event in events:
                if event.code == 'ABS_Y':
                    left_joystick_y = event.state / MAX_JOY_VAL  # normalize between -1 and 1
                elif event.code == 'ABS_X':
                    left_joystick_x = event.state / MAX_JOY_VAL  # normalize between -1 and 1

                  # Apply deadband
                if abs(left_joystick_x) < DEADBAND_THRESHOLD:
                    left_joystick_x = 0
                if abs(left_joystick_y) < DEADBAND_THRESHOLD:
                    left_joystick_y = 0

    monitor_thread = threading.Thread(target=monitor_left_joystick)
    monitor_thread.daemon = True
    monitor_thread.start()

    while True:
        yield left_joystick_x, left_joystick_y

# Robot control 
def control_robot():
    for x, y in read_left_joystick():
        # Assuming the robot has two wheels and speed can be controlled independently
        left_wheel_speed = y + x
        right_wheel_speed = y - x
        
        # Limit the speed between -1 and 1
        left_wheel_speed = max(min(left_wheel_speed, 1), -1)
        right_wheel_speed = max(min(right_wheel_speed, 1), -1)
        
        # Use the calculated speeds to control the robot's wheels        
        print("Left Wheel Speed:", left_wheel_speed)
        print("Right Wheel Speed:", right_wheel_speed)

        # Send data to all motors
        Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(None,int(left_wheel_speed * 1000000),0)
        Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(None,int(right_wheel_speed * -1000000),0)

        for i in range(1, 4):  # read up to 3 replies
            message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
            print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

            # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
            if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
                
                Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
                print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, speed is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].speed}")

        time.sleep(0.05)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    control_robot()

```


---

# Quadruped robot guide

## Intro
In this guide we will show you how you can control a leg of any quadruped robot using Spectral micro BLDC drivers. <br />If you can control one of them you can control all the rest!<br />

**After you finish this guide you will be able to do something like this:** [video](https://youtu.be/g9rHJr9-tok)<br />

!!! tip "Python API and toolbox"
    This guide leverages [Spectral BLDC python API](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main) and [Source robotics toolbox](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Source-Robotics-Toolbox)

![The robot leg: two motors, each with its driver, on one CAN bus](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/LEG_wiring.webp)

!!! note "Building the LEG"
    In this guide we only recommend you the hardware you can use to build the robot you designed. We do not offer already made designs you can build!

This guide will cover:

* How to define the robot leg kinematic chain
* How to execute simple trajectories with the leg

What you will need:

* 2 x spectral micro BLDC 
* Wires to connect everything up: [CAN wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [Power wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable)
* 2 x BLDC motors
* 1 x [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter)
* 1 x 24V power supply
* A Laptop or raspberry pi

![Two drivers daisy-chained on power and CAN, with the CAN adapter to the PC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/leg_setup.webp)

The setup will be the same for any kind of quadruped leg. You will need to follow the diagram above to wire everything up.

* First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using. 
* After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
* Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
* Connect the power to both drivers. (Use daisy chain)

## Leg kinematics

![The coordinate frames of the leg and its DH table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/robot_leg_dh_table.webp)

First you will need to assign coordinate frames to your leg model.
We already did it but if you want to learn more on how and why check this [Link](https://automaticaddison.com/how-to-assign-denavit-hartenberg-frames-to-robotic-arms/)<br />

Now we will need to find DH (Denavit-Hartenberg) table values. You can learn more on how and why we did it [Here!](https://automaticaddison.com/how-to-find-denavit-hartenberg-parameter-tables/)

value l1 is 0.112 meters and value l2 is 0.1 meters. The frame 2 is the end / foot of our leg.

## Testing / Calibrating the leg

Before running the main code lets check if the comms are working and get initial position values of our robot leg. This code will try to get data from the 2 motors of our robot leg.

We are most interested in position data of those 2 motors. Position the leg like shown in this image. Run the leg_calib code and write down position values of each motor. 

![The leg in its reference pose and the positions leg_calib.py prints](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/leg_terminal.webp)

``` py title="leg_calib.py"

import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM6', bitrate=1000000)
Motor = []

Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1)) 

timeout_setting = 0.00005

while True:

    Motor[0].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    Motor[1].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()

    for i in range(1, 7):  # read up to 6 replies
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        print(f"unpack {i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
            #print(Motor)
            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID [0]}, speed is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].speed}, current is {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].current },pos is {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            """
            print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, speed is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].speed}")
            print(f"Error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].error}")
            print(f"Temperature rror is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].temperature_error}")
            print(f"Encoder error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].encoder_error}")
            print(f"Vbus error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].vbus_error}")
            print(f"Driver error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].driver_error}")
            print(f"Velocity error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].velocity_error}")
            print(f"Current error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].current_error}")
            print(f"Estop error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].estop_error}")
            print(f"Watchdog error is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].watchdog_error}")
            print(f"Calibrated is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].calibrated}")
            print(f"Activated is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].activated}")
            """

    time.sleep(0.5)
``` 

## Follow a specific trajectory

Joint level control involves directly controlling the angles or positions of the robot's individual joints. Each joint is treated as an independent actuator, and the control system sends commands to each joint to achieve the desired angles. 

For this example we will not use joint level control but a different method called Task/Cartesian Level Control.<br />
 Task or cartesian level control focuses on controlling the position and orientation of the robot's end-effector in a Cartesian coordinate system (X, Y, Z coordinates and orientations).

In our robot leg case we don't have Z axes (or orientation) and our end-effector is foot (end of our robot leg).

In this example we will follow a circle trajectory i X,Y plane.
We defined that trajectory with our function generate_circle_coords and with parameters: 

* center - Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters
* radius - Radius of the circle in meters
* speed - Speed of the end-effector in meters per second
* time_var - Elapsed time in seconds

![The circle the foot follows at a speed of 1 and of 3](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/circ_2.webp)

How precise you follow the trajectory depends on the speed you set. With low speeds you can track the circle perfectly. With larger speeds the system can't keep up and overshoots. This is due multiple reaseons like:

* Inertia and Momentum: At higher speeds, the inertia and momentum of the robot leg increase, making it harder to change directions quickly and accurately.
* Centrifugal and Coriolis Forces
* Trajectory Planning and Execution - at higher speeds our trajectory has less points to create a full circle. This is due a fixed rate we send data to our motors eg. every 20ms. 
* Feedforward Control: Lack of proper feedforward control can lead to errors in trajectory tracking, as the controller might not anticipate the required accelerations and decelerations.

You can see that from the example with speed set to 1 and 3.

## Example code

This code will make your robot leg draw the above circles. It might look complicated but it is not. Once you understand how this example works you can use it as a base for building more complicated projects. 

``` py title="2DOF_leg_demo.py"
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
# We are using v1.1.0
from roboticstoolbox import DHRobot, RevoluteDH, ERobot, ELink, ETS
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from oclock import Timer, loop, interactiveloop
import math
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast
INTERVAL_S = 0.02

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([14000,2430]) # These are the positions we got from calib code
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 0.90476190] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

# Setup your CAN coms. Change the channel to match your CAN adapter
Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM6', bitrate=1000000)

# Define our motors
Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

# Define the joints
Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = -np.pi/2, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

testing = 5

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])
received_ids = [0,0]

# robot length values (metres)
l = [0.112, 0.1]

alpha_DH = [0,0]

# Create robot model using DH params
L1 = RevoluteDH(a=l[0],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[0])
L2 = RevoluteDH(a=l[1],d = 0,alpha=alpha_DH[1])
robot = DHRobot([L1,L2], name="Two link")

prev_pos = np.array([0,0])
speed_var = np.array([0,0])

def generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time):
  """
  Generates x,y coordinates for a circle at a given time, considering constant speed.

  Args:
      center: Tuple representing the center coordinates (x, y) in meters.
      radius: Radius of the circle in meters.
      speed: Speed of the end-effector in meters per second.
      time: Elapsed time in seconds.

  Returns:
      Tuple containing the x and y coordinates in meters.
  """

  # Calculate angular displacement based on speed and time
  angular_displacement = speed * time

  # Use parametric equations for a circle to generate coordinates
  x = center[0] + radius * math.cos(angular_displacement)
  y = center[1] + radius * math.sin(angular_displacement)

  return (x, y)

def save_xy_data(filename, xy_data):
  """
  Saves a list of x,y coordinates to a text file.

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file to save the data to.
      xy_data (list): A list of tuples containing x and y coordinates.
  """

  with open(filename, 'a') as file:
    for x, y in xy_data:
      file.write(f"{x},{y}\n")
  
# Example usage with update loop (adjust update_interval for your needs)
center = (-0.04, -0.17)
radius = 0.03
speed = 0.8
time_var = 0

# We are using oclock module to generate stable interval defined with INTERVAL_S
timer = Timer(interval=INTERVAL_S, warnings=False, precise=True)
while timer.elapsed_time < 1100000:

    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    #Motor[0].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    #Motor[1].Send_Respond_Encoder_data()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = Needed_joint_pos[0],Speed = speed_var[0], Current = 0)
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = Needed_joint_pos[1],Speed = speed_var[1], Current = 0)

    # Handles data we get from the motors
    for i in range(1, 3):  # read up to 2 replies
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
            
            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # Generate desired x,y coordinates with respect to time_var
    x, y = generate_circle_coords(center, radius, speed, time_var)

    # Create a matrix with those x,y coordinates
    T2 = SE3(x, y, 0)
    # Perform inverse kinematics (get joint data from x,y data)
    q1 = robot.ik_LM(T2, q0 = [-0.8,-1],mask = [1,1,0,0,0,0])
    Needed_joint_pos[0] = Joint[0].get_encoder_position(q1[0][0])
    Needed_joint_pos[1] = Joint[1].get_encoder_position(q1[0][1])  
    speed_var[0] = ((Needed_joint_pos[0] - prev_pos[0]) / INTERVAL_S)
    speed_var[1] = ((Needed_joint_pos[1] - prev_pos[1]) / INTERVAL_S)
    print(speed_var)
    prev_pos[0] = Needed_joint_pos[0]
    prev_pos[1] = Needed_joint_pos[1]
    # Process or visualize the generated coordinates (x, y)
    #print(f"Time: {time_var:.2f}s, Coordinates: ({x:.4f}, {y:.4f})")

    # Update time
    time_var += INTERVAL_S

    t2 = time.perf_counter()
    #print(f"total time is {t2-t1}")

    T = robot.fkine(position_values)
    xy = T.t
    #print(f"{xy[0]},{xy[1]}")
    xy_data = [(xy[0], xy[1])]  # Assuming xy is a single pair of coordinates
    # Save data to a txt file
    save_xy_data('my_data.txt', xy_data)
    #time.sleep(0.05)

```

## Plot data

Script that will plot the data of your leg:

``` py title="plot_leg_data.py"

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_data(filename):
  """
  Plots data from a text file in the format:
  x1, y1
  x2, y2
  ...

  Args:
      filename (str): The name of the text file containing the data.
  """

  try:
    with open(filename, 'r') as file:
      data = file.readlines()

    x_data = []
    y_data = []
    for line in data:
      # Split the line based on comma (",")
      values = line.strip().split(',')

      # Check if there are exactly two values per line
      if len(values) != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid line format in file '{filename}': {line}")

      try:
        x = float(values[0])
        y = float(values[1])
      except ValueError:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid data type in file '{filename}': {line}")

      x_data.append(x)
      y_data.append(y)

    # Ensure equal x and y scales
    plt.axis('equal')

    # Create the plot
    plt.plot(x_data, y_data)

    # Customize the plot (optional)
    plt.xlabel('X-Position')
    plt.ylabel('Y-Position')
    plt.title('Data Plot from ' + filename)

    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

  except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: File '{filename}' not found.")
  except (ValueError, TypeError) as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

# Example usage
filename = 'C:\\Users\\xx\\Desktop\\test_code\\env\\Robot_leg\\data_2.txt'  # Replace with your actual filename
plot_data(filename)

```

# Gravity compensation

<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ax6jpcH3168?si=d5UKeyYru_Y35xdS" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

## What is Gravity Compensation?

Gravity compensation is a fundamental concept in robotic control that helps counteract the effects of gravity on a robot's joints and links. By applying the necessary motor current to balance this torque, the robotic joint can remain stationary at any position without additional external forces.

## Why is it so important?

In robotics, a significant portion of motor power is consumed just fighting against gravity. Gravity compensation algorithms are standard in all industrial robots and collaborative robot arms because they provide: improved position accuracy and control, smoother motion planning, and more precise force control applications.

The gravity compensation algorithm works as a feedforward component to the motor PID control loops, reducing their computational load and improving overall performance.

## The Approach

In this example, we use the Robotics Toolbox for Python to model a "robotic arm" with a single revolute joint. We compute the required torque using the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) and convert this torque into a motor current/torque that the motor controller will command the motor.

For more info check the full guide here:  [https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/gravity-compensation-in-robotics](https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/gravity-compensation-in-robotics)

Github repos with examples are here: [Github repo](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/blob/main/examples/Advanced/Gravity%20compensation/BOM.md), [Github repo2](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples/Advanced/Gravity%20compensation)

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/guides/bilateral-teleoperation/ -->

# Bilateral teleoperation guide

## What is bilateral teleoperation?
Bilateral teleoperation is a concept that Involves two-way communication where both the operator and the remote device send and receive feedback. The operator controls the device remotely and receives sensory feedback (such as force) from the device to adjust their actions.

The two grippers are virtually coupled to each other, allowing either to act as the master (the haptic interface) or the slave (the manipulator) in the system. We are not using a force sensor at the grippers but are relying on proprioception.

![Two motors coupled by bilateral teleoperation: each follows the other and feels its force](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/bil_tel.webp)

Watch these example videos to get a "feel" of the concept:

- [Gripper bilateral](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8jfgFuEFNdI) 
- [2DOF arm bilateral](https://twitter.com/SourceRobotics/status/1812872129148342691)

!!! note "What is this used for?"
    These kind of setup is perfect for: Teleoperation, Imitation learning, Virtual Environments...

## The algorithm
The magic of this setup is done with these 2 simple formulas.

 We got them from amazing Ben Katz paper, creator of mini cheetah quad: [Link to the paper](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/118671?show=full)

 𝜏1,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃2,𝑖 − 𝜃1, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃2,𝑖 − ˙𝜃1,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃1,𝑖)

 𝜏2,𝑖 = 𝐾𝑝(𝜃1,𝑖 − 𝜃2, 𝑖) + 𝐾𝑑( ˙𝜃1,𝑖 − ˙𝜃2,𝑖) − 𝐾( ˙𝜃2,𝑖)

!!! tip "Learn more!"
    You can read more on how it works in our [blog post!](https://source-robotics.com/blogs/blog/force-sensitive-grippers-for-teleoperation-and-imitation-learning)

## What you will need

We recommend these items to create a simple test jig:

* 2 x spectral micro BLDC - one for each motor or gripper
* Wires to connect everything up: [CAN wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [Power wires](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable)
* 2 x BLDC motors or SSG48 grippers
* 1 x [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter)
* 1 x 24V power supply
* A Laptop or raspberry pi
* [UART adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter)

## Setup

Here we are showing you the setup for any 2 motors, for example we are using 2 x [ssg48 grippers](https://source-robotics.com/products/compliant-gripper) that are connected in exactly the same setup.

![Two drivers daisy-chained on power and CAN, with the CAN adapter to the PC](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/110/assets/leg_setup.webp)

You will need to follow the diagram above to wire everything up.

* First you need to calibrate your Spectral BLDC drivers with the motors you are using. 
* After that change the CAN ids of one of the drivers to CAN 1. You can do it by using UART commands: #CANID 1 and after that #Save
* Now connect CAN adapters CAN bus to one of the drivers and then from that driver connect to the second driver. Make sure that last driver in chain has its CAN termination resistor in "ON" state
* Connect the power to both drivers. You can daisy chain it or use 2 separate wires.

## The code

This code will run on your PC and it will communicate with the drivers from the CAN adapter.

!!! danger "Advanced example"
    More advanced code that allows communication over UDP can be found here: [Link](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python/tree/main/examples/Advanced/SSG48%20gripper%20bilateral%20teleop) 

``` py title="bilateral_teleoperation.py"
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as SourceRoboticsToolbox
import time
import numpy as np
from math import pi, sin, cos
from spatialmath import *
from typing import Union, Any, List, Optional, cast

Needed_joint_pos = np.array([100,100]) # If using gripper you will need to adjust this
Joint_reduction_ratio = [1, 1] # Reduction ratio we have on our joints

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM123', bitrate=1000000)

Motor: list[Union[Spectral.SpectralCAN,Spectral.SpectralCAN]] = []
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1))
Motor.append(Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=1, communication=Communication1))

Joint: list[Union[SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint,SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint]] = []
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[0], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[0], offset = 0, dir = 0))
Joint.append(SourceRoboticsToolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution = 14, master_position=Needed_joint_pos[1], gear_ratio = Joint_reduction_ratio[1], offset = 0, dir = 0))

timeout_setting = 0.001

initial = 0
initial_setup = [0,0]

# Initialize position values
position_values =  np.array([0.0,0.0])
Motor_values = np.array([0,0])

speed_values = np.array([0,0])

position_send = np.array([0,0])
speed_send = np.array([0,0])
T0 = 0
T1 = 0

received_ids = [0,0] 
Kp = 650
Kd = 0.00550 #  0.0060
Kk = 0.0003 #0.0003

while(1):
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    Motor[0].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T0))
    Motor[1].Send_data_pack_1(Position = None,Speed = None, Current = int(T1))

    for i in range(1, 3):  # read up to 2 replies
        message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=timeout_setting)
        #print(f"unpack{i} is: {UnpackedMessageID}")

        # Check if UnpackedMessageID is not None 
        if UnpackedMessageID is not None:
            
            # Update received id index; meaning that we received response from that CAN ID
            received_ids[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
            Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].UnpackData(message,UnpackedMessageID)
            #print(f"Motor {UnpackedMessageID[0]}, position is: {Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position}")
            unwrapped_position_raw = Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].unwrap_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)
            Motor_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position
            position_values[UnpackedMessageID[0]] =  Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].get_joint_position(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

            if initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] == 0:
                initial_setup[UnpackedMessageID[0]] = 1
                Joint[UnpackedMessageID[0]].determine_sector(Motor[UnpackedMessageID[0]].position)

    # The magic
    T0 = Kp*( position_values[1] -  position_values[0]) + Kd*(Motor[1].speed - Motor[0].speed) - Kk*(Motor[0].speed)
    T1 = Kp*( position_values[0] -  position_values[1]) + Kd*(Motor[0].speed - Motor[1].speed) - Kk*(Motor[1].speed)
    # There are no delays here, we send as fast as possible!

```
